text: Font Info data Complete font metadata.
title: fontlab.Info

text: Info is the metadata wrapper for all the descriptive information about your font that gets embedded in the file: the family name, style name, designer's name, copyright notice, license, all the OpenType metric values, PostScript hinting parameters, and much more. It follows the UFO (Unified Font Object) specification for attribute names, which means the property names like openTypeNameDesigner , openTypeOS2WeightClass , and postscriptFontName correspond directly to documented UFO 3 attributes. If you know UFO, you already know this interface. Access Info through package.info on an flPackage wrapper: package = fl . flPackage ( fl . CurrentFont ()) info = package . info print ( info . familyName ) info . copyright = "© 2026 My Foundry" All properties read/write the font's metadata storage directly. There is no need to call a save method — changes take effect immediately in the in-memory font.
title: What is Info?

text: These are the most important fields for most type designers. Name Type Description Access familyName string The primary family name shown in application font menus (e.g. "Helvetica", "Times New Roman"). All styles in the family should share this name. read/write styleName string The style name within the family (e.g. "Regular", "Bold Italic", "Condensed Light"). read/write styleMapFamilyName string The "linked family" name used for bold/italic style mapping in older applications. Applications that only understand the 4-style model (Regular/Bold/Italic/BoldItalic) use this to group styles. read/write styleMapStyleName string The style position within the linked family group. Must be one of exactly four values: "regular" , "italic" , "bold" , or "bold italic" . read/write copyright string The full copyright statement embedded in the font file (e.g. "Copyright 2026 My Foundry. All rights reserved."). read/write trademark string The trademark statement, if any. read/write note string Arbitrary free-text note about the font. Not shown to end users; used for internal documentation. read/write unitsPerEm int/float Units per em — the scale of the design grid. read/write descender int/float The descender value for this font's default UPM-relative metrics. read/write ascender int/float The ascender value. read/write xHeight int/float The x-height value. read/write capHeight int/float The cap height value. read/write italicAngle int/float The italic angle in degrees, measured counter-clockwise from vertical. 0 for upright fonts; typically -12 to -15 for italic. read/write versionMajor int The major version number of the font (e.g. the 1 in version 1.012 ). read/write versionMinor int The minor version number. read/write year int Year of creation. Deprecated in UFO 3 in favour of openTypeHeadCreated , but still supported. read/write panose string Legacy PANOSE classification — 10 space-separated numbers. Most modern workflows ignore PANOSE, but it is required for some font delivery platforms. read/write

Should be short, no spaces, no special characters. read/write postscriptFullName string The PostScript full name ( FullName in the font dictionary). read/write postscriptWeightName string The PostScript weight string (e.g. "Regular" , "Bold" ). read/write postscriptUniqueID int PostScript unique ID number. read/write postscriptIsFixedPitch bool True if the font is monospaced — all glyphs have the same advance width. read/write postscriptForceBold bool The ForceBold flag in the CFF Private dictionary. read/write postscriptDefaultWidthX int/float Default advance width for glyphs. Used to save space in the CFF data when most glyphs share one width. read/write postscriptNominalWidthX int/float The "nominal" width deviation stored in CFF. read/write postscriptBlueValues list Up to 14 blue zone values (in pairs). These define the horizontal bands used for PS alignment-zone hinting. Example: [0, 10, 490, 500, 690, 700] for baseline+overshoot, x-height+overshoot, capHeight+overshoot. read/write postscriptOtherBlues list Up to 10 "other blues" values — the downward-facing alignment zones (for the descender area). read/write postscriptFamilyBlues list Family-level blue values, shared across all styles to ensure consistent zone snapping. read/write postscriptFamilyOtherBlues list Family-level other blues. read/write postscriptStemSnapH list Up to 12 representative horizontal stem widths. text:
import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () info = font . info # FontInfo object — direct read/write access # ============================================================ # 1. Read the most important identification fields. # ============================================================ print ( "--- Font Identification ---" ) print ( f "Family: { info . familyName } " ) print ( f "Style: { info . styleName } " ) print ( f "Designer: { info . openTypeNameDesigner } " ) print ( f "Copyright: { info . copyright } " ) print ( f "Version: { info . versionMajor } . { info . versionMinor : 03d } " ) print ( f "UPM: { info . unitsPerEm } " ) # ============================================================ # 2. Check the key vertical metrics. # ============================================================ print ( " 
 --- Vertical Metrics ---" ) print ( f "Ascender: { info . ascender } " ) print ( f "Descender: { info . descender } " ) print ( f "x-Height: { info . xHeight } " ) print ( f "Cap Height: { info . capHeight } " ) print ( f "Italic Angle: { info . italicAngle } °" ) # ============================================================ # 3. Check OS/2 classification fields. # These determine how the font appears in weight/width menus. # ============================================================ print ( " 
 --- OS/2 Classification ---" ) print ( f "Weight class: { info . openTypeOS2WeightClass } " f "(400=Regular, 700=Bold)" ) print ( f "Width class: { info . openTypeOS2WidthClass } " f "(5=Normal, 3=Condensed)" ) print ( f "Vendor ID: ' { info . openTypeOS2VendorID } '" ) # ============================================================ # 4. Update copyright and license fields. # This is one of the most common pre-export scripts. # ============================================================ info . copyright = "Copyright 2026 My Foundry. All rights reserved." info . openTypeNameDesigner = "Jane Smith" info . openTypeNameDesignerURL = "https://myfoundry.example.com" info . openTypeNameManufacturer = "My Foundry" info . openTypeNameManufacturerURL = "https://myfoundry.example.com" info . openTypeNameLicense = ( "This Font Software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License, " "Version 1.1. This license is available with a FAQ at: " "https://scripts.sil.org/OFL" ) info . openTypeNameLicenseURL = "https://scripts.sil.org/OFL" info . versionMajor = 1 info . versionMinor = 0 print ( " 
 Identification fields updated." ) # ============================================================ # 5. Read PostScript hinting metadata. # These are the font-level values (separate from per-master # flHintingParameters, which override these). # ============================================================ print ( " 
 --- PostScript Blues ---" ) print ( f "BlueValues: { info . postscriptBlueValues } " ) print ( f "OtherBlues: { info . postscriptOtherBlues } " ) print ( f "StemSnapH: { info . postscriptStemSnapH } " ) print ( f "StemSnapV: { info . postscriptStemSnapV } " ) # ============================================================ # 6. Set the PostScript font name (required for OTF export). # The PS name should have no spaces and no special characters. # ============================================================ family = ( info . familyName or "MyFont" ) . replace ( " " , "" ) style = ( info . styleName or "Regular" ) . replace ( " " , "" ) info . postscriptFontName = f " { family } - { style } " info . postscriptFullName = f " { info . familyName } { info . styleName } " print ( f " 
 PS name set to: ' { info . postscriptFontName } '" )

text: import fontlab as fl package = fl . flPackage ( fl . CurrentFont ()) info = package . info required = { "familyName" : info . familyName , "styleName" : info . styleName , "copyright" : info . copyright , "openTypeNameDesigner" : info . openTypeNameDesigner , "openTypeNameManufacturer" : info . openTypeNameManufacturer , "openTypeNameLicense" : info . openTypeNameLicense , "postscriptFontName" : info . postscriptFontName , "openTypeOS2VendorID" : info . openTypeOS2VendorID , } print ( "--- Required fields check ---" ) all_ok = True for field , value in required . items (): status = "✓" if value else "✗ MISSING" if not value : all_ok = False print ( f " { status } { field } : ' { value or '' } '" ) if all_ok : print ( " \n All required fields are filled." ) else : print ( " \n Some fields are missing — fill them before export." )

text: Property Type Access Meaning nametablePath str or None read/write Font-wide custom .nam path; assignment reloads the mapping. Empty/None selects the standard mapping. otherData dict read/write Snapshot of additional settings; assign a dictionary to patch selected entries. font.info.nametablePath reads or sets the font-wide .nam path shown in Font Info > Other. Assignment reloads the mapping immediately. Use "" or None to restore the standard mapping. Relative paths resolve from the font's folder; an unreadable file retains its configured path and uses standard mapping with a warning. font.info.otherData returns a dictionary snapshot of the current master's Other settings (including loop resolution and TrueType hinting controls), plus the font-wide nametablePath . Assign a dictionary to patch selected entries; mutating the returned snapshot alone does not update the font. PANOSE retains its existing font.info.panose / font.info.openTypeOS2Panose access. font . info . nametablePath = "names/custom.nam" font . info . otherData = { "nametablePath" : "names/custom.nam" } font . info . otherData = { "nametablePath" : None } # standard mapping MCP uses set_font_info with {"font_info": {"other_data": {"nametablePath": "names/custom.nam"}}} . otherData is also accepted. get_font_info returns the configured value in other_data.nametablePath . This setting applies to every master; do not put it inside masters[] . text: A parametric range on a contour.
title: fontlab.Interval

text: Imagine "selecting" a portion of a contour — not a node, but a stretch of curve from 25% to 75% of the way along the path. An Interval stores exactly that: two parametric values t0 and t1 defining a sub-range of a Bézier contour. Intervals are used internally by the node selection system, by split-curve operations, and by any tool that needs to work with a portion of a contour rather than whole segments. You will mostly encounter them when writing custom canvas tools that deal with selecting or cutting parts of curves.
title: What is Interval?

text:
from fontlab import Interval # ============================================================ # Create an interval covering the middle third of a contour. # This represents parametric positions 33.3% to 66.7% along # the contour arc. # ============================================================ iv = Interval () iv . setT0T1 ( 0.333 , 0.667 ) print ( f "Interval: t0= { iv . t0 : .3f } t1= { iv . t1 : .3f } " ) print ( f "Length: { iv . d : .3f } " ) print ( f "Midpoint: { iv . middle () : .3f } " ) print ( f "Is empty: { iv . isEmpty () } " ) # ============================================================ # Map a relative position within the interval to an # absolute contour position. # "Where is the 1/4 point of this interval on the contour?" # ============================================================ # 0.25 = 1/4 of the way through [0.333, 0.667] quarter_abs = iv . toAbsolute ( 0.25 ) print ( f " 
 1/4 through interval → absolute t = { quarter_abs : .3f } " ) # Expected: 0.333 + 0.25 * (0.667 - 0.333) = ~0.417 # Map back: given absolute t=0.5, where is that in the interval? fraction = iv . toInterval ( 0.5 ) print ( f "Absolute t=0.5 → interval fraction = { fraction : .3f } " ) # Expected: (0.5 - 0.333) / (0.667 - 0.333) = ~0.5 # ============================================================ # Reverse the interval — same coverage, opposite direction. # Useful when you need to iterate a selection in reverse. # ============================================================ rev = iv . reversed () print ( f " 
 Reversed: t0= { rev . t0 : .3f } t1= { rev . t1 : .3f } " ) # ============================================================ # An empty interval — covers nothing. # This is what you get when a hit test lands exactly on a node. # ============================================================ empty_iv = Interval () empty_iv . setT0T1 ( 0.5 , 0.5 ) print ( f " 
 Empty interval: isEmpty= { empty_iv . isEmpty () } d= { empty_iv . d } " )
title: Tutorial

text: from fontlab import Interval iv = Interval () iv . setT0T1 ( 0.2 , 0.8 ) def contains ( interval , t ): return interval . t0 <= t <= interval . t1 print ( contains ( iv , 0.5 )) # True print ( contains ( iv , 0.1 )) # False
title: Check whether a parametric position falls within an interval

text: from fontlab import Interval iv = Interval () iv . setT0T1 ( 0.0 , 1.0 ) third = iv . d / 3.0 parts = [] for i in range ( 3 ): part = Interval () part . setT0T1 ( iv . t0 + i * third , iv . t0 + ( i + 1 ) * third ) parts . append ( part ) print ( f "Part { i } : [ { part . t0 : .3f } , { part . t1 : .3f } ]" ) Constructors: Native bases: object Captured native MRO: Interval, object Native new allocation evidence (not an init overload): ( args, *kwargs) Create and return a new object. text: A LocationValue is the value stored for a single axis in an flLocation . For the vast majority of uses, a LocationValue is just a number — you set it to 400 and read it back as 400 . But it can also be anisotropic , which means it carries two slightly different numbers.
title: What is a LocationValue?

text: Isotropic (the normal case): a single number. Both sides of the default on the axis use the same value. When you write loc["wght"] = 700 , you're creating an isotropic LocationValue with x == y == 700 . Anisotropic : two numbers, x and y . These represent the value on the approach side (coming from the default toward the minimum) and the departure side (going from the default toward the maximum). This is used for rare cases like optical-size axes where the interpolation behavior at the default point is asymmetric — the letter shapes transition differently when you go up vs. down from the default. In practice, you'll almost always use isotropic values. Anisotropic values are a niche feature. # Isotropic (normal): v = LocationValue ( 400 ) print ( float ( v )) # 400.0 # Anisotropic (rare, advanced): v2 = LocationValue ( 400 , 450 ) # x=400 on one side of the default, y=450 on the other When x == y , a LocationValue displays and accepts as a plain number. When x != y , it appears as a (x, y) tuple.
title: Isotropic vs anisotropic

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flLocation , LocationValue font = fl . CurrentFont () # ============================================================ # 1. Creating a location from scratch # ============================================================ # The simplest approach: start with an empty location, then # add axis values one by one, just like filling a dictionary. loc = flLocation () loc [ "wght" ] = 400 # Weight axis at Regular (400) loc [ "wdth" ] = 100 # Width axis at Normal (100) print ( "My location:" , dict ( loc )) # {'wght': 400.0, 'wdth': 100.0} # ============================================================ # 2. Creating a location from a dict (most convenient) # ============================================================ # You can pass a plain Python dict directly to the constructor. # This is the cleanest way to build a location in one line. bold_loc = flLocation ({ "wght" : 700 , "wdth" : 100 }) condensed_loc = flLocation ({ "wght" : 400 , "wdth" : 75 }) bold_condensed = flLocation ({ "wght" : 700 , "wdth" : 75 }) print ( "Bold location:" , dict ( bold_loc )) # ============================================================ # 3. Reading values from a location # ============================================================ # Use the axis tag as the key, just like a dictionary. # The value comes back as a LocationValue, but it acts like a number. wght_val = bold_loc [ "wght" ] print ( f "Weight: { wght_val } " ) # prints: 700 (or similar) print ( f "As float: { float ( wght_val ) } " ) # explicitly convert to float # ============================================================ # 4. Updating values in a location # ============================================================ loc [ "wght" ] = 600 # change weight to Semibold print ( "Updated weight:" , float ( loc [ "wght" ])) # 600.0 # ============================================================ # 5. Checking what axes are in a location # ============================================================ print ( "Axes in location:" , list ( loc . keys ())) print ( "Has wght?" , "wght" in loc ) print ( "Has opsz?" , "opsz" in loc ) # False if optical size not set print ( "Number of axes:" , len ( loc )) # ============================================================ # 6. Iterating over a location # ============================================================ # Iterate just like a dict — you get the axis tags, and then # look up each value. print ( "All axis values:" ) for tag in loc : print ( f " { tag } = { float ( loc [ tag ]) : .0f } " ) # Or iterate over .items() for tag+value pairs: for tag , val in loc . items (): print ( f " { tag } → { float ( val ) : .1f } " ) # ============================================================ # 7. Removing an axis from a location # ============================================================ # If you want a location that only specifies some axes, # you can remove others with del. loc2 = flLocation ({ "wght" : 300 , "wdth" : 75 , "ital" : 0 }) del loc2 [ "ital" ] # remove the italic axis print ( "After removing ital:" , list ( loc2 . keys ())) # ["wght", "wdth"] # ============================================================ # 8. LocationValue — isotropic vs anisotropic # ============================================================ # Normally you'll just use plain numbers. But here's how # LocationValue works if you need to inspect it directly. # Isotropic (the everyday case): v_iso = LocationValue ( 400 ) print ( "Isotropic value:" , float ( v_iso )) # 400.0 # Anisotropic (rare — for axes with asymmetric interpolation): v_aniso = LocationValue ( 400 , 450 ) # Use this in a location: loc [ "opsz" ] = v_aniso # ============================================================ # 9. Reading the current design-space location # ============================================================ # font.currentLocation() tells you which location the font # editor is currently showing. This is useful if you want to # run a script that operates on "wherever the designer is right now." cur_loc = font . currentLocation () print ( " \n Currently viewing:" ) for tag in cur_loc : print ( f " { tag } = { float ( cur_loc [ tag ]) : .0f } " ) # ============================================================ # 10. Reading instance locations # ============================================================ # Each named instance has a location that defines exactly where # it lives in design space. You can read and compare these. print ( " \n All named instances:" ) for inst in font . instances : loc_parts = [ f " { tag } = { float ( inst . location [ tag ]) : .0f } " for tag in inst . location ] print ( f " ' { inst . name } ': { ', ' . join ( loc_parts ) } " ) # ============================================================ # 11. Building a location to navigate to a specific master # ============================================================ # Use setCurrentLocation to move the editor view to a specific # point in design space. This is equivalent to dragging the # axis sliders in the Variations panel. # Navigate to Bold: # font.setCurrentLocation(bold_loc) # Navigate to Condensed: # font.setCurrentLocation(condensed_loc) # ============================================================ # 12. Converting a location to a plain Python dict # ============================================================ # Sometimes you need a plain dict — for JSON export, for printing, # or to pass to code that doesn't know about flLocation. plain_dict = { tag : float ( loc [ tag ]) for tag in loc } print ( "As plain dict:" , plain_dict ) fl . Update ()
title: Tutorial

text: # Useful when you want to know which named preset the user # is currently looking at, even if they've dragged a slider away. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () cur = font . currentLocation () def location_distance ( loc_a , loc_b ): """Simple Euclidean distance between two locations in design space.""" total = 0.0 for tag in loc_a : if tag in loc_b : diff = float ( loc_a [ tag ]) - float ( loc_b [ tag ]) total += diff * diff return total ** 0.5 closest = min ( font . instances , key = lambda inst : location_distance ( cur , inst . location )) print ( f "Closest instance to current view: ' { closest . name } '" )
title: Find the instance closest to the current location

text: # If you have axis names ("Weight") rather than tags ("wght"), # this helper converts them for you. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flLocation font = fl . CurrentFont () axes_by_name = { a . name : a for a in font . axes } def location_from_names ( name_dict ): """Build an flLocation from a dict keyed by axis name.""" loc = flLocation () for axis_name , value in name_dict . items (): if axis_name in axes_by_name : loc [ axes_by_name [ axis_name ] . tag ] = value return loc loc = location_from_names ({ "Weight" : 700 , "Width" : 75 }) print ( "Built location:" , { k : float ( v ) for k , v in loc . items ()})
title: Build a location from a dict of axis names (not tags)

text: # Show what each instance looks like in the OpenType # normalized range (−1, 0, 1 scale). import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () axes_by_tag = { a . tag : a for a in font . axes } for inst in font . instances : normals = {} for tag , val in inst . location . items (): if tag in axes_by_tag : normals [ tag ] = round ( axes_by_tag [ tag ] . normalize ( float ( val )), 3 ) print ( f "' { inst . name } ': { normals } " )
title: Print all axis values as normalized numbers

text: # Compare two locations to see if they point to the same place. from fontlab import flLocation def locations_equal ( a , b , tolerance = 0.01 ): if set ( a . keys ()) != set ( b . keys ()): return False return all ( abs ( float ( a [ tag ]) - float ( b [ tag ])) < tolerance for tag in a ) loc1 = flLocation ({ "wght" : 700 , "wdth" : 100 }) loc2 = flLocation ({ "wght" : 700 , "wdth" : 100 }) loc3 = flLocation ({ "wght" : 700 , "wdth" : 75 }) print ( locations_equal ( loc1 , loc2 )) # True print ( locations_equal ( loc1 , loc3 )) # False
title: Check whether two locations are identical

text: # Identify which instances are at the min or max of any axis. # These are your "extreme" corner masters. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () axes_by_tag = { a . tag : a for a in font . axes } for inst in font . instances : edges = [] for tag , val in inst . location . items (): if tag in axes_by_tag : if axes_by_tag [ tag ] . onEdge ( float ( val )): edges . append ( tag ) if edges : print ( f "' { inst . name } ' is on the edge of: { edges } " ) else : print ( f "' { inst . name } ' is in the interior of design space" )
title: Walk all instances and print whether they're at an axis edge

text: # Automatically create instances at every combination of # axis stops in a two-axis Weight × Width font. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flInstance , flLocation font = fl . CurrentFont () weight_stops = [ 300 , 400 , 600 , 700 ] # Light, Regular, Semibold, Bold width_stops = [ 75 , 100 , 125 ] # Condensed, Normal, Extended weight_names = { 300 : "Light" , 400 : "Regular" , 600 : "Semibold" , 700 : "Bold" } width_names = { 75 : "Condensed" , 100 : "" , 125 : "Extended" } for wght in weight_stops : for wdth in width_stops : inst = flInstance () # Combine weight + width name, strip extra spaces parts = [ weight_names [ wght ], width_names [ wdth ]] inst . name = " " . join ( p for p in parts if p ) inst . exportable = True loc = flLocation () loc [ "wght" ] = wght loc [ "wdth" ] = wdth inst . location = loc font . addInstance ( inst ) print ( f "Added: ' { inst . name } ' wght= { wght } wdth= { wdth } " ) fl . text: Brush settings for drawing tools.
title: fontlab.PaintBrush

text: The PaintBrush defines the shape of the brush used by FontLab's scribble and colour-font drawing tools. It controls how thick the brush stroke is, whether it is circular or elliptical, and at what angle. You can script brush settings to create consistent stroke effects programmatically.
title: What is PaintBrush?

text: from fontlab import PaintBrush # A calligraphic-style brush at 45 degrees: brush = PaintBrush () brush . init () brush . size = 40.0 brush . flatness = 0.2 # very flat, like a broad-nib pen brush . angle = 45.0 # classic calligraphic angle brush . render ( 1.0 ) print ( f "Brush: { brush . toString () } " ) # A round brush: round_brush = PaintBrush () round_brush . init () round_brush . size = 20.0 round_brush . flatness = 1.0 round_brush . angle = 0.0

text: Interactive Bounding Frame.
title: fontlab.TransformFrame

text: The TransformFrame is the rectangular selection bounding box you see in FontLab when you choose the Transform tool and select objects. It has eight handles (four corners plus four mid-edge points) that you can drag to scale, rotate, slant, or reflect the selected content. The box can be freely rotated, so it is not always axis-aligned. In scripts, TransformFrame lets you compute what transform to apply based on dragging one handle to a new position — essentially implementing the math behind FontLab's Transform tool in your own scripts. You build a frame, manipulate it, then call getTransform() to get the resulting QTransform that you apply to the actual geometry.
title: What is TransformFrame?

text: Signature Description QPointF mt() Returns the mid-top handle position — the midpoint of the top edge. QPointF mb() Returns the mid-bottom handle position — the midpoint of the bottom edge. QPointF ml() Returns the mid-left handle position. QPointF mr() Returns the mid-right handle position. QPolygonF polygon() Returns the frame as a four-point polygon (the four corners in order: TL, TR, BR, BL). double lh() The height of the left side of the frame (distance from bl to tl ). double mh() The average height: (lh() + rh()) / 2 . Useful when the frame is slightly non-rectangular due to floating-point rounding. double rh() The height of the right side of the frame (distance from br to tr ). double tw() The width of the top edge (distance from tl to tr ). double mw() The average width: (tw() + bw()) / 2 . double bw() The width of the bottom edge (distance from bl to br ). QRectF boundingRect() Returns the axis-aligned bounding rectangle that fully contains the (possibly rotated) frame.
title: Handle Query Methods

text: Signature Description TransformFrame getMapped(QTransform t) Returns a new TransformFrame with all four corners mapped through the transform t . Use this to preview what the frame will look like after a transformation, without modifying the original frame. QPointF getControlPos(TransformFrameControls) Returns the current canvas position of one of the eight control handles. Pass a TransformFrameControls enum value: TL , TR , BL , BR , MT , MB , ML , or MR . void translate(QPointF) Moves the entire frame by the given offset vector. All four corners are shifted by the same amount. void rotate(double) Rotates the frame by the given angle in degrees , counter-clockwise. The frame rotates around its centre point cr . void scale(QPointF s) Scales the frame: s.x() is the horizontal scale factor, s.y() is the vertical. Values greater than 1 enlarge; values less than 1 shrink. Scaling is relative to the frame's centre. void slant(double angle, double angle) Applies an oblique (slant) transform using the given horizontal and vertical angle values. This is what the Slant action uses internally. void horizontalReflection() Mirrors the frame horizontally: left becomes right, right becomes left. The centre stays fixed. void verticalReflection() Mirrors the frame vertically: top becomes bottom. The centre stays fixed. void flipHorizontal() Flips the frame horizontally (same effect as horizontalReflection ). void flipVertical() Flips the frame vertically (same as verticalReflection ). void rotate180() Rotates the frame exactly 180 degrees. Equivalent to both a horizontal and a vertical flip. void initCenter() Recomputes the centre point cr from the current corner positions. Always call this after manually repositioning corners so that rotations and scales pivot correctly. void doTransformation(int code, QPointF value) Applies a transformation identified by code (a TransformFrameControls integer) by the delta value . This is the core method behind drag-to-transform interactions — it is what gets called when you drag a handle in the editor. QTransform getTransform() Returns the net QTransform that maps the original (pre-interaction) frame to its current state. Apply this transform to the selected objects to commit the change to the geometry. void prepareTransformations([TransformFrameControls control, QPointF p,] double scale) Prepares the frame for an interactive transformation session. scale is the current canvas zoom factor. Optionally constrain to one control point and provide the starting mouse position p . void setControlPos([TransformFrameControls control,] QPointF position, bool reflection, bool proportional, bool fixed) Moves a handle to position . reflection mirrors the change to the opposite handle symmetrically; proportional locks the aspect ratio; fixed locks the opposite side in place. void setProjectionPos([TransformFrameControls control,] QPointF position, bool reflection, bool proportional, bool fixed) Like setControlPos but uses perspective-preserving (projection) mathematics for the handle movement. Used for the Perspective transformation.
title: Transformation Methods

text: Name Type Access Description tl QPointF rw Top-left corner of the frame. tr QPointF rw Top-right corner of the frame. bl QPointF rw Bottom-left corner of the frame. br QPointF rw Bottom-right corner of the frame. cr QPointF rw Centre point of the frame. This is the pivot used for rotations and scales. Call initCenter() to recompute it from corners.
title: Corner Properties

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import TransformFrame # ============================================================ # Goal: Scale a shape 2× horizontally using TransformFrame. # # The workflow is: # 1. Get the shape's bounding box # 2. Build a TransformFrame that matches it # 3. Apply a transformation to the frame # 4. Retrieve the resulting QTransform via getTransform() # 5. Apply that QTransform to the actual shape geometry # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] bbox = shape . boundingBox # returns a QRectF in glyph units print ( f "Shape bounding box: { bbox } " ) # ============================================================ # Step 1: Build a frame from the bounding box corners. # We set the four corners manually, then call initCenter() # so that rotations and scales use the correct pivot point. # ============================================================ frame = TransformFrame () frame . tl = QPointF ( bbox . left (), bbox . top ()) frame . tr = QPointF ( bbox . right (), bbox . top ()) frame . bl = QPointF ( bbox . left (), bbox . bottom ()) frame . br = QPointF ( bbox . right (), bbox . bottom ()) frame . initCenter () # compute centre from corners print ( f "Frame centre: { frame . cr } " ) print ( f "Frame width: { frame . mw () : .0f } " ) print ( f "Frame height: { frame . mh () : .0f } " ) # ============================================================ # Step 2: Scale the frame — 2× wide, same height. # scale() takes a QPointF where x = horizontal factor, # y = vertical factor. # ============================================================ frame . scale ( QPointF ( 2.0 , 1.0 )) print ( f " \n After 2× horizontal scale:" ) print ( f " New width: { frame . mw () : .0f } " ) # ============================================================ # Step 3: Get the net transform and apply it to the shape. # getTransform() returns the QTransform that maps the # original frame to the current (scaled) frame. # ============================================================ tx = frame . getTransform () print ( f "Net transform: { tx } " ) shape . transformBy ( tx ) fl . Update () print ( "Done — shape scaled 2× horizontally." )

text: PythonQtInstanceWrapper object Dockable panel system.
title: fontlab.YPanelManager

text: FontLab's sidebar and panel system is managed by YPanelManager . Every dockable panel you see in FontLab — the Layers panel, the Glyph panel, the Properties panel — is registered with and managed by this singleton. If you want to create a custom side panel that always appears in the FontLab UI (rather than a separate window), you subclass YPanelWidget and register it with YPanelManager.instance() .
title: What is YPanelManager?

text: There is always exactly one YPanelManager in a running FontLab: from fontlab import YPanelManager pm = YPanelManager . instance ()
title: Getting the instance

text: YPanelManager lets you open, close, and inspect FontLab's dockable panels. Here is how to work with both the built-in panels and your own custom ones. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import YPanelManager , YPanelWidget # ============================================================ # Get the panel manager singleton. # ============================================================ pm = YPanelManager . instance () print ( f "Registered panels: { len ( pm . registeredPanels ) } " ) for panel in pm . registeredPanels : visible = pm . panelVisible ( panel ) status = "open" if visible else "closed" print ( f " [ { status } ] id= { panel . id : 3d } ' { panel . title } '" ) print ( f " \n Currently open: { len ( pm . panels ) } " ) # ============================================================ # Toggle a panel open/closed by its title. # ============================================================ target_title = "Layers" # change to any panel title you see above target_panel = next ( ( p for p in pm . registeredPanels if p . title == target_title ), None ) if target_panel : if pm . panelVisible ( target_panel ): pm . closePanel ( target_panel ) print ( f "Closed ' { target_title } '" ) else : pm . openPanel ( target_panel ) print ( f "Opened ' { target_title } '" ) else : print ( f "Panel ' { target_title } ' not found." ) # ============================================================ # Create and register a minimal custom panel. # (Full UI requires Qt widgets from PyQt5 or PySide2.) # ============================================================ # class MyInfoPanel(YPanelWidget): # def __init__(self): # super().__init__() # self.title = "Glyph Info" # self.defaultEdge = 2 # right side # self.minimumPanelSize = fl.QSize(200, 150) # # panel = MyInfoPanel() # pm.registerPanel(panel) # pm.openPanel(panel) # print(f"Custom panel id={panel.id}")

text: YPanelWidget is the content class for a dockable panel. Subclass it to create a panel that appears in FontLab's sidebar. You are responsible for setting the title, icon, and minimum size, and for building the Qt widget hierarchy that populates the panel.
title: What is YPanelWidget?

Run this in the scripting panel. # ============================================================ pm = YPanelManager . instance () print ( f "Registered panels: { len ( pm . registeredPanels ) } " ) for panel in pm . registeredPanels : is_visible = pm . panelVisible ( panel ) status = "open" if is_visible else "closed" print ( f " [ { status } ] id= { panel . id } title=' { panel . title } '" ) print () print ( f "Currently open: { len ( pm . panels ) } " ) # ============================================================ # Part 2: Open, close, and toggle a panel by id. # # Replace 42 with the actual id from the output above. # ============================================================ # panel = pm.registeredPanel(42) # find by id # if panel: # if pm.panelVisible(panel): # pm.closePanel(panel) # print(f"Closed '{panel.title}'") # else: # pm.openPanel(panel) # print(f"Opened '{panel.title}'") # ============================================================ # Part 3: Create a simple custom panel. # # In a real plugin this would be more elaborate, but this # shows the minimum needed to get a panel appearing in FontLab. # ============================================================ # class MyScriptPanel(YPanelWidget): # def __init__(self): # super().__init__() # self.title = "My Script Panel" # self.defaultEdge = 2 # dock on the right # self.minimumPanelSize = fl.QSize(200, 300) # # def setupUI(self): # # Called once the widget is ready. # # Create Qt widgets and add them to self. # pass # # my_panel = MyScriptPanel() # pm.registerPanel(my_panel) # pm.openPanel(my_panel) # print("Custom panel opened!")

title: fontlab.fgSymbol

text: Every slot in a text string that FontLab renders in the metrics view is represented by an fgSymbol . Think of it as a small ticket that says "show me the glyph for the letter 'A' (Unicode 0x0041)." It also carries a glyph ID (the slot index in the font), a layer name (which master to use), and can hold arbitrary custom data. You will encounter fgSymbol objects mainly when working with fgSymbolList (a complete string of characters) or through flGlyphInfo.symbol (the symbol for a rendered glyph slot in the metrics view).
title: What is fgSymbol?

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import fgSymbol # ============================================================ # Create a symbol for the letter 'A' and inspect it. # You normally get symbols from an fgSymbolList rather than # creating them manually, but this shows the structure. # ============================================================ sym = fgSymbol () sym . id = 0x0041 # set to Unicode code point for 'A' print ( f "Unicode: { hex ( sym . unicode ) } " ) # 0x41 print ( f "Name: ' { sym . name } '" ) print ( f "Empty: { sym . empty } " ) print ( f "Has unicode: { sym . hasUnicode } " ) # ============================================================ # Attach custom data to a symbol. # DataCode is just an integer key you choose — use any number. # This is useful for tagging symbols during batch processing. # ============================================================ sym . setData ( 1 , "needs-review" ) print ( f "Has data at code 1: { sym . containsData ( 1 ) } " ) print ( f "Data: { sym . data ( 1 ) } " ) # Clear the data when done: sym . clearData ( 1 ) print ( f "After clear: { sym . containsData ( 1 ) } " ) # ============================================================ # Resolve a symbol within a specific font. # Call computeID() to find out which glyph slot 'A' occupies # in the currently open font. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () sym2 = fgSymbol () sym2 . id = 0x0041 # 'A' found = sym2 . computeID ( font ) if found : print ( f "'A' is at glyph index { sym2 . glyphIndex } in font ' { font . info . familyName } '" ) else : print ( "Glyph 'A' not found in current font" ) # ============================================================ # Check if two symbols refer to the same character. # Useful when searching a symbol list. # ============================================================ sym3 = fgSymbol () sym3 . id = 0x0042 # 'B' print ( f "sym2 == sym2: { sym2 . compare ( sym2 ) } " ) # True print ( f "sym2 == sym3: { sym2 . compare ( sym3 ) } " ) # False
title: Tutorial

text: Master selection uses the master/layer name ; fgSymbol has no master property. Repeated occurrences of the same glyph can carry different overrides. import fontlab as fl light = fl . fgSymbol ( "a" ) light . setLayerOverride ( "Light" ) instance = fl . fgSymbol ( "a" ) instance . setLocation ( fl . flLocation ({ "wt" : 450 })) symbols = fl . fgSymbolList ([ light , instance ]) print ( symbols [ 0 ] . layerName ) # Light print ( symbols [ 1 ] . hasLocation ) # True print ( symbols [ 1 ] . location [ "wt" ]) # 450 # List access returns a copy: assign the edited symbol back. symbol = symbols [ 0 ] symbol . setLayerOverride ( "Bold" ) symbols . set ( 0 , symbol ) symbol = symbols [ 1 ] symbol . clearPresentationOverride () symbols . set ( 1 , symbol ) location also returns a copy. To change coordinates, construct a new flLocation from a dictionary and pass it to symbol.setLocation() . Coordinates use the font's design space; axis short names such as "wt" are supported. flGlyphInfo.symbol is a copy as well. To change a displayed occurrence, use flGlyphInfo.setActiveLayer(layer) , setLocation(location) , or clearPresentationOverride() on the flGlyphInfo itself.
title: Choose a master or location for each symbol

text: from fontlab import fgSymbol sym = fgSymbol () sym . id = 0x000D # carriage return print ( "Is CR:" , sym . cr )
title: Check if a symbol is a line break

text: from fontlab import fgSymbol sym = fgSymbol () sym . id = 0x0041 font_a = fl . CurrentFont () sym . computeID ( font_a ) # resolve in font A # Now move to font B: sym . clearID () # discard font-A-specific IDs font_b = ... # another open font sym . computeID ( font_b ) # resolve in font B

text: A string of characters.
title: fontlab.fgSymbolList

text: An fgSymbolList is an ordered, mutable sequence of fgSymbol objects — essentially, a text string at the font object level. Where Python's str stores Unicode code points and knows nothing about your font, fgSymbolList stores symbols that are already resolved to specific glyphs in a specific font. You use fgSymbolList when you need to: - Programmatically set the text string in a metrics view text block - Inspect which characters are selected in a metrics view - Build a sequence of glyphs for batch measurement or spacing work
title: What is fgSymbolList?

text:
import fontlab as fl from fontlab import fgSymbol , fgSymbolList # ============================================================ # Build a symbol list from a Unicode string — the easiest way. # This creates one symbol per character in the string. # ============================================================ sl = fgSymbolList () sl . setString ( "HAMBURGEFONS" ) # a classic font-testing string print ( f "String: ' { sl . string ( False ) } ' ( { sl . size () } chars)" ) # ============================================================ # Iterate symbols and print each character's name and unicode. # ============================================================ for i in range ( sl . size ()): s = sl . at ( i ) print ( f " [ { i } ] U+ { s . unicode : 04X } ' { s . name } '" ) # ============================================================ # Build a list from Unicode code points directly. # Useful when you have a list of codepoints from another source. # ============================================================ sl2 = fgSymbolList () sl2 . setUnicodeList ([ 0x0041 , 0x0042 , 0x0043 ]) # A, B, C print ( f " 
 From unicodes: ' { sl2 . string ( False ) } '" ) # ============================================================ # Build a list from glyph names. # Useful when working with non-unicode glyphs like ligatures. # ============================================================ sl3 = fgSymbolList () sl3 . setNamesList ( "H A M B U R G" ) print ( f "From names: ' { sl3 . string ( False ) } ' ( { sl3 . size () } symbols)" ) # ============================================================ # Extract a sub-string — like Python's slicing. # ============================================================ sub = sl . mid ( 0 , 7 ) # first 7 characters: "HAMBURG" print ( f " 
 First 7: ' { sub . string ( False ) } '" ) # ============================================================ # Append one list to another. # ============================================================ tail = fgSymbolList () tail . setString ( " test" ) sl . append ( tail ) print ( f "After append: ' { sl . string ( False ) } ' ( { sl . size () } chars)" ) # ============================================================ # Compare two lists for equality. # ============================================================ sl_a = fgSymbolList () sl_a . setString ( "ABC" ) sl_b = fgSymbolList () sl_b . setString ( "ABC" ) sl_c = fgSymbolList () sl_c . setString ( "ABD" ) print ( f " 
 ABC == ABC: { sl_a . equals ( sl_b ) } " ) # True print ( f "ABC == ABD: { sl_a . equals ( sl_c ) } " ) # False # ============================================================ # Remove a range of symbols. # ============================================================ sl4 = fgSymbolList () sl4 . setString ( "Hello World" ) sl4 . remove ( 5 , 6 ) # remove " World" (index 5, count 6) print ( f "After remove: ' { sl4 . string ( False ) } '" ) # "Hello" # ============================================================ # Use symbols() to get a plain Python list for iteration. # ============================================================ all_syms = sl_a . symbols () # returns a Python list for sym in all_syms : print ( f " { sym . name } " )

text: Inline canvas widget editor.
title: fontlab.flAbstractEditor

text: flAbstractEditor is the base class for small input widgets that appear directly inside the glyph editor canvas. The most familiar example is the metric value field that pops up when you click on a sidebearing line in metrics editing mode — you can type a new value without leaving the canvas. FontLab creates these inline editors by subclassing flAbstractEditor . If you are building a custom canvas tool that needs inline numeric input (for example, a dialog-free way to let the user type a value at a specific canvas position), you subclass flAbstractEditor and implement the widget using Qt.
title: What is flAbstractEditor?

text: The typical pattern for an inline editor in a custom tool is: detect a click on an editable value → activate the editor → commit or cancel on key press. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flAbstractEditor # ============================================================ # flAbstractEditor is a base class — you subclass it to create # a real inline editor. This example shows the lifecycle. # # In a real plugin, your editor subclass would: # 1. Set up a Qt QLineEdit (or similar) as its widget # 2. Override activate() to show and position the widget # 3. Override deactivate() to hide it and process the input # ============================================================ # Check whether any item on the canvas has an active editor: ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas : gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if gi : print ( f "Active glyph: ' { gi . name } '" ) # In a real tool, you would detect a click on a sidebearing # line and activate a metric editor like this: # # class MetricEditor(flAbstractEditor): # def __init__(self): # super().__init__() # self._line_edit = QtWidgets.QLineEdit() # # ... set up the widget # # def activate(self): # self._line_edit.show() # self._line_edit.setFocus() # # def deactivate(self): # new_value = int(self._line_edit.text()) # # apply new_value to the glyph metrics # self._line_edit.hide() # # editor = MetricEditor() # editor.activate() print ( "(No inline editor created — subclass flAbstractEditor to build one.)" ) # ============================================================ # Check whether the currently hovered canvas item has an editor. # This is how tools decide whether a click should open editing. # ============================================================ if canvas : # flVisualItem.haveEditor(pos) tells you if clicking at a # specific canvas position would trigger inline editing: test_pos = QPointF ( 300 , 200 ) # (would call item.haveEditor(test_pos) on each visible item) print ( "Use item.haveEditor(canvas_pos) to check before activating." )

text: Guideline-anchored nodes.
title: fontlab.flAbstractVectorNode

text: A vector node (called a "vector point" in the FontLab UI) is a special node that is pinned to a guideline. When the guideline moves, the node moves with it — automatically, across all glyphs that reference that guideline. This is the mechanism behind FontLab's power guidelines : you draw a guideline, attach nodes from multiple glyphs to it, and moving the guideline moves all the attached nodes at once. This makes vector nodes a powerful tool for variable font design. If you define a guideline at the x-height and attach the top of your lowercase letters to it, raising the x-height guideline automatically raises every attached node in every glyph. flAbstractVectorNode is the base class (provides the interface); flVectorNode is the concrete implementation you create and use in scripts.
title: What are vector nodes?

text: Signature Description flVectorNode createInstance() Creates a detached flVectorNode ready to be attached to a guideline. bool isVectorNode(flObject) Returns True if the given object is an flVectorNode . Use this for type checking when iterating mixed node lists.

text: Vector nodes are most useful in variable fonts where you want multiple glyphs to share a common alignment target. Here is how to check for and inspect existing vector nodes in a glyph. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flVectorNode # ============================================================ # Check whether any nodes in the active glyph are vector nodes # (i.e. attached to guidelines). # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'a' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] print ( f "Checking ' { glyph . name } ' for vector nodes:" ) found = 0 for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if flVectorNode . isVectorNode ( node ): vn = node # it IS an flVectorNode print ( f " Vector node at ( { vn . x : .0f } , { vn . y : .0f } )" f " attached to guideline: { vn . guideline } " ) found += 1 if found == 0 : print ( " No vector nodes found in this glyph." ) # ============================================================ # Create a vector node and attach it to a guideline. # ============================================================ # First, find or create a guideline to attach to: x_height_guide = next ( ( g for g in font . guidelines if g . expression == "=xHeight" ), None ) if x_height_guide : # Create a vector node at the x-height position: vn = flVectorNode . createInstance () vn . setPosition ( QPointF ( 250 , x_height_guide . centerPoint . y ())) print ( f " \n Created vector node at ( { 250 } , { x_height_guide . centerPoint . y () : .0f } )" ) print ( "Attach this node to a contour via contour.addVectorNode(vn)." ) else : print ( " \n No x-height expression guideline found." ) print ( "Create one first: guide.expression = '=xHeight'" )
title: Tutorial

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flVectorNode font = fl . CurrentFont () total = 0 for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if flVectorNode . isVectorNode ( node ): total += 1 print ( f "Total vector nodes in font: { total } " )
title: Count vector nodes across the entire font

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flVectorNode font = fl . CurrentFont () used_guides = set () for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if flVectorNode . isVectorNode ( node ): gl = node . guideline if gl : used_guides . add ( id ( gl )) print ( f " { len ( used_guides ) } guideline(s) have attached vector nodes." )

text: flAnchor is a geometric attachment link — it records a connection between a shape and another object (a guideline, another shape, or a specific node). FontLab uses these internally in its smart component and composite shape system to keep shapes locked to each other or to guidelines. You'll encounter flAnchor objects if FontLab passes one to you in a callback. They are managed internally and are not enumerable from Python — there is no shape.anchors() method in the scripting API. You don't create them by hand; FontLab creates and destroys them as you build composites in the editor.
title: fontlab.flAnchor

text: Property Type Description Access anchorCode quint64 A unique hash that identifies this anchor's geometry. Two anchors with the same code attach to the same geometric position read anchorPoint QPointF The attachment point's position in font units read isGlobal bool True if this is a font-level anchor (rather than glyph-level) read fixHorzDirection bool True if this anchor constrains horizontal movement — the attached shape cannot move left or right independently of what it's anchored to read fixVertDirection bool True if this anchor constrains vertical movement read
title: Properties (Read-only)

text: flPinPoint is the Python class for named mark-to-base anchors on layers (what you access via layer.anchors ). flAnchor (above) is a different, internal-only class for geometric shape attachments.
title: flPinPoint Properties

text: Property Type Description point QPointF The anchor's position in font units. Set this to move the anchor to a specific coordinate. cloudEnabled bool When True , the anchor position is recalculated from the nearest point on the outline each time the outline changes. Use for variable fonts where glyph geometry shifts between masters. anchor bool Internal flag that controls whether this point acts as an attachment anchor. Normally True for all anchors you create. appearance int A numeric appearance code that controls how the anchor is drawn in the editor. expressionX str A formula that determines the anchor's X position, e.g. "=lsb + (width - lsb - rsb) / 2" . When set, the X coordinate is computed from the expression rather than stored as a fixed value. expressionY str A formula that determines the anchor's Y position, e.g. "=xHeight" .
title: Read-write

text: Property Type Description hasExpression bool True if either expressionX or expressionY is set. Check this before assuming the point coordinates are fixed values. style PinPointStyle The visual style used to draw this anchor in the editor (e.g. cross, circle). isLatch bool True if this anchor is in "latch" mode — locked to a specific node on the outline.

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flPinPoint font = fl . CurrentFont () # ============================================================ # 1. Creating anchors on a combining mark # ============================================================ # A combining mark like acutecomb needs a "_top" anchor to tell # FontLab where to align it when it attaches to a base letter. # The underscore prefix means "I am the mark's attachment point." acute_glyph = font [ 'acutecomb' ] acute_layer = acute_glyph . layers [ 0 ] # Create the mark anchor at the visual bottom of the acute accent # (this is where it will "sit on" the base letter's top anchor). mark_anchor = flPinPoint ( QPointF ( 250 , 0 )) mark_anchor . name = "_top" # underscore = I'm a mark anchor acute_layer . addAnchor ( mark_anchor ) print ( f "Added ' { mark_anchor . name } ' anchor at { mark_anchor . point } " ) # ============================================================ # 2. Creating anchors on a base letter # ============================================================ # The base letter needs a matching anchor WITHOUT the underscore. # This says: "I accept marks named 'top' at this position." base_glyph = font [ 'a' ] base_layer = base_glyph . layers [ 0 ] # Place the top anchor near the top of the letter, optically centered. base_anchor = flPinPoint ( QPointF ( 220 , 600 )) base_anchor . name = "top" # no underscore = I'm a base anchor base_layer . addAnchor ( base_anchor ) print ( f "Added ' { base_anchor . name } ' anchor at { base_anchor . point } " ) # Now acutecomb._top will align with a.top to produce áCorrect # ============================================================ # 3. Adding multiple anchors for different mark types # ============================================================ # A base letter can have anchors for many different diacritics. # Add them all to the same layer. anchor_positions = { "top" : ( 220 , 600 ), # for above marks (acute, grave, etc.) "bottom" : ( 220 , - 10 ), # for below marks (cedilla, etc.) } for name , ( x , y ) in anchor_positions . items (): a = flPinPoint ( x , y ) a . name = name base_layer . addAnchor ( a ) # List everything that's on this layer now: for a in base_layer . anchors : print ( f " ' { a . name } ' at ( { a . point . x () : .0f } , { a . point . y () : .0f } )" ) # ============================================================ # 4. Repositioning an anchor # ============================================================ # You can reposition anchors by setting .point directly, or # nudge them with .translate() for small adjustments. a = base_layer . anchors [ 0 ] # Move to an absolute position: a . point = QPointF ( 225 , 610 ) # Nudge by a relative offset (10 units right, 5 units up): a . translate ( QPointF ( 10 , 5 )) print ( f "Repositioned ' { a . name } ' to { a . point } " ) # ============================================================ # 5. Expression anchors — positions driven by formulas # ============================================================ # Expression anchors are incredibly useful for variable fonts # or for glyphs that exist in many widths. Instead of hardcoding # coordinates, you write a formula. # # Font metric variables you can use in expressions: # lsb — left side-bearing # rsb — right side-bearing # xHeight, capHeight, ascender, descender # width — advance width a . expressionX = "=lsb + (width - lsb - rsb) / 2" # horizontal center a . expressionY = "=xHeight" # exactly at x-height print ( "Expression-driven?" , a . hasExpression ) # True # ============================================================ # 6. Cloud mode — let the anchor follow the outline # ============================================================ # With cloud mode, the anchor's position is recalculated from # the nearest point on the outline each time the outline changes. # This is great for variable fonts where the outline shape # varies between masters. mark_anchor . cloudEnabled = True print ( "Cloud mode active:" , mark_anchor . cloudEnabled ) # ============================================================ # 7. Listing and inspecting all anchors on a layer # ============================================================ for glyph in font . glyphs : layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] anchors = layer . anchors if anchors : print ( f " \n Glyph ' { glyph . name } ':" ) for a in anchors : mode = "cloud" if a . cloudEnabled else "fixed" print ( f " ' { a . name } ' ( { a . point . x () : .0f } , { a . point . y () : .0f } ) " f "mode= { mode } hasExpr= { a . hasExpression } " ) # ============================================================ # 8. Removing an anchor # ============================================================ acute_layer . removeAnchor ( mark_anchor ) print ( "Anchors remaining on acutecomb:" , len ( acute_layer . anchors )) # ============================================================ # 9. Working with flAnchor (geometric shape anchors) # ============================================================ # flAnchor objects represent geometric attachment links inside # FontLab's composite/smart-corner system. They are NOT the same # as flPinPoint (mark-to-base anchors on layers). # flAnchor objects are managed internally by FontLab and are NOT # directly enumerable via Python — there is no shape.anchors() # method in the Python API. If you receive an flAnchor in a # callback, its read-only properties (anchorPoint, anchorCode, # isGlobal, fixHorzDirection, fixVertDirection) are accessible. fl . Update ()

text: # A quick script to add "top" and "bottom" anchors to all # glyphs in a range. Adjust y-positions for your font's metrics. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flPinPoint font = fl . CurrentFont () # Map glyph names to the anchor positions you want. # You'd typically generate these from the actual glyph geometry. lowercase = [ g for g in font . glyphs if g . unicode and 0x61 <= int ( g . unicode , 16 ) <= 0x7A ] for glyph in lowercase : layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] # Skip glyphs that already have a "top" anchor if any ( a . name == "top" for a in layer . anchors ): continue # Approximate center-x from metrics cx = ( glyph . advanceWidth or 500 ) / 2 a = flPinPoint ( cx , 600 ) a . name = "top" layer . addAnchor ( a ) fl . Update ()
title: Add top/bottom anchors to all lowercase letters

text: # Use an expression to keep every "top" anchor horizontally # centered in each glyph's advance width. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () for glyph in font . glyphs : layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for a in layer . anchors : if a . name in ( "top" , "_top" ): a . expressionX = "=lsb + (width - lsb - rsb) / 2" fl . Update ()

CurrentFont () print ( "Glyph" . ljust ( 20 ), "Anchor" . ljust ( 15 ), "X" , "Y" ) print ( "-" * 50 ) for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for a in layer . anchors : print ( glyph . name . ljust ( 20 ), a . name . ljust ( 15 ), f " { a . point . x () : .0f } " . rjust ( 6 ), f " { a . point . y () : .0f } " . rjust ( 6 ), )

text: # In a multi-master setup, copy the anchor names and # relative positions from the Regular layer to the Bold layer. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flPinPoint font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'a' ] src = glyph . layers [ 0 ] # Regular dst = glyph . layers [ 1 ] # Bold # Remove existing anchors from the destination layer first for a in list ( dst . anchors ): dst . removeAnchor ( a ) # Copy each anchor from source to destination for a in src . anchors : new_a = flPinPoint ( a . point ) new_a . name = a . name dst . addAnchor ( new_a ) fl . Update ()

text: # Turn on cloud mode for every anchor whose name starts with "_" # (i.e., all mark attachment anchors). This is useful in variable # fonts where the outline geometry shifts significantly. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for a in layer . anchors : if a . name . startswith ( "_" ): a . cloudEnabled = True fl . Update ()

text: Represents one finding from FontLab's built-in font audit system. Each flAuditInfo wraps a FaBasic record that describes a specific problem (an open contour, an almost-flat curve, a wrong-direction path, etc.) and can point you to the exact location in the glyph.

text: When you want to programmatically run the audit and process or fix the results. Combine with FaBasic.fix() to auto-fix all fixable issues in a batch.
title: When do you use it?

text:
The code below shows how to build a simple interactive tool function that works with info objects. You can run parts of it in the scripting panel when a glyph window is open. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # First, make sure a glyph window is open. # Everything that follows requires an active canvas. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Please open a glyph window first (double-click any glyph)." ) raise SystemExit # ============================================================ # 1. Get the glyph that is currently being edited. # This is your main entry point into the canvas info system. # ============================================================ glyph_info = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if not glyph_info : print ( "No active glyph — click inside the glyph editor." ) raise SystemExit print ( f "Active glyph: ' { glyph_info . name } '" ) print ( f " Canvas bounds: { glyph_info . brectOnCanvas } " ) print ( f " Is active: { glyph_info . isActive } " ) # ============================================================ # 2. Find all contours within 60 canvas pixels of a point. # This simulates what a snap-to-outline tool would do: # given the mouse position, find the nearest contour. # ============================================================ test_point = QPointF ( 200 , 400 ) # a canvas-space point nearby = glyph_info . getNearbyContours ( test_point , 60.0 , "" ) print ( f " 
 Contours within 60px of { test_point } : { len ( nearby ) } " ) for ci in nearby : pt = ci . paramExT () # extended parametric position of closest point print ( f " Contour canvas bounds: { ci . brectOnCanvas () } " ) # ============================================================ # 3. Work with selected nodes. # canvas.selectedNodes() gives you every selected node as # an flNodeInfo. You can read its glyph position and move it. # ============================================================ selected = canvas . selectedNodes () print ( f " 
 Selected nodes: { len ( selected ) } " ) for ni in selected : # Read current position in glyph units: pos = ni . getGlyphPoint ( True ) # True = round to nearest integer print ( f " Node at glyph ( { pos . x () : .0f } , { pos . y () : .0f } )" ) # Check which shape and contour this node belongs to: si = ni . shapeInfo () print ( f " → in shape with canvas bounds { si . boundingBox () } " ) # Move the node 10 units to the right: new_pos = QPointF ( pos . x () + 10 , pos . y ()) ni . setGlyphPoint ( new_pos ) # After moving nodes, tell FontLab to refresh the display: if selected : fl . Update () print ( "Moved all selected nodes 10 units right." ) # ============================================================ # 4. Hit test: find which shape is under a canvas point. # Useful in custom tools to implement "click to select shape". # ============================================================ hit_pt = QPointF ( 150 , 300 ) # simulate a mouse click position hit_shape = glyph_info . getTopHitShape ( hit_pt ) if hit_shape : print ( f " 
 Shape hit at { hit_pt } : bounds = { hit_shape . boundingBox () } " ) else : print ( f " 
 No shape at { hit_pt } " ) # ============================================================ # 5. Align selected nodes to the same Y value (horizontal align). # This is a practical designer script: select nodes in the # glyph editor, run this, and they all snap to the same height. # ============================================================ selected = canvas . selectedNodes () if len ( selected ) >= 2 : # Use the average Y of all selected nodes as the target: avg_y = sum ( ni . getGlyphPoint ( False ) . y () for ni in selected ) / len ( selected ) print ( f " 
 Aligning { len ( selected ) } nodes to Y = { avg_y : .1f } " ) for ni in selected : pos = ni . getGlyphPoint ( False ) ni . setGlyphPoint ( QPointF ( pos . x (), avg_y )) fl . Update () print ( "Done — nodes aligned." )

text: A design axis is one dimension of variation in a variable font. Think of it as a slider. At one end of the slider lives one extreme of your design; at the other end lives the opposite extreme. As you drag the slider, the letterforms interpolate smoothly between those two extremes. Some common axes and what they control: Axis Tag Typical range What it does Weight wght 100–900 Light ↔ Bold Width wdth 50–200 Condensed ↔ Extended Italic ital 0–1 Upright ↔ Italic Slant slnt −90–0 Oblique angle Optical Size opsz 6–144 Caption ↔ Display Custom any any Whatever you design Every axis has: A 4-character tag (like wght or wdth ) that the OpenType spec defines for registered axes, or a custom uppercase tag (like XOPQ ) for private axes. A name — the human-readable label shown in font editors and CSS ( "Weight" , "Width" , etc.). A numeric range : minimum, default, and maximum values. An optional design-space vs user-space mapping for non-linear interpolation.
title: What is a design axis?

text: Sometimes the numbers designers think in (user space) don't map linearly to the underlying interpolation math (design space). For example, a Weight axis might run from 100–900 in user space (CSS weight values), but internally the interpolation happens between masters at design-space values of 0–1000. The map property stores this piecewise-linear translation. If your axis is simple and linear, user space and design space are the same, and you don't need the map.
title: User space vs design space

text: Axes are what turn a static font into a variable font. Here is how to read and manipulate axis definitions. import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Read all axes defined in the current font. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () if not font . axes : print ( "This font has no axes — it is not a variable font." ) raise SystemExit print ( f "Axes in ' { font . fontName } ':" ) for axis in font . axes : print ( f " tag=' { axis . tag } ' name=' { axis . name } '" ) print ( f " min= { axis . minimal } default= { axis . default } max= { axis . maximum } " ) print ( f " hidden= { axis . hidden } registered= { axis . tag in ( 'wght' , 'wdth' , 'ital' , 'slnt' , 'opsz' ) } " ) # ============================================================ # Create a new custom axis. # ============================================================ from fontlab import flAxis new_axis = flAxis () new_axis . tag = "XHGT" # four uppercase letters = private axis new_axis . name = "X-Height" new_axis . minimal = 0 new_axis . default = 100 new_axis . maximum = 200 # font.axes.append(new_axis) # uncomment to actually add it print ( f " \n New axis prepared: { new_axis . tag } ' { new_axis . name } ' " f "[ { new_axis . minimal } , { new_axis . default } , { new_axis . maximum } ]" ) # ============================================================ # Move to a specific location along an axis. # ============================================================ loc = font . currentLocation () print ( " \n Current location:" ) for tag in loc : print ( f " { tag } : { loc [ tag ] } " )

text: Base class for editor tools.
title: fontlab.flBasicTool

text: Every tool in FontLab's toolbar — the Pointer, the Pen, the Knife, the Eraser, the Text tool — is an flBasicTool under the hood. This class defines the minimum interface that all canvas tools share: the ability to activate and deactivate, and an identifier for the cursor shape to display while the tool is active. If you want to write a custom editor tool that handles mouse and keyboard events on the canvas, you subclass flBasicTool and implement event handler methods ( mousePressEvent , mouseMoveEvent , keyPressEvent , etc.). You then receive flEvent objects in those methods describing exactly what the user did. For most designers writing utility scripts, you will never create a tool — you call methods on model objects directly. But if you want a persistent tool that always lives in the toolbar and responds to drawing gestures in real time, flBasicTool is your starting point.
title: What is flBasicTool?

text: The most common scripting use of flBasicTool is activating a built-in tool programmatically. The tool instances are accessible through the workspace. import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # List all available tools in the current workspace. # Each tool is an flBasicTool subclass registered with the # workspace tool manager. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () tools = ws . tools # list of registered flBasicTool objects print ( f "Available tools ( { len ( tools ) } ):" ) for tool in tools : active = " [ACTIVE]" if tool == ws . currentTool else "" print ( f " { type ( tool ) . __name__ : 30s } cursor= { tool . cursorId }{ active } " ) # ============================================================ # Activate a specific tool by name. # Replace 'flPointerTool' with the tool class you want. # ============================================================ pointer = next (( t for t in tools if 'Pointer' in type ( t ) . __name__ ), None ) if pointer : pointer . activateTool () print ( f " \n Activated: { type ( pointer ) . __name__ } " ) else : print ( " \n Pointer tool not found." ) # ============================================================ # Subclassing example (not runnable in the scripting panel, # but shows the structure for a real plugin): # ============================================================ # # class MyMeasureTool(fl.flBasicTool): # def __init__(self): # super().__init__() # self._start = None # # def mousePressEvent(self, event): # # Convert canvas click to glyph coordinates: # canvas = fl.flWorkspace.instance().currentCanvas # self._start = canvas.canvasToGlyph(event.origin) # # def mouseMoveEvent(self, event): # if self._start and event.buttons: # canvas = fl.flWorkspace.instance().currentCanvas # current = canvas.canvasToGlyph(event.global) # dx = current.x() - self._start.x() # dy = current.y() - self._start.y() # import math # dist = math.hypot(dx, dy) # print(f"Distance: {dist:.1f} units") # # my_tool = MyMeasureTool() # fl.flWorkspace.instance().registerTool(my_tool) # my_tool.activateTool()
