text: A canvas is one editor window in FontLab — a glyph editor, a metrics window, or a text window. When you're drawing nodes in a glyph editor, you're looking at a canvas. flCanvas gives you scripting access to that window: its zoom level, what's selected, what's visible, and the coordinate mapping between the screen and your font data. You get the active canvas from the workspace: ws = flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas ()
title: fontlab.flCanvas

text: This is the most important conceptual thing to understand about flCanvas . There are two coordinate systems in play whenever a glyph is on screen: Glyph (font unit) coordinates — the "real" coordinates stored in your font. A node at x=250, y=700 is at those coordinates in font units, regardless of how zoomed in you are. Canvas (screen pixel) coordinates — where that node actually appears on screen, in pixels, taking zoom and scroll position into account. When you're writing code that interacts with the visual display — checking what's under the mouse, doing hit testing, or snapping to canvas positions — you need to be able to move between these two systems. flCanvas provides the conversion methods: glyphToCanvas(point) — takes a point in font units, returns where it appears on screen (in canvas pixels). canvasToGlyph(point) — takes a screen pixel position, returns the corresponding font unit coordinate. Example: if a node is at glyph position (250, 700), and you're zoomed to 200%, glyphToCanvas might return something like (480, 300) in screen pixels. canvasToGlyph does the reverse — if the mouse is at screen pixel (480, 300), canvasToGlyph tells you the glyph coordinate underneath it. This matters for: - Hit testing — "did the user click near this node?" - Snap-to-point — "snap this to the nearest canvas grid point" - Custom drawing — drawing overlays or decorations that need to match glyph positions on screen
title: Two coordinate systems — and why they matter

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF from fontlab import flWorkspace ws = flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : raise RuntimeError ( "Open a glyph window first." ) # Check zoom level print ( "Current zoom:" , canvas . scale ()) # e.g. 2.0 for 200% # Convert: glyph coords → screen position import fontlab as fl node_pos_in_font = QPointF ( 250 , 700 ) screen_pos = canvas . mapToViewport ( node_pos_in_font ) # Convert: mouse position → glyph coords mouse_screen = canvas . mousePosition () mouse_glyph = canvas . mapFromViewport ( mouse_screen ) # Get selected nodes nodes = canvas . selectedNodes () for ni in nodes : print ( ni ) # Force a full redraw canvas . refresh () # Deselect everything canvas . unselectAll () # Ensure a specific glyph bounding box is visible # canvas.ensureVisible(some_rect)
title: Common Scripting Patterns

text:
from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF , QRectF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flWorkspace , flCanvas # ============================================================ # 1. Get the active canvas # ============================================================ # Always check that a canvas is open before proceeding. # Scripts that assume a canvas is open will crash otherwise. ws = flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "No glyph window is open. Please open a glyph to edit." ) raise SystemExit print ( "Got canvas:" , canvas ) print ( "Is active:" , canvas . isActiveCanvas ()) print ( "Has focus:" , canvas . isFocusedCanvas ()) # ============================================================ # 2. Zoom level # ============================================================ # scale() returns a float: 1.0 = 100%, 2.0 = 200%, etc. current_zoom = canvas . scale () print ( f " 
 Current zoom: { current_zoom * 100 : .0f } %" ) # Zoom to 400% centered on the origin # canvas.zoomTo(QPointF(0, 0), 4.0, fl.ViewPointAlignment.Center) # ============================================================ # 3. Coordinate mapping — the most important canvas skill # ============================================================ # These two systems are always in play: # - Glyph (font unit) coords: stored in the font, e.g. x=250, y=700 # - Canvas (screen pixel) coords: where that point appears on screen # A specific point in glyph/font units: glyph_pt = QPointF ( 250 , 700 ) # Where does it appear on screen right now? # mapToViewport takes a canvas-space point and returns a screen pixel point. # (For glyph coords, the canvas transform includes zoom + pan.) screen_pt = canvas . mapToViewportF ( glyph_pt ) print ( f " 
 Glyph point { glyph_pt } appears on screen at { screen_pt } " ) # And the reverse: what glyph coords is this screen position? back = canvas . mapFromViewport ( screen_pt ) print ( f "Screen point { screen_pt } maps back to glyph { back } " ) # scaled() tells you how many screen pixels = 1 font unit at current zoom: pixels_per_unit = canvas . scaled ( 1.0 ) print ( f "At current zoom: 1 font unit = { pixels_per_unit : .2f } screen pixels" ) # ============================================================ # 4. Selection — reading what the user has selected # ============================================================ # selectedNodes() gives you canvas-level proxies (flNodeInfo) # for each selected node. selected = canvas . selectedNodes () print ( f " 
 Selected nodes: { len ( selected ) } " ) for ni in selected : # Each flNodeInfo knows where the node is on-screen print ( f " Node proxy: { ni } " ) # Check if there's anything selected at all: if canvas . haveSelectedNodes (): print ( "Nodes are selected." ) else : print ( "No nodes selected." ) # Deselect everything: canvas . unselectAll () print ( "Deselected all." ) # ============================================================ # 5. Mouse position # ============================================================ # mousePosition() returns canvas (screen pixel) coordinates. # Use mapFromViewport to get the glyph-unit position under the cursor. mouse_canvas = canvas . mousePosition () mouse_glyph = canvas . mapFromViewport ( mouse_canvas ) print ( f " 
 Mouse: screen= { mouse_canvas } , glyph coords= { mouse_glyph } " ) # ============================================================ # 6. Built-in edit operations # ============================================================ # These are equivalent to menu commands — they operate on # whatever is currently selected in the canvas. # Example: select all nodes first (requires glyph to be open) # canvas.selectAll() # Then apply an operation: # canvas.operationReverseContours() # reverse contour direction # canvas.operationSimplify() # remove redundant nodes # canvas.operationToBeziers() # convert to cubic beziers # canvas.operationFlipHorizontal() # mirror left/right # ============================================================ # 7. Forcing a redraw # ============================================================ # After making edits with other API calls, tell the canvas to # refresh so the user sees the updated state. canvas . refresh () # standard full-canvas redraw # canvas.refreshAll() # heavier: clears all render caches too # ============================================================ # 8. Highlight a region # ============================================================ # Useful for drawing attention to a specific area — e.g. # after finding a problem spot in the glyph. problem_area = QRectF ( 200 , 600 , 100 , 150 ) # x, y, w, h in glyph units canvas . highlight ( problem_area ) # Remove the highlight when done: # canvas.resetHighlight() print ( " 
 Canvas tutorial complete." )

text: appendPythonPainter(callback[, order]) -> int registers an overlay and returns a cleanup token. callback(painter, canvas) receives a borrowed QPainter whose transform has been reset for viewport coordinates. The default order is flCanvas.UnderOwner (0); flCanvas.OverOwner (1) draws above the owner. removePythonPainter(token) -> bool removes a callback from the same canvas and requests repainting. import fontlab as fl canvas = fl . flWorkspace . instance () . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is not None : def overlay ( painter , callback_canvas ): painter . drawText ( 12 , 24 , "Python overlay" ) painter_token = canvas . appendPythonPainter ( overlay , fl . flCanvas . OverOwner ) # Keep canvas and painter_token while the overlay is needed. # Later, during cleanup: canvas . removePythonPainter ( painter_token ) Register and remove hooks on the GUI thread. Keep the token for cleanup; do not retain the borrowed painter beyond its callback or assume its wrapper remains valid. The native hook saves and restores painter state and guards against recursive painting. Exceptions are reported through Python's error output.

text: A contour is the closed or open path that forms a letter's shape . Everything you see when you look at a glyph in the editor — the outer edge of an "H", the bowl of a "p", the counter inside an "O" — is a contour. Each contour is made up of an ordered sequence of flNode objects connected by curve and line segments. The contour is the level at which you think about the overall shape of a letter part, while nodes are the individual control points that define exactly where the path goes. Inherits from flObject .
title: fontlab.flContour

text: Open vs. closed contours. Most glyphs consist entirely of closed contours — the path's last node connects back to its first node, enclosing an area. Closed contours are what you use for all regular letterforms. An open contour, by contrast, has two free endpoints that don't connect. Open contours appear in some decorative or component-based designs, in stroke-based workflows where a skeleton is later expanded, and in glyphs built from paths that are meant to be processed further rather than filled directly. The closed property tells you which kind you have. Winding direction and why it matters. In digital type, a filled shape is defined not just by its path but by the direction the path travels — clockwise or counter-clockwise. FontLab follows the PostScript convention: outer contours wind counter-clockwise and counter-shapes (holes) wind clockwise . The letter "O", for example, is built from two contours: the outer oval winds counter-clockwise, and the inner counter-oval winds clockwise — together they create a filled ring. If you get the directions wrong, the font renderer may fill the hole or leave the outer shape empty. The clockwise property and the setStartPoint method (combined with a direction reversal) are your tools for managing this. When scripting, always verify and normalize winding direction after building contours programmatically.
title: What Is a Contour?

text: The letter "O" is the classic test case for understanding contour structure in font design. It requires exactly two contours: the outer oval (counter-clockwise, the positive shape) and the inner counter-oval (clockwise, the hole). This tutorial builds a simplified circular "O" from scratch using flContour and flNode , demonstrating the key concepts of contour construction, node types, smooth nodes, and winding direction. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flContour , flNode font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'O' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] # ── Step 1: Understand the existing "O" ───────────────────────────────────── # A real "O" glyph will already have two contours. Let's inspect them to # understand what winding direction and node count to expect. for i , contour in enumerate ( shape . contours ): direction = "clockwise (inner)" if contour . clockwise else "counter-clockwise (outer)" print ( f "Contour { i } : { contour . nodesCount } nodes, { direction } , closed= { contour . closed } " ) # ── Step 2: Build the outer oval (counter-clockwise) ──────────────────────── # A circle in Bézier representation needs 4 on-curve nodes (at 12, 3, 6, 9 o'clock) # and 8 off-curve handles. The magic constant 0.5523 gives excellent circle approximation. # We place nodes counter-clockwise: top → left → bottom → right. k = 0.5523 # Bézier circle approximation constant cx , cy = 250 , 350 # center of the O rx , ry = 200 , 250 # horizontal and vertical radii outer = flContour () outer . closed = True # Top on-curve node (12 o'clock), going counter-clockwise outer . add ( flNode ( cx , cy + ry , nodeType = 'on' )) # top outer . add ( flNode ( cx - rx * k , cy + ry , nodeType = 'off' )) # outgoing handle outer . add ( flNode ( cx - rx , cy + ry * k , nodeType = 'off' )) # incoming handle outer . add ( flNode ( cx - rx , cy , nodeType = 'on' )) # left outer . add ( flNode ( cx - rx , cy - ry * k , nodeType = 'off' )) # outgoing handle outer . add ( flNode ( cx - rx * k , cy - ry , nodeType = 'off' )) # incoming handle outer . add ( flNode ( cx , cy - ry , nodeType = 'on' )) # bottom outer . add ( flNode ( cx + rx * k , cy - ry , nodeType = 'off' )) # outgoing handle outer . add ( flNode ( cx + rx , cy - ry * k , nodeType = 'off' )) # incoming handle outer . add ( flNode ( cx + rx , cy , nodeType = 'on' )) # right outer . add ( flNode ( cx + rx , cy + ry * k , nodeType = 'off' )) # outgoing handle outer . add ( flNode ( cx + rx * k , cy + ry , nodeType = 'off' )) # incoming handle # (path closes back to the top node) print ( f "Outer contour: { outer . nodesCount } nodes, clockwise= { outer . clockwise } " ) # ── Step 3: Make the on-curve nodes smooth ─────────────────────────────────── # Setting smooth=True on the on-curve nodes ensures the handles are treated as # collinear — producing the fluid, tangent-continuous curve transitions that # make a circle look like a circle, not a polygon. for node in outer . nodes (): if node . isOn (): node . smooth = True # ── Step 4: Build the inner counter (clockwise) ───────────────────────────── # The inner oval is smaller and must wind in the OPPOSITE direction to create # a hole. We build it clockwise: top → right → bottom → left. # Using smaller radii for the counter. irx , iry = 130 , 170 # inner radii inner = flContour () inner . closed = True # Top on-curve node, going CLOCKWISE: top → right → bottom → left inner . add ( flNode ( cx , cy + iry , nodeType = 'on' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx + irx * k , cy + iry , nodeType = 'off' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx + irx , cy + iry * k , nodeType = 'off' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx + irx , cy , nodeType = 'on' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx + irx , cy - iry * k , nodeType = 'off' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx + irx * k , cy - iry , nodeType = 'off' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx , cy - iry , nodeType = 'on' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx - irx * k , cy - iry , nodeType = 'off' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx - irx , cy - iry * k , nodeType = 'off' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx - irx , cy , nodeType = 'on' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx - irx , cy + iry * k , nodeType = 'off' )) inner . add ( flNode ( cx - irx * k , cy + iry , nodeType = 'off' )) # Make on-curve nodes smooth for node in inner . nodes (): if node . isOn (): node . smooth = True print ( f "Inner contour: { inner . nodesCount } nodes, clockwise= { inner . clockwise } " ) # ── Step 5: Verify winding directions ──────────────────────────────────────── # Before adding the contours, make sure winding is as expected. # Outer should be counter-clockwise (False), inner should be clockwise (True). # getSquare() returns positive for CCW, negative for CW. print ( f "Outer area (positive = CCW): { outer . getSquare () : .1f } " ) print ( f "Inner area (negative = CW): { inner . getSquare () : .1f } " ) # ── Step 6: Add both contours to the shape and update ─────────────────────── # clearNodes on existing contours first if this is a re-run of the script: for existing in list ( shape . contours ): shape . removeContour ( existing ) shape . addContour ( outer ) shape . addContour ( inner ) fl . Update () print ( "Done! The letter O has been rebuilt." )
title: Tutorial: Building the Letter "O" from Two Contours

text: These self-contained examples solve the tasks that come up most often when working with contours in scripts.
title: Common Scripting Patterns

text: When importing outlines, the winding direction can come in wrong. This script identifies any clockwise outer contour (which should be counter-clockwise) and any counter-clockwise inner contour (which should be clockwise) and fixes them. The heuristic used here is area: the largest contour by area is assumed to be the outer shape. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'O' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : contours = shape . contours if not contours : continue # Find the contour with the largest absolute area — that's the outer shape. areas = [( abs ( c . getSquare ()), c ) for c in contours ] areas . sort ( reverse = True ) outer_contour = areas [ 0 ][ 1 ] for area , contour in areas : is_outer = ( contour is outer_contour ) # Outer should be CCW (clockwise=False); inners should be CW (clockwise=True) if is_outer and contour . clockwise : contour . reverse () print ( f "Reversed outer contour in ' { glyph . name } '" ) elif not is_outer and not contour . clockwise : contour . reverse () print ( f "Reversed inner contour in ' { glyph . name } '" ) fl . Update ()
title: Reverse winding direction of all counter-shapes

text: Open contours are usually unintentional in a production font. This script lists every open contour by glyph name so you can investigate and close them. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () open_found = [] for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : if not contour . closed : first = contour . getFirstPoint () last = contour . getLastPoint () open_found . append ( f " { glyph . name } [ { layer . name } ]: " f "open contour with { contour . nodesCount } nodes, " f "start=( { first . x () : .0f } , { first . y () : .0f } ), " f "end=( { last . x () : .0f } , { last . y () : .0f } )" ) if open_found : print ( f "Found { len ( open_found ) } open contour(s):" ) for line in open_found : print ( " " , line ) else : print ( "No open contours found." )
title: Find all open contours in the font

text: Extremum nodes — points at the topmost, bottommost, leftmost, and rightmost positions of a curve — are required for correct PostScript hinting. This script inserts them where they are missing by using insertNodeTo at the parametric position of each extremum. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'O' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : nodes = contour . nodes () for node in nodes : if node . isOn (): # isExtreme(x=False) checks vertical extremes (top/bottom) # isExtreme(x=True) checks horizontal extremes (left/right) if not node . isExtreme ( x = False ) and not node . isExtreme ( x = True ): pass # node is not at an extreme; no action needed # The above just inspects — to *add* missing extremes, use: # FontLab has a built-in method on the shape for this: # shape.addExtremes() # adds extremum nodes to all contours in the shape fl . Update ()
title: Add extremum nodes to all contours

text: After auto-tracing or importing from SVG, outlines often contain far too many nodes. This script applies the simplify method to each contour to reduce node count while preserving the visual shape within a tolerance of 1 em unit. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () tolerance = 1.0 # maximum deviation from original shape, in em units for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for shape in layer . shapes : original_count = sum ( c . nodesCount for c in shape . contours ) for contour in shape . contours : contour . simplify ( tolerance , lossy = False , # keep within tolerance extremes = True # always preserve extreme nodes ) new_count = sum ( c . nodesCount for c in shape . contours ) if new_count < original_count : print ( f " { glyph . name } : { original_count } → { new_count } nodes" ) fl . Update ()
title: Simplify all contours by removing redundant nodes

text: Variable font masters must have the same number and type of nodes on each corresponding contour. This script compares the first two masters of a variable font and reports any incompatible glyphs. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyphs = font . glyphs for glyph in glyphs : if len ( glyph . layers ) < 2 : continue layer_a = glyph . layers [ 0 ] layer_b = glyph . layers [ 1 ] contours_a = [ c for s in layer_a . shapes for c in s . contours ] contours_b = [ c for s in layer_b . shapes for c in s . contours ] if len ( contours_a ) != len ( contours_b ): print ( f "INCOMPATIBLE { glyph . name } : " f " { len ( contours_a ) } vs { len ( contours_b ) } contours" ) continue for i , ( ca , cb ) in enumerate ( zip ( contours_a , contours_b )): if not ca . isCompatible ( cb , strong = True ): print ( f "INCOMPATIBLE { glyph . name } contour { i } : " f " { ca . nodesCount } vs { cb . nodesCount } nodes" )
title: Check contour compatibility across masters for variable fonts

title: fontlab.flContourInfo

text: flContourInfo represents one contour on the FontLab canvas. It extends flShapeInfo with per-contour node queries and a parametric "where along the contour" tracker — the mechanism that lets tools show a preview point on a contour as the mouse moves over it (as in a knife or add-node tool). While flContour stores the model data (nodes and segments in font units), flContourInfo knows where the contour appears on screen . It provides the canvas-space bounding rect for the contour, access to node info objects, and hit-testing at a specific mouse position.
title: What is flContourInfo?

text: The most practical use of flContourInfo in a custom tool is the parametric hover-point system: as the mouse moves, you find the nearest parametric position on a contour and show a small indicator there. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Simulate a knife-tool hover: # Given a canvas mouse position, find the nearest point on any # contour and display its parametric position (exT value). # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Open a glyph window first." ) raise SystemExit gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if gi is None : print ( "No active glyph." ) raise SystemExit # Simulate a mouse position: mouse_pos = QPointF ( 250 , 350 ) # Get nearby contours within 20 canvas pixels: nearby = gi . getNearbyContours ( mouse_pos , 20.0 , "" ) if not nearby : print ( f "No contours within 20 px of ( { mouse_pos . x () : .0f } , { mouse_pos . y () : .0f } )." ) else : # The closest one (smallest dist): ci = min ( nearby , key = lambda c : c . dist ) print ( f "Closest contour dist= { ci . dist : .1f } px" ) print ( f " Canvas bounds: { ci . brectOnCanvas () } " ) # The parametric position of the closest point: ex_t = ci . paramExT () t = ci . paramT () print ( f " Extended t: { ex_t : .4f } Segment t: { t : .4f } " ) # Update the hover indicator (for tool paint): ci . setExT ( ex_t ) repaint_rect = ci . getUpdateRect ( ex_t ) print ( f " Repaint rect: { repaint_rect } " ) # ============================================================ # Get all node info objects for this contour to draw handles: # ============================================================ nodes_info = ci . getNodesInfo () print ( f " \n Nodes in this contour ( { len ( nodes_info ) } ):" ) for ni in nodes_info : print ( f " Node type= { ni . node . type } " f "canvas=( { ni . canvasPoint . x () : .1f } , { ni . canvasPoint . y () : .1f } )" )
title: Tutorial

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if canvas else None if gi : mouse_pos = QPointF ( 300 , 400 ) nearby = gi . getNearbyContours ( mouse_pos , 50.0 , "" ) hit_node = None for ci in nearby : ni = ci . getHitNode ( mouse_pos ) if ni is not None : hit_node = ni break if hit_node : print ( f "Nearest node: type= { hit_node . node . type } " f "at ( { hit_node . node . x : .0f } , { hit_node . node . y : .0f } )" ) else : print ( "No node hit within 50px of cursor." )

title: fontlab.flEvent

text: flEvent is the small native event record used by the editor's own tools. It records a native event category and Qt modifier-key flags. The mouse-specific data is exposed separately by flMouseEvent . Callback tools registered with flWorkspace.registerPythonTool() receive Qt QMouseEvent/QKeyEvent wrappers rather than this native record. See the tool callback contract. flEvent exposes only type and modifiers . For mouse coordinates, buttons and movement, use flMouseEvent.
title: What is flEvent?

text: Name Type Access Description type EventType rw What kind of event this is. The class dictionary flEvent.EventType contains MouseEvent , WheelEvent and MovementEvent . These are native categories, not Qt event IDs. modifiers int rw A bitmask of which modifier keys were held when the event fired. Combine with Qt's modifier constants: Qt.ShiftModifier , Qt.ControlModifier (Ctrl/Cmd), Qt.AltModifier (Alt/Option), Qt.MetaModifier . Example: bool(event.modifiers & Qt.ShiftModifier) — is Shift held?

text: Formula string for axis-driven values.
title: fontlab.flExpression

text: An flExpression stores and evaluates a text formula that can reference design-space axis values and font metric names. For example: "ascender * 0.7" "xHeight + stemWidth" "weight < 400 ? 50 : 100" When FontLab evaluates an expression, it substitutes the current values of axis tags (like wght , wdth ) and metric names (like ascender , xHeight , capHeight ) for the variable names in the formula, then computes the result. Expressions are used by guidelines, anchors, and parametric shape nodes to make their positions vary smoothly across the design space.
title: What is flExpression?

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flExpression # ============================================================ # 1. Create an expression and inspect it. # This is standalone — not yet attached to any object. # ============================================================ expr = flExpression () expr . expression = "ascender * 0.7" print ( "Has expression:" , expr . hasExpression ()) # True print ( "Has error:" , expr . hasError ()) # False (not yet evaluated) print ( "Is ready:" , expr . ready ) # False (not yet evaluated) # ============================================================ # 2. Inspect which variables the formula depends on. # ============================================================ deps = expr . variables ({}) # {} = no alias substitution print ( "Depends on:" , deps ) # ['ascender'] # ============================================================ # 3. Rename variables for human-friendly display. # Useful if you are showing the expression in a UI panel. # ============================================================ alias_map = { "ascender" : "Ascender Height" } friendly = expr . expression ( alias_map ) print ( "Friendly formula:" , friendly ) # "Ascender Height * 0.7" # ============================================================ # 4. Read an expression from an existing guideline. # Guidelines can be formula-driven — for example, the # x-height guideline might use "xHeight" as its expression. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () for gl in font . guidelines : # flGuideLine exposes its expression through the y-property: e = gl . expressionY # returns flExpression if e and e . hasExpression (): print ( f "Guideline at y= { gl . centerPoint . y () : .0f } : " f "formula = ' { e . expression } '" ) if e . hasError (): from fontlab import flPropertiesProcessor err_msg = flPropertiesProcessor . errorToStr ( e . error ) print ( f " ERROR: { err_msg } " ) # ============================================================ # 5. Assign an expression to a guideline. # Make a horizontal guideline track the x-height # so it always sits at the right height in every master. # ============================================================ from fontlab import flGuideLine # Create a new guideline at y=500 initially: gl = flGuideLine ( 0.0 , QPointF ( 0 , 500 )) font . appendGuideline ( gl ) # Now attach an expression so it tracks xHeight automatically: gl . expressionY . expression = "xHeight" gl . expressionY . resetReady () # force re-evaluation fl . Update () print ( "Guideline is now tracking xHeight." )

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flExpression font = fl . CurrentFont () # Test expressions before applying: for formula in [ "=xHeight" , "=capHeight * 0.5" , "=badVariable + 100" ]: expr = flExpression () expr . expression = formula valid = expr . validate ( font ) # check against font's variable scope print ( f "' { formula } ': valid= { valid } " )

text: A glyph is your font's record for one character — the letter "A", the numeral "3", an ampersand, or any other symbol you draw. Think of it as a folder: the glyph holds your drawings (called layers ), the character code it maps to ( unicodes ), the spacing information ( metrics ), and any organisational labels ( tags ) you want to attach. Inherits from flObject .
title: fontlab.flGlyph

text: The glyph itself doesn't contain drawing data directly. Instead it holds one or more layers . Each layer is a snapshot of the character at a particular design stage or design-space location: Master layers (one per master in a variable font) are the interpolatable drawings that define your design space. In a simple single-master font there is just one — often called "Regular". Service layers are helpers: the mask, reference drawings, or intermediate states used during editing. They do not export. So when you draw the letter "A", you are drawing on a layer inside the glyph, not on the glyph itself. This distinction matters when scripting: to read or change actual node coordinates you go glyph → layer → shape → contour → node .
title: The shape of a glyph

text: A unicode is the number that maps your glyph to a character in the Unicode standard. "A" is 0x0041 , "α" is 0x03B1 . A glyph can have more than one unicode (for example the standard "A" and its fullwidth variant "Ａ" can share a single drawing). The font system uses unicodes to figure out which glyph to show when text is set.
title: Unicodes

text: The advance width is how much horizontal space the glyph occupies — including any side-bearings. The left sidebearing is the gap between the glyph's left edge and the start of its outline; the right sidebearing is the gap on the other side. You can set these as raw numbers or as expressions that reference other glyphs (e.g. "=n" means "copy the left sidebearing from the glyph n"). Expressions let you keep spacing consistent across a family without maintaining numbers by hand.
title: Metrics

text: Tags are free-form labels you attach to a glyph. They are invaluable for organising large font projects: tag all diacritics as "diacritic" , all small caps as "sc" , all glyphs that still need review as "todo" . You can then filter or select glyphs by tag in the font window.
title: Tags

text: font = fl . CurrentFont () for glyph in font . glyphs : if not glyph . hasBody : print ( f "Empty glyph: { glyph . name } " )
title: Iterating every glyph and checking content

text: glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] # first (usually Regular) master layer print ( layer . name , layer . advanceWidth )
title: Finding a glyph and reading its active layer

text: # Tag all glyphs that still need spacing work for glyph in font . glyphs : if glyph . advanceWidth == 0 : glyph . setTag ( "no-width" , True ) # Later, remove the tag after fixing glyph . setTag ( "no-width" , False )
title: Adding and removing tags

text: # Make every lowercase letter inherit its left bearing from 'n' import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () lowercase = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz" for name in lowercase : g = font . findName ( name ) if g : g . metricsLeft = "=n"
title: Batch-setting sidebearings with a metric expression

text: from fontlab import flGlyph original = font [ 'A' ] copy = flGlyph ( original ) # independent clone copy . name = "A.ss01" font . addGlyph ( copy )
title: Copying a glyph

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flGlyph , flLayer , flShape , flContour , flNode # ============================================================ # Get the current font and look at a glyph # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () # Access the glyph for the letter 'A'. The font acts like a # dictionary — you can look glyphs up by name. glyph = font [ 'A' ] # The advance width is the total horizontal space this character # takes up in a line of text (left sidebearing + outline + right # sidebearing). print ( f "Glyph: ' { glyph . name } '" ) print ( f "Advance width: { glyph . advanceWidth } units" ) # ============================================================ # Layers — one per master, plus service layers # ============================================================ # Each glyph can have several layers. In a variable font you'll # see one per master (e.g. "Light", "Regular", "Bold"). In a # single-master font there is usually just one. for layer in glyph . layers : print ( f " Layer ' { layer . name } ' — width: { layer . advanceWidth } " ) # The active layer is the one shown in the glyph editor right now. active = glyph . activeLayer print ( f "Active layer: ' { active . name } '" ) # ============================================================ # Tags — organise your glyph set # ============================================================ # Add a tag to mark this glyph for review: glyph . setTag ( "needs-review" , True ) # Read back the tags: print ( "Tags:" , glyph . tags ) # explicit tags you set print ( "Auto-tags:" , glyph . virtualTags ()) # tags FontLab derives automatically # Remove a tag once work is done: glyph . setTag ( "needs-review" , False ) # ============================================================ # Metrics — read and write sidebearings # ============================================================ # Read both sidebearings at once (no italic transform needed here): from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform identity = QTransform () lsb , rsb = glyph . getSB ( identity ) print ( f "Left SB: { lsb } Right SB: { rsb } " ) # Set the left sidebearing directly: glyph . setLSB ( 40.0 , False , identity ) # Or use metric expressions so this glyph inherits spacing from 'H': glyph . metricsLeft = "=H" glyph . metricsRight = "=H" # Now tell FontLab to re-evaluate the expressions: glyph . updateSidebearings ( True ) # ============================================================ # OpenType glyph classification # ============================================================ # Mark a glyph as a ligature (two components): ligature = font . findName ( "f_i" ) if ligature : ligature . otGlyphClass = 2 # 2 = ligature ligature . otLigaturesCount = 2 # composed of 2 glyphs (f + i) # Mark a glyph as a combining mark: acute = font . findName ( "acutecomb" ) if acute : acute . otGlyphClass = 3 # 3 = mark # ============================================================ # Creating a brand new glyph from scratch # ============================================================ # Create a detached glyph object: new_glyph = flGlyph () new_glyph . name = "diamond" new_glyph . mark = 3 # colour-mark it so it's easy to spot # Build a layer to hold the outline: layer = flLayer () layer . name = "Regular" layer . advanceWidth = 400 # advance width for this master # Build the outline: a diamond shape made of 4 on-curve nodes. # The path goes: bottom → right → top → left, closed. shape = flShape () contour = flContour () contour . closed = True for x , y in [( 200 , 0 ), ( 400 , 300 ), ( 200 , 600 ), ( 0 , 300 )]: contour . add ( flNode ( x , y , nodeType = 'on' )) shape . addContour ( contour ) layer . addShape ( shape ) # Attach the layer to the glyph, then add the glyph to the font: new_glyph . addLayer ( layer ) font . addGlyph ( new_glyph ) # Tell FontLab to refresh the UI: fl . Update ()
title: Tutorial

text: glyph.glyphMark exposes the existing FontLab integer, not a Glyphs label index. Nonpositive values render as no mark. Values 1–360 encode hue ( value - 1 ). Values above 360 render as gray, with channel value min(255, lightness // 2 + max(0, value - 1000) // 2) using the current mark lightness setting. Thus 1000 uses the base gray and 1100 is 50 channel units lighter; neither specifies a fixed RGB gray across preferences. VFJ stores the integer. There is no categorical conversion from Glyphs label 11 to a FontLab charcoal label. Converting an achromatic QColor through the hue-based color adapter yields no mark and is not a substitute for this integer property. The raw property is suitable when the caller manages change notification and history. Ordinary glyph history can import geometry to serialize a full snapshot. This binding does not provide a geometry-free metadata transaction, cross-document atomicity, or automatic rollback. Do not emulate glyph-only writes by changing mark and restoring layers: that can make inherited layer marks explicit. Existing scripts that use mark retain its previous behavior.
title: Glyph-only mark encoding and history

text: The binding exposes the native Sigma metadata used for authored interpolation adjustments: Method Result and behavior getSigmaData() Return an editable dictionary snapshot of the glyph's Sigma metadata. setSigmaData(data) Validate and apply a complete dictionary through the native Sigma authoring path; invalid data raises ValueError . The native operation records the edit in history. clearSigmaData() Remove authored Sigma curves through the native editing path; errors raise ValueError . initializeSigma() Bind compatible master points for Sigma, record the initialization in history, and return None . Errors raise ValueError . Read the dictionary with getSigmaData() before editing it; retain unrelated keys and use the native validator rather than inventing a metadata schema. setSigmaData() and clearSigmaData() also return None on success. The current registration docstring for initializeSigma() says dict , but the implementation returns None ; call getSigmaData() afterward to inspect the initialized data. text: Canvas proxy for a rendered glyph.
title: fontlab.flGlyphInfo

text: flGlyphInfo is the top-level entry point into the canvas info system. When a glyph is displayed in the metrics view or glyph editor, FontLab wraps it in an flGlyphInfo that knows everything about how it appears on screen: its bounding rectangle in pixels, its screen position, whether it is currently active for editing, and where all its shapes, contours, and nodes are. This is the class you reach for when writing interactive tools or canvas decorators. canvas.activeGlyphInfo() is the single most important call for tool code — it gives you the live rendering context for whatever glyph the user is currently editing. flGlyphInfo is the root of the canvas info hierarchy: flGlyphInfo ← top-level proxy for one rendered glyph slot ├── flLayerInfo ← canvas proxy for a layer (bounding rect) └── (via shapes/contours) flShapeInfo ← shape-level: move, hit-test, composite queries └── flContourInfo ← per-contour: node list, parametric hover point └── flNodeInfo ← per-node: move in glyph space, repaint rect The base info classes ( flSearchInfo , flGraphicsInfo ) hold shared infrastructure — distance values and canvas transform matrices — and are described in their own files.
title: What is flGlyphInfo?

text: canvas.activeGlyphInfo() is the single most useful call for interactive tool code. It gives you the currently-being-edited glyph's canvas context — its screen position, bounds, and the full tree of shapes, contours, and nodes with canvas coordinates.
title: When do you use it?

text:
The standard flow in any canvas tool starts with getting the flGlyphInfo for the active glyph, then querying it for shapes, contours, or nodes near the mouse position. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Step 1: Get the active glyph info from the canvas. # This works in both the glyph editor and the metrics view. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Open a glyph window first." ) raise SystemExit gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if gi is None : print ( "No glyph is currently active for editing." ) raise SystemExit print ( f "Active glyph: ' { gi . name } '" ) print ( f "Is active: { gi . isActive } " ) print ( f "Canvas bounds: { gi . brectOnCanvas } " ) print ( f "Body rect (UPM): { gi . bodyRectOnCanvas } " ) print ( f "Null glyph: { gi . isNullGlyph } " ) # ============================================================ # Step 2: Hit-test — did the user click inside the glyph? # This is the fastest way to answer "is this click on ink?" # ============================================================ mouse_pos = QPointF ( 250 , 400 ) # canvas-space click position hit = gi . hitToShape ( mouse_pos ) print ( f " 
 Point ( { mouse_pos . x () : .0f } , { mouse_pos . y () : .0f } ) inside glyph: { hit } " ) # ============================================================ # Step 3: Find the nearest shape to a mouse position. # ============================================================ top_shape = gi . getTopHitShape ( mouse_pos ) if top_shape : print ( f "Top hit shape canvas bounds: { top_shape . brectOnCanvas () } " ) # ============================================================ # Step 4: Find nearby contours (the magnetic snap pattern). # This is how knife tools and add-node tools find the curve # to snap to. # ============================================================ nearby = gi . getNearbyContours ( mouse_pos , 30.0 , "" ) if nearby : nearest = min ( nearby , key = lambda c : c . dist ) print ( f " 
 Nearest contour at { nearest . dist : .1f } px from mouse" ) print ( f " Parametric position (exT): { nearest . paramExT () : .3f } " ) nodes = nearest . getNodesInfo () print ( f " Contour has { len ( nodes ) } node(s)" ) # ============================================================ # Step 5: Access the model data through .glyph. # ============================================================ glyph = gi . glyph layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] print ( f " 
 Glyph ' { glyph . name } ' has { len ( layer . shapes ) } shape(s) " f "on layer ' { layer . name } '" )

text: Canvas-transform-aware info object.
title: fontlab.flGraphicsInfo

text: flGraphicsInfo extends flSearchInfo with the one thing that makes canvas rendering possible: the transformation matrix ( transform ) that maps from glyph-space coordinates (font units) to canvas-space coordinates (screen pixels at the current zoom level). Once you have an flGraphicsInfo , you can convert any glyph-space point to its screen position by applying the transform. Conversely, you can map screen coordinates back to glyph coordinates using the inverse transform. Every shape, contour, and node info object inherits from flGraphicsInfo , which is why all of them can answer "where on screen am I?". Most scripting that works with canvas positions will receive flGraphicsInfo (or one of its subclasses like flShapeInfo , flContourInfo , or flNodeInfo ) back from a query method rather than constructing one directly.
title: What is flGraphicsInfo?

text: The transform property is the bridge between the mathematical world of font units and the visual world of the screen. Here is how to use it to map points between the two coordinate systems. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Get the canvas transform for a specific shape on screen. # flShapeInfo inherits from flGraphicsInfo, so every shape # info object has a .transform property. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Open a glyph window first." ) raise SystemExit gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if gi is None : print ( "No active glyph." ) raise SystemExit # Get shape infos through a broad contour query: all_contours = gi . getNearbyContours ( QPointF ( 0 , 0 ), 99999 , "" ) if all_contours : ci = all_contours [ 0 ] si = ci . shapeInfo # flShapeInfo, which has transform # The transform maps glyph units → canvas pixels: tx = si . transform # Map a glyph-space point to canvas space: glyph_pt = QPointF ( 100 , 500 ) # 100 units right, 500 units up canvas_pt = tx . map ( glyph_pt ) # apply the transform print ( f "Glyph ( { glyph_pt . x () : .0f } , { glyph_pt . y () : .0f } ) " f "→ Canvas ( { canvas_pt . x () : .1f } , { canvas_pt . y () : .1f } )" ) # Map back from canvas → glyph space using the inverse: inverse_tx = tx . inverted ()[ 0 ] # inverted() returns (QTransform, bool_ok) back = inverse_tx . map ( canvas_pt ) print ( f "Canvas ( { canvas_pt . x () : .1f } , { canvas_pt . y () : .1f } ) " f "→ Glyph ( { back . x () : .1f } , { back . y () : .1f } )" )

text: Guidelines are the non-printing reference lines you draw across your canvas to help align things. They are the blue (or custom-colored) lines that mark cap height, x-height, descender, optical margins, stem axes, and any other alignment target you care about. FontLab has two scopes of guidelines: Font-level guidelines live in flPackage.guidelines . They appear in every glyph you open — they are global to the whole font. These are perfect for metrics references like ascender, cap height, x-height, descender, and baseline, because those values are relevant to every glyph. Glyph-level guidelines live in flLayer.guidelines . They only appear when that specific glyph (and layer) is open in the editor. Use these for glyph-specific construction lines, like the exact center of a capital O, or the shoulder angle on a lowercase n. Beyond simple horizontal and vertical lines, guidelines can be: Angled — any angle in degrees. Useful for italic slant guides or diagonal construction lines. Expression-based — a guideline whose position is tied to a font metric by a formula, like "=xHeight" . If you change xHeight, the guideline moves with it automatically. Power guides — guidelines that FontLab auto-generates from the extremes of your outlines. They snap to the tops, bottoms, and sides of your contours, making it easy to align multiple glyphs to common optical heights.
title: What is a guideline?

text: flSnapLine is the technical base class that handles all the snap and measurement geometry — the center node, the vector node, the snap flags, and the distance/offset math. You rarely need to interact with flSnapLine directly; flGuideLine inherits everything from it and adds the extra features (color, tags, style, expressions) that you'll actually use. Think of flSnapLine as the engine and flGuideLine as the car.
title: What is flSnapLine?

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF from PythonQt.QtGui import QColor import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flGuideLine font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'H' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] # ============================================================ # 1. Font-level (global) guidelines # ============================================================ # Font-level guidelines appear in every glyph. They're ideal for # shared metrics references like cap height, ascender, x-height, # and descender. Add them once and they show up everywhere. # Create a horizontal guideline at y = 700 (cap height reference). # angle=0 means horizontal; the QPointF gives the position. h_guide = flGuideLine ( 0.0 , QPointF ( 0 , 700 )) font . addGuideline ( h_guide ) print ( "Font-level guidelines:" , len ( font . guidelines )) # Create a vertical guideline at x = 300 (a stem axis reference). # angle=90 means vertical. v_guide = flGuideLine ( 90.0 , QPointF ( 300 , 0 )) font . addGuideline ( v_guide ) # ============================================================ # 2. Glyph-level guidelines # ============================================================ # Glyph-level guidelines only appear in the one glyph where you # add them. Great for construction lines specific to that letter — # like the shoulder angle on a lowercase 'n', or the center of a # round letter's bowl. # A 45° diagonal guideline through the point (100, 100): a_guide = flGuideLine ( 45.0 , QPointF ( 100 , 100 )) layer . appendGuidelines ([ a_guide ]) print ( "Glyph-level guidelines in this layer:" , len ( layer . guidelines )) # ============================================================ # 3. Inspecting guidelines # ============================================================ # Loop through all font-level guides and print their properties. for gl in font . guidelines : print ( f " angle= { gl . angle : .1f } ° " f "pos= { gl . centerPoint } " f "vertical= { gl . isVertical () } " f "horizontal= { gl . isHorizontal () } " ) # ============================================================ # 4. Moving a guideline with a transform # ============================================================ # The guideline doesn't have a simple ".y = 720" setter, so you # move it with applyTransform(). QTransform().translate(dx, dy) # shifts it by (dx, dy) in font units. gl = font . guidelines [ 0 ] print ( "Before move:" , gl . centerPoint ) from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform gl . applyTransform ( QTransform () . translate ( 0 , 20 )) # move up 20 units print ( "After move:" , gl . centerPoint ) # ============================================================ # 5. Coloring guidelines # ============================================================ # You can assign any color to a guideline to help distinguish it. # Red for construction guides, blue for metrics, green for # opticals — whatever helps your visual system. gl . color = QColor ( 220 , 60 , 60 ) # a warm red print ( "Has custom color:" , gl . hasColor ) # True # ============================================================ # 6. Expression-based guidelines # ============================================================ # An expression ties the guideline's position to a font metric. # When you update the metric (e.g. change xHeight in Font Info), # the guideline follows automatically. The expression string starts # with "=" followed by a metric name or arithmetic formula. gl . expression = "=xHeight" print ( "Expression:" , gl . expression ) print ( "Position controlled by expression:" , gl . hasExpression ) # You can also use arithmetic: h_guide . expression = "=capHeight * 0.5" # midpoint of cap height # ============================================================ # 7. Tagging guidelines for filtering # ============================================================ # Tags let you group guides by purpose so your scripts can # work on just a subset without touching everything. h_guide . tags = { "metrics" , "horizontal" } v_guide . tags = { "construction" } # Find all guides tagged "metrics": metric_guides = [ g for g in font . guidelines if "metrics" in g . tags ] print ( "Metric guides:" , len ( metric_guides )) # ============================================================ # 8. Snap geometry (distanceTo, offsetTo) # ============================================================ # You can query how far a point is from a guideline, or get the # snap vector that would move a point onto the guide. # This is useful if you want to measure how far a node is # from an alignment target. pt = QPointF ( 100 , 680 ) dist = gl . distanceTo ( pt , 0 ) # perpendicular distance, signed offset = gl . offsetTo ( pt , 0 ) # vector to snap onto the guide print ( f "Distance from point to guide: { dist : .1f } units" ) print ( f "Snap offset: ( { offset . x () : .1f } , { offset . y () : .1f } )" ) # ============================================================ # 9. Markers on a guideline # ============================================================ # Some guidelines carry measurement markers — tick marks that # label distances or stem widths. If you're scripting metrics # or stem analysis, you can read them here. for m in gl . markers : print ( f " Marker at position= { m . position } " ) # ============================================================ # 10. Power guides (auto-generated from outlines) # ============================================================ # Power guides are automatically created from the extreme points # of your contours. They snap to the optical tops, bottoms, and # sides of your shapes — useful for aligning multiple glyphs # to a shared optical height. # # flGuideLine.createPowerGuides(font, layer, # horizontal=True, ← capture top/bottom extremes # vertical=True, ← capture left/right extremes # diagonal=False) ← skip diagonal tangent points ok = flGuideLine . createPowerGuides ( font , layer , True , True , False , use_glyph_guides = True , use_font_guides = True ) print ( "Power guides created:" , ok ) print ( "Layer guides after power-guide generation:" , len ( layer . guidelines )) # ============================================================ # 11. Sorting guidelines # ============================================================ # Sort font guidelines from bottom to top (ascending y position): sorted_guides = flGuideLine . sortGuideLines ( list ( font . guidelines ), True ) for g in sorted_guides : print ( f " y= { g . centerPoint . y () : .0f } angle= { g . angle : .0f } °" ) # ============================================================ # 12. Removing a guideline # ============================================================ font . removeGuideline ( v_guide ) print ( "Font guidelines remaining:" , len ( font . guidelines )) fl . Update ()

text: PostScript hinting settings.
title: fontlab.flHintingParameters

text: PostScript (CFF/Type 1) hinting makes your fonts look crisper at small sizes on screen by snapping certain features to pixel boundaries. The hinting parameters control exactly how aggressive or conservative that snapping is. If you are a type designer who cares about these settings, you already know what BlueFuzz, BlueShift, and BlueScale mean. If you are not sure: the default values work well for most fonts — FontLab's autohinting engine will set them appropriately when you run autohint. The settings here correspond directly to the Private dictionary in CFF/Type 1 fonts and to certain fields in the OpenType maxp and head tables (for TrueType hinting). Access hinting parameters on a font via: hp = font . hintingParameters ( master_name )
title: What is flHintingParameters?

text: These are the values written into the Private dictionary of a CFF/Type 1 font. Name Type Access Description forceBold bool rw If True , the rasterizer will artificially thicken strokes at very small sizes (below forceBoldTreshold ). Rarely needed for modern screen rendering, but sometimes useful for bitmap-targeted fonts. Adobe's recommendation is False . forceBoldTreshold double rw The display size (in PPEM) below which forceBold takes effect. Only matters if forceBold is True . blueFuzz int rw Extends each blue zone by this many character-space units on each side, giving the zone a wider "fuzzy" capture region. A value of 0 means zones have sharp edges. Adobe recommends 0 for most fonts. blueShift int rw The minimum distance between an overshoot and the alignment zone boundary for the overshoot to be suppressed at small sizes. Adobe recommends 7 . blueScale double rw The PPEM size at which overshoots are no longer suppressed and the full design curve is shown without snapping. Adobe recommends 0.039625 (corresponding to roughly 25 PPEM). flex bool rw If True , nearly-horizontal curves (like the slight curve of a capital S at the mid-stroke) are eligible for the CFF flex hint, which reduces visual weight at small sizes by treating the nearly-flat curve as truly flat. zonePPM int rw The minimum PPEM at which alignment zone hinting is active. Below this size, zone snapping is disabled. stemSnapLimit int rw The maximum number of stems that can be included in the StemSnap arrays. CFF limits StemSnapH and StemSnapV to 12 values each. codePPM int rw The PPEM at which code-level (glyph instruction) hinting engages. dropoutPPM int rw The PPEM below which dropout control (a technique that improves rendering of thin diagonal strokes) is applied.
title: PostScript / CFF Hinting Properties

text: These values are written into the OpenType binary and affect TrueType hinting behaviour and font metadata. Name Type Access Description lowestRecPPEM int rw The "lowest recommended pixel-per-em" value written to the OpenType head table. This tells applications the minimum display size at which the font is intended to be used. Typical values: 8–12 for body text fonts. fontDirectionHint int rw Writing direction hint written to the head table. 2 = strongly left-to-right (Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, etc.), -2 = strongly right-to-left (Arabic, Hebrew), 0 = mixed. Most fonts use 2 . maxZones int rw Maximum number of TrueType hinting zones used by the glyph programs. Written to maxp . maxTwilightPoints int rw Maximum number of "twilight zone" points used by the TrueType hint program. The twilight zone holds temporary reference points. Written to maxp . maxStorage int rw Maximum number of storage area locations (variables) the TrueType hint program uses. Written to maxp . maxFunctionDefs int rw Maximum number of functions defined in the TrueType hint program's FPGM table. Written to maxp . maxInstructionDefs int rw Maximum number of instruction definitions (IDEF). Written to maxp . maxStackElements int rw Maximum stack depth during TrueType hint program execution. Written to maxp .

text: A named instance is a preset — a specific location in design space that you've given a name to, like "Regular", "Bold", "Light Italic", or "SemiBold Condensed". Named instances are the styles that end users see in their font menu when they install your variable font. They're also what get exported as separate font files when you generate a family of static fonts from your variable font source. Each named instance has: - A name (the style name the user sees) - A location (where it sits on all your axes, as an flLocation dict) - Export flags (should it be included when you export?) - Style-linking values (is this the bold of another style? The italic?) - Typographic naming (how it fits into OpenType name table entries) For example, in a Weight+Width variable font, you might have instances at: - Regular: {wght: 400, wdth: 100} - Bold: {wght: 700, wdth: 100} - Condensed: {wght: 400, wdth: 75} - Bold Condensed: {wght: 700, wdth: 75}
title: What is a named instance?

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flAxis , flInstance , flLocation font = fl . CurrentFont () # ============================================================ # 1. Inspecting existing axes # ============================================================ # Start by seeing what axes are already defined in your font. # Most variable fonts have at least one — probably Weight. print ( "Design axes:" ) for axis in font . axes : print ( f " ' { axis . name } ' tag= { axis . tag } " f "min= { axis . minimal } " f "default= { axis . default } " f "max= { axis . maximum } " f "range= { axis . getRange () } " ) # ============================================================ # 2. Creating a new Weight axis # ============================================================ # Here we build a weight axis from scratch and add it to the font. # The tag "wght" is the registered OpenType tag for weight. wt_axis = flAxis () wt_axis . name = "Weight" wt_axis . tag = "wght" wt_axis . minimal = 100 # the lightest extreme (Thin) wt_axis . default = 400 # Regular — the "zero" of the normalized range wt_axis . maximum = 900 # the heaviest extreme (Black) # After setting the name, you can ask FontLab to re-derive the tag: wt_axis . updateTag () font . addAxis ( wt_axis ) print ( f "Added axis ' { wt_axis . name } ' ( { wt_axis . tag } )" ) # ============================================================ # 3. Normalizing a value # ============================================================ # The normalize() method converts a user-space value to the # normalized range: -1 at min, 0 at default, +1 at max. # This is the range that OpenType interpolation actually uses. print ( f "400 normalized: { wt_axis . normalize ( 400 ) : .2f } " ) # 0.0 (default) print ( f "700 normalized: { wt_axis . normalize ( 700 ) : .2f } " ) # ~0.6 print ( f "100 normalized: { wt_axis . normalize ( 100 ) : .2f } " ) # -1.0 (min) print ( f "900 normalized: { wt_axis . normalize ( 900 ) : .2f } " ) # 1.0 (max) # ============================================================ # 4. Checking and clamping values # ============================================================ # Is a value at the edge of the axis range? print ( "On edge (100):" , wt_axis . onEdge ( 100 )) # True print ( "On edge (400):" , wt_axis . onEdge ( 400 )) # False # Clamp an out-of-range value: clamped = wt_axis . checkValue ( 1200 ) print ( f "Clamped 1200 → { clamped } " ) # 900 # ============================================================ # 5. Inspecting existing named instances # ============================================================ # Named instances are the "presets" visible in font menus. print ( " \n Named instances:" ) for inst in font . instances : print ( f " ' { inst . name } ' " f "location= { dict ( inst . location ) } " f "exportable= { inst . exportable } " f "bold= { inst . bold } italic= { inst . italic } " ) # ============================================================ # 6. Creating named instances # ============================================================ # Add instances for Light, Regular, Semibold, and Bold. instance_specs = [ ( "Light" , 300 , False , False ), ( "Regular" , 400 , False , False ), ( "Semibold" , 600 , False , False ), ( "Bold" , 700 , True , False ), ] for inst_name , wght_val , is_bold , is_italic in instance_specs : inst = flInstance () inst . name = inst_name inst . bold = is_bold inst . italic = is_italic inst . exportable = True # Build the location (where this instance sits in design space) loc = flLocation () loc [ "wght" ] = wght_val inst . location = loc font . addInstance ( inst ) print ( f " Added instance ' { inst . name } ' at wght= { wght_val } " ) # ============================================================ # 7. Auto-generating style names from the OS/2 table # ============================================================ # FontLab can auto-compute style names and linking values for you. bold_inst = font . instances [ - 1 ] # the Bold instance we just added print ( "Auto TSN:" , bold_inst . autoTSN ()) print ( "Auto SLV:" , bold_inst . autoSLV ()) # ============================================================ # 8. Finding an instance by axis value # ============================================================ # Use instanceIndex and styleName to look up instances by value. idx = wt_axis . instanceIndex ( 700 ) name = wt_axis . styleName ( 700 ) print ( f "Nearest instance to wght=700: index= { idx } name=' { name } '" ) # And the reverse: what value does "Regular" correspond to? val = wt_axis . styleValue ( "Regular" ) print ( f "'Regular' is at wght= { val } " ) # ============================================================ # 9. Generating a human-readable location name # ============================================================ loc = flLocation () loc [ "wght" ] = 700 loc_name = flAxis . locationName ( list ( font . axes ), loc ) print ( f "Location name: ' { loc_name } '" ) # e.g. "Bold" # ============================================================ # 10. Updating axis tags and short names # ============================================================ wt_axis . updateTag () wt_axis . updateShortName () print ( f "Tag: { wt_axis . tag } ShortName: { wt_axis . shortName } " ) fl . Update ()

text: flItems is FontLab's application-wide event megaphone . Whenever anything happens in the application — a glyph is activated, a selection changes, a font is opened, a canvas gets focus — flItems broadcasts a signal so that all the UI panels, inspectors, and displays can react and update themselves. As a type designer writing scripts, you use flItems to tell FontLab that your script has changed something , so the displays refresh correctly. Without these calls, the screen won't update — you might edit 50 glyphs and see no change until you click somewhere. You access it as a class with static methods — no instance needed: from fontlab import flItems # Tell FontLab a glyph was updated (triggers display refresh) flItems . notifyGlyphUpdated ( package_id , glyph_id ) # Request that a specific UI dialog opens flItems . requestFontInfoDlg ()
title: fontlab.flItems

text: These two prefixes mean very different things: notify* — "I just changed something. Please update your displays." You call these after making a change. They're announcements: "glyph data changed", "the active layer changed", "preferences changed". FontLab's UI listens for these signals and refreshes whatever needs refreshing. request* — "Please do this for me." You call these to ask FontLab to perform an action — open a dialog, activate a glyph, load a font, run an operation. The difference from calling the operation directly is that request* goes through the normal UI pipeline, complete with undo recording, validation, and UI state management. A useful way to think about it: notify* is telling the application about the past ("this already happened"), while request* is asking it to do something in the future ("please do this now").
title: notify vs request — what's the difference?

text: from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flItems # ============================================================ # Understanding flItems: the "please update" and "please do" # system. Two categories of calls: # # notify* = "I changed data, please refresh displays" # request* = "please run this operation for me" # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () # ============================================================ # 1. The most important pattern: notify after editing # ============================================================ # Whenever a script edits a glyph directly (moving nodes, # changing contours, adjusting metrics), FontLab's UI # won't know until you fire a notification. glyph = font [ 'A' ] # Make a change (example: shift the first shape) layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] if layer . shapes : shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] shape . transform = QTransform () . translate ( 10 , 0 ) # NOW tell FontLab what happened: flItems . notifyGlyphUpdated ( font . id , glyph . id ) # The font window, glyph window, and all panels will refresh. # ============================================================ # 2. Batch editing — use the batch notification for speed # ============================================================ # Calling notifyGlyphUpdated inside a loop is wasteful. # Collect changed glyph IDs and notify all at once. changed_ids = set () for name in [ 'A' , 'B' , 'C' , 'D' , 'E' ]: g = font [ name ] if not g or not g . layers : continue layer = g . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : shape . transform ( QTransform () . translate ( 5 , 0 )) changed_ids . add ( g . id ) # One notification for all the changed glyphs: flItems . notifyGlyphsUpdated ( font . id , changed_ids ) print ( f "Notified { len ( changed_ids ) } glyph(s) updated." ) # ============================================================ # 3. Making edits undoable # ============================================================ # notifyChangesApplied tells the undo system to record an # undo step. Pass a label (shown in Edit > Undo) and the # object(s) that changed. Call BEFORE making the change # so the undo system captures the before-state. glyph_b = font [ 'B' ] flItems . notifyChangesApplied ( "Nudge B" , glyph_b ) # ... now make the change ... if glyph_b . layers and glyph_b . layers [ 0 ] . shapes : glyph_b . layers [ 0 ] . shapes [ 0 ] . transform ( QTransform () . translate ( 20 , 0 )) flItems . notifyGlyphUpdated ( font . id , glyph_b . id ) # The user can now Cmd+Z to undo "Nudge B". # ============================================================ # 4. Showing a progress bar for long operations # ============================================================ # For scripts that process many glyphs, show a progress bar # so the user knows the script is running. all_glyphs = list ( font . glyphs ) flItems . requestProgressShow ( True ) flItems . requestProgressRange ( len ( all_glyphs )) for i , g in enumerate ( all_glyphs ): flItems . requestProgressMessage ( f "Processing { g . name } ( { i + 1 } / { len ( all_glyphs ) } )..." ) flItems . requestProgressValue ( i + 1 ) # ... do something with g ... # Always hide the bar when done flItems . requestProgressShow ( False ) print ( "Done — progress bar hidden." ) # ============================================================ # 5. Opening dialogs via request* # ============================================================ # These go through the normal UI pipeline, triggering # the same behavior as clicking the menu item. # Open the Font Info dialog: # flItems.requestFontInfoDlg() # Activate the node editor tool: # flItems.requestActivateNodesTool() # Ask FontLab to open a glyph by its IDs: # flItems.requestGlyphActivate(font.id, font['A'].id) # ============================================================ # 6. After changing preferences, notify the system # ============================================================ # If your script changes flPreferences values, call this # so all panels and displays refresh to use the new settings. # from fontlab import flPreferences # prefs = flPreferences.instance() # prefs.snapToGuidelines = True # flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged() # ============================================================ # 7. The workspace property # ============================================================ ws = flItems . instance () . workspace print ( "Workspace from flItems:" , ws )

text: In FontLab, a layer is the container inside a glyph that holds the actual drawing for one master. If your font has a Light master and a Bold master, then every glyph has (at least) two layers — one for each master. The layer is where shapes live, where metrics are set, and where anchors and guidelines for that specific master are stored. Inherits from flObject .
title: fontlab.flLayer

text: Think of layers as the per-master "slots" inside a glyph: font └── glyph "A" ├── layer "Light" ← shapes, metrics, anchors for the Light master ├── layer "Regular" ← shapes, metrics, anchors for the Regular master └── layer "Bold" ← shapes, metrics, anchors for the Bold master
title: What is a Layer?

text: Not every layer is a master. FontLab supports several layer types, each with a different role: Layer type What it's for Master layer ( isMasterLayer = True ) The real drawing layers that correspond to design-space masters. These are the layers that participate in interpolation. Service layer ( isService = True ) Non-printing helper layers — for example a layer storing reference artwork or construction guides. They show up in the editor but don't export. Mask layer ( isMaskLayer = True ) A special overlay layer for each master used during manual hinting and for storing reference outlines. Accessible via getMaskLayer() . Image layer ( isImgLayer = True ) A dedicated layer for raster image data attached to a glyph — typically a scan or reference image to draw on top of. Body layer ( isBodyLayer = True ) The primary drawing layer for a glyph in simple (non-variable) fonts. Auto layer ( autoLayer = True ) A layer whose content is generated automatically, usually by an interpolation recipe. You can read its content but manual edits may be overwritten.
title: Layer Types

text: A layer is not just outlines. It holds everything that can vary between masters: Shapes — the contours and composite references that define the glyph drawing Metrics — the advance width, left sidebearing (LSB), and right sidebearing (RSB) Anchors — named attachment points used for mark positioning and component composition Guidelines — per-glyph guidelines (as opposed to font-wide guidelines) Stems and zones — PS hint stems and alignment zones for this master TrueType hinting — the TTH command program for this master A note — freeform text you can attach to this layer for editorial comments
title: What Lives on a Layer

text: This script shows a real workflow: finding every glyph named "A" in the font, iterating over all its master layers, and setting a consistent advance width on each one. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flLayer font = fl . CurrentFont () TARGET_GLYPH = "A" NEW_WIDTH = 620 # desired advance width in font units glyph = font [ TARGET_GLYPH ] if glyph is None : print ( f "Glyph ' { TARGET_GLYPH } ' not found" ) else : for layer in glyph . layers : # Only touch master layers — skip mask, service, and image layers if not layer . isMasterLayer : continue old_width = layer . advanceWidth layer . advanceWidth = NEW_WIDTH print ( f " [ { layer . name } ] " f "width { old_width : .0f } → { NEW_WIDTH } " ) glyph . changed () fl . Update () print ( "Done." ) Extending the same pattern to all glyphs in the font: import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () # Set all capital letters to a consistent side-bearing on the Regular master REGULAR_MASTER = "Regular" TARGET_LSB = 70 for glyph in font . glyphs : if not glyph . name [ 0 ] . isupper (): continue for layer in glyph . layers : if layer . name != REGULAR_MASTER : continue if not layer . isMasterLayer : continue # Clear any expression so we can set a numeric value # Set a numeric LSB via the metrics expression string layer . resetMetricsLeft () layer . metricsLeft = str ( TARGET_LSB ) glyph . changed () fl . Update () print ( f "Set LSB= { TARGET_LSB } on all uppercase glyphs in ' { REGULAR_MASTER } '." )
title: Tutorial: Set Width of All "A" Glyphs Across All Masters

text: Iterate only master layers for layer in glyph . layers : if layer . isMasterLayer : print ( f " { layer . name } : width= { layer . advanceWidth } " ) Read metrics in all masters font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ "n" ] print ( f " { 'Master' : <20 } { 'Width' : >8 } { 'LSB' : >8 } { 'RSB' : >8 } " ) print ( "-" * 46 ) for layer in glyph . layers : if layer . isMasterLayer : ib = layer . inkBox () lsb = ib . x () rsb = layer . advanceWidth - ( ib . x () + ib . width ()) print ( f " { layer . name : <20 } { layer . advanceWidth : >8.1f } { lsb : >8.1f } { rsb : >8.1f } " ) Set a metrics expression (link LSB to another glyph) # Link the 'n' glyph's LSB to the 'H' glyph on all master layers for layer in font [ 'n' ] . layers : if layer . isMasterLayer : layer . metricsLeft = "=H" font [ 'n' ] . changed () fl . Update () Add an anchor to all master layers from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF from fontlab import flPinPoint import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ "a" ] for layer in glyph . layers : if not layer . isMasterLayer : continue # Remove existing "top" anchor if present, then add a new one existing = layer . findAnchor ( "top" ) if existing : layer . removeAnchor ( existing ) # Position the anchor at the bounding-box top center bb = layer . inkBox () x = bb . x () + bb . width () / 2 y = bb . y () + bb . height () layer . createAnchor ( "top" , QPointF ( x , y ), 0 ) glyph . changed () fl . Update () Check interpolation compatibility across all masters font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ "g" ] layers = [ l for l in glyph . layers if l . isMasterLayer ] reference = layers [ 0 ] for layer in layers [ 1 :]: ok = reference . isCompatible ( layer , strong = True ) status = "OK" if ok else "INCOMPATIBLE" print ( f " { reference . name } ↔ { layer . name } : { status } " ) Leave an editorial note on a layer for layer in glyph . layers : if layer . name == "Bold" and layer . isMasterLayer : layer . note = "Optical correction needed on right shoulder — see ticket #42" break Count total nodes across all master layers font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ "g" ] for layer in glyph . layers : if layer . isMasterLayer : n = layer . nodesCount () print ( f " { layer . name } : { n } nodes" ) Constructors: flLayer() flLayer(flObject) flLayer(flGlyph) flLayer('title') Native bases: object Captured native MRO: flLayer, object Native new allocation evidence (not an init overload): ( args, *kwargs) Create and return a new object. title: fontlab.flLayerInfo

text: flLayerInfo is the canvas-aware wrapper around an flLayer . While an flLayer stores the model data (shapes, guidelines, metrics, nodes in font units), an flLayerInfo knows where all of that content is on screen at the current zoom level. Its primary purpose is providing the brectOnCanvas() method — the bounding rectangle in screen pixels that contains everything on the layer. You typically get an flLayerInfo from the canvas engine rather than creating one yourself. It is used in tool code when you need to know the full on-screen footprint of the active layer — for example, to draw an overlay, zoom to fit, or calculate a repaint region.
title: What is flLayerInfo?

text: flLayerInfo is most useful when you need the full on-screen bounds of a layer's content — for example, to draw a custom overlay frame or to check whether anything is visible in the current viewport. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flLayerInfo # ============================================================ # Get the canvas bounding rect of the active layer. # This is the screen rectangle that encloses all shapes. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Open a glyph window first." ) raise SystemExit gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if gi is None : print ( "No active glyph." ) raise SystemExit # Get a layer info — create one and attach the layer: layer = gi . glyph . layers [ 0 ] li = flLayerInfo . createInstance () li . layer = layer bbox_canvas = li . brectOnCanvas () print ( f "Layer canvas bounds:" ) print ( f " x: { bbox_canvas . left () : .1f } .. { bbox_canvas . right () : .1f } " ) print ( f " y: { bbox_canvas . top () : .1f } .. { bbox_canvas . bottom () : .1f } " ) print ( f " width: { bbox_canvas . width () : .1f } px height: { bbox_canvas . height () : .1f } px" ) # ============================================================ # Use the bounding rect to check if the glyph is in the # current viewport (e.g. for selective rendering). # ============================================================ viewport = canvas . rect () # viewport rectangle in canvas coords if bbox_canvas . intersects ( viewport ): print ( "Layer is visible in the current viewport." ) else : print ( "Layer is scrolled out of view." )
