text: A location is a coordinate in design space. It answers the question: "Which specific style am I looking at right now?" If your font has two axes — Weight ( wght ) and Width ( wdth ) — then every style you can imagine in that font lives somewhere in a 2D grid. The Regular lives at {wght: 400, wdth: 100} . The Bold Condensed lives at {wght: 700, wdth: 75} . The Thin Extended lives at {wght: 100, wdth: 125} . Each of those coordinates is an flLocation . Think of it as a Python dictionary where: - Keys are axis tags (strings like "wght" , "wdth" , "ital" ) - Values are numbers representing where you sit on that axis loc = flLocation ({ "wght" : 700 , "wdth" : 100 }) # This describes the Bold style in a Weight+Width variable font flLocation is used throughout FontLab's scripting API wherever you need to specify or navigate to a particular point in design space: - Named instances ( flInstance.location ) — where does the "Bold" preset live? - The current editor view ( font.currentLocation() ) — which master/location am I viewing? - Variation layer lookups — which layer corresponds to this design-space point? - Interpolation calls — evaluate the font at this location
title: What is a location?

text: flLocation supports the full Python mapping protocol. You can treat it almost exactly like a plain Python dict : loc = flLocation () loc [ "wght" ] = 400 # set a value loc [ "wdth" ] = 100 x = loc [ "wght" ] # read a value del loc [ "ital" ] # remove a key for tag in loc : # iterate over keys print ( tag , loc [ tag ]) print ( len ( loc )) # number of axes set print ( "wght" in loc ) # check for a key The main difference from a plain dict: the values are LocationValue objects, not raw floats. For simple cases (the vast majority), they behave like numbers. For advanced cases, they can be anisotropic — see the LocationValue section below.
title: How wzxhzdk:18 behaves like a dictionary

text: flLocation behaves like a Python dict keyed by axis tag ( str ): loc = flLocation ({ "Weight" : 100 , "Width" : 75 }) loc [ "Weight" ] # → LocationValue (reads as 100) loc [ "Optical" ] = ( 12 , 14 ) # anisotropic value as (x, y) tuple len ( loc ) # → number of axes set "Weight" in loc # → True
title: Mapping Protocol

text: flLocation is the everyday currency for navigating variable font design space. Here is how to create, read, and use locations in practical scenarios. import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Read the current design-space location in the active editor. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () loc = font . currentLocation () print ( "Current location:" ) for tag in loc : val = loc [ tag ] print ( f " { tag } : { val } " ) # LocationValue prints as a number # ============================================================ # Create a location dictionary and navigate to it. # ============================================================ if font . axes : # Build a location at a specific point in design space: target = fl . flLocation () for axis in font . axes : # Place each axis at the midpoint of its range: mid = ( axis . minimal + axis . maximum ) / 2.0 target [ axis . tag ] = mid print ( f " { axis . tag } : { mid : .0f } (midpoint of [ { axis . minimal } , { axis . maximum } ])" ) # Navigate to this location in the editor: font . setCurrentLocation ( target ) fl . Update () print ( "Navigated to midpoint location." ) else : print ( "This font has no axes — it's not a variable font." ) # ============================================================ # Inspect the locations of all named instances. # ============================================================ print ( " \n Named instances:" ) for inst in font . instances : loc = inst . location coords = " " . join ( f " { tag } = { loc [ tag ] } " for tag in loc ) print ( f " ' { inst . name } ': { coords } " ) # ============================================================ # Compare two locations. # ============================================================ if len ( font . instances ) >= 2 : loc_a = font . instances [ 0 ] . location loc_b = font . instances [ 1 ] . location same = all ( loc_a [ tag ] == loc_b [ tag ] for tag in loc_a if tag in loc_b ) print ( f " \n Instances at same location: { same } " )
title: Tutorial

text: import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () if font . axes : # Quick construction from a dict — values can be plain floats: loc = fl . flLocation ({ axis . tag : axis . default for axis in font . axes }) print ( "Default location:" , { tag : float ( loc [ tag ]) for tag in loc })
title: Build a location from a plain Python dict

title: fontlab.flMarkerPoint

text: Guidelines in FontLab can carry measurement markers — small tick marks that represent stem widths, zone boundaries, or sidebearing measurements. An flMarkerPoint is one such tick mark. It sits at a specific position along the guideline and carries flag bits that describe what kind of measurement it represents. Most designers interact with markers through the Snap/Measure panel rather than in scripts. But if you are writing a tool that programmatically creates or analyses measurement data attached to guidelines, flMarkerPoint gives you direct access to each marker's position and role flags.
title: What is flMarkerPoint?

text: import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Inspect all marker points on all guidelines in the current # glyph layer. Each guideline can carry zero or more markers. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'H' ] # 'H' often has stems worth measuring layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for guide in layer . guides : markers = guide . markers # list of flMarkerPoint if not markers : continue print ( f "Guideline at angle { guide . angle : .0f } °:" ) for m in markers : kind = "stem" if m . isStem else "other" sel = " [selected]" if m . isSelected else "" print ( f " position= { m . position : .0f } type= { kind } " f "key= { m . key } flags= { m . markerFlags : #010b }{ sel } " ) # ============================================================ # Create a new stem marker and attach it to the first guide. # ============================================================ if layer . guides : guide = layer . guides [ 0 ] new_marker = fl . flMarkerPoint . createInstance () new_marker . position = 80.0 # 80 units from guideline centre new_marker . isStem = True # mark it as a stem edge guide . addMarker ( new_marker ) fl . Update () print ( f " \n Added stem marker at position 80 to first guideline." )
title: Tutorial

text: import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () for glyph in font . glyphs : layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for guide in layer . guides : for m in guide . markers : if str ( m . key ) == 'HandMarker' : print ( f " { glyph . name } : hand marker at { m . position : .0f } " )
title: List all hand-placed markers across all glyphs

text: import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'H' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for i , guide in enumerate ( layer . guides ): stem_markers = [ m for m in guide . markers if m . isStem ] print ( f "Guide { i } : { len ( stem_markers ) } stem marker(s)" ) Inherited binding members: flObject. text: Think of flModel as FontLab's type registry — its internal catalogue of every kind of object that can exist in a font. Every node, contour, shape, glyph, layer, guideline, and anchor has a numeric type ID registered here. flModel lets you look those IDs up, create objects dynamically by type, and most importantly, send "something changed" signals to the rest of the application after you've made scripted edits. As a type designer writing scripts, you'll reach for flModel in two situations: After editing glyph data — call notifyGlyphChanged() so FontLab refreshes its displays (metrics, previews, the glyph window). Type checking — use ModelType IDs and typeToStr() to confirm what kind of object you're holding. The class is a singleton; you don't need an instance. All methods are called directly on the class, like flModel.notifyGlyphChanged(fg_id) .
title: fontlab.flModel

title: Common Scripting Patterns

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flModel # ============================================================ # 1. Identifying object types # ============================================================ # Every font object has a .type property — an integer code. # typeToStr() turns that code into a human-readable name. font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] node = shape . contours [ 0 ] . nodes ()[ 0 ] for obj , label in [( glyph , 'glyph' ), ( layer , 'layer' ), ( shape , 'shape' ), ( node , 'node' )]: type_id = obj . type type_name = flModel . typeToStr ( type_id ) print ( f " { label } : type= { type_id } name=' { type_name } '" ) # Using ModelType to get type IDs by name: print ( "Node type ID:" , flModel . ModelType [ "Node" ]) print ( "Shape type ID:" , flModel . ModelType [ "Shape" ]) print ( "GuideLine ID:" , flModel . ModelType [ "GuideLine" ]) # ============================================================ # 2. Creating objects dynamically # ============================================================ # You can create a new, blank object by its type ID. # This is useful for building objects programmatically. node_type_id = flModel . ModelType [ "Node" ] new_node = flModel . createObject ( node_type_id ) if new_node is not None : print ( "Created a new:" , flModel . typeToStr ( new_node . type )) # ============================================================ # 3. Class mask checks (advanced) # ============================================================ # isClassMask tells you if a type constant is a bitmask # (abstract base class) rather than a concrete type: print ( "Is 'Node' a class mask?" , flModel . isClassMask ( flModel . ModelType [ "Node" ])) # False — it's concrete print ( "Is 'Object' a class mask?" , flModel . isClassMask ( flModel . ModelType [ "Object" ])) # True — it's abstract # getClassMask: what abstract base categories does a type belong to? mask = flModel . getClassMask ( flModel . ModelType [ "Shape" ]) print ( "Shape class mask:" , bin ( mask )) # ============================================================ # 4. Notifying FontLab after scripted edits # ============================================================ # This is the most important real-world use of flModel. # After you change glyph data from a script, FontLab's UI # doesn't know about it until you send a notification. # Get the fontgate glyph ID (not Unicode, not array index): fg_id = glyph . id # Lightweight: just refresh the visual display flModel . notifyGlyphUpdate ( fg_id ) # Full update: recalculate metrics, refresh previews, etc. # Use this after actually changing node positions or outlines. flModel . notifyGlyphChanged ( fg_id ) # Batch update — efficient for multi-glyph scripts: changed_ids = { font [ 'A' ] . id , font [ 'B' ] . id , font [ 'C' ] . id } flModel . notifyGlyphsChanged ( changed_ids ) # ============================================================ # 5. Browsing ObjectParameter constants # ============================================================ print ( "ObjectParameter constants:" ) for k , v in flModel . ObjectParameter . items (): print ( f " { k } = { v } " ) All registered methods are static and take positional arguments. text: Clipboard operations.
title: fontlab.flModelProducer

text: flModelProducer handles copying and pasting font objects. It can serialise a list of shapes, contours, or glyphs into a binary blob, write that blob to the system clipboard, and later deserialise it back into live objects. All of its methods are static — you never create an instance, you just call the methods directly. The most common scripting use-case is programmatic copy/paste : capture the shapes of one glyph, then paste them into another, possibly with a transform applied.
title: What is flModelProducer?

text: from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flModelProducer # ============================================================ # SCENARIO: Copy the shapes of glyph 'A' and paste them # into glyph 'B' (moved 100 units to the right). # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () # Step 1: Get the shapes you want to copy. src_layer = font [ 'A' ] . layers [ 0 ] shapes_to_copy = list ( src_layer . shapes ) print ( f "Copying { len ( shapes_to_copy ) } shape(s) from 'A'" ) # Step 2: Serialise them into a binary blob. blob = flModelProducer . getClipboardData ( font . id , font . upm , shapes_to_copy ) print ( f "Serialised to { len ( blob ) } bytes" ) # Step 3: Deserialise the blob back into new objects. # This gives you fresh, independent copies of the shapes. copies = flModelProducer . getObjectsFromData ( blob ) if not copies : print ( "Deserialisation failed." ) raise SystemExit print ( f "Got { len ( copies ) } object(s) back" ) # Step 4: Apply a transform and add to the destination glyph. dst_layer = font [ 'B' ] . layers [ 0 ] for obj in copies : # Move 100 units right before adding: obj . transformBy ( QTransform () . translate ( 100 , 0 )) dst_layer . addShape ( obj ) fl . Update () print ( "Shapes pasted into 'B'." ) # ============================================================ # ALTERNATIVE: Put shapes on the system clipboard so the # user can paste them into another font with Cmd+V. # ============================================================ flModelProducer . copyToClipboard ( font . id , shapes_to_copy ) print ( "Shapes are now on the clipboard — use Edit → Paste to paste." )
title: Tutorial

text: # Count glyphs in a blob before deserialising: count = flModelProducer . countGlyphsInData ( blob ) print ( f "Blob contains { count } glyph(s)" ) # Paste from the clipboard into the current glyph: pasted = flModelProducer . getObjectsFromClipboard () if pasted : layer = fl . CurrentGlyph () . layers [ 0 ] for obj in pasted : layer . addShape ( obj ) fl . Update ()

CurrentGlyph () if glyph : producer = flModelProducer () layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] if layer . shapes : data = producer . shapeToString ( layer . shapes [ 0 ]) print ( data [: 300 ]) # show first 300 chars

text: Two static methods expose the existing FontLab object transport without reading or changing the system clipboard: producer = fontlab . flModelProducer data = producer . getClipboardDataJson ( 0 , 1000.0 , [ contour , layer , glyph ]) objects = producer . getObjectsFromJsonData ( data ) getClipboardDataJson(package_id, upm, objects) returns a QByteArray . getObjectsFromJsonData(data) accepts a wrapped QByteArray , Python bytes , bytearray , or str (encoded as UTF-8). It returns detached native objects, or None when the native reader fails or returns no objects. None and unsupported argument types raise TypeError ; incorrect argument counts raise IndexError . Neither method attaches the results to a document or creates a history entry. This is the existing permissive UI JSON format, not a strict typed flJson API. The reader does not validate the dataType discriminator. The writer omits images and collapses a single-item batch to the singleton wire representation. It is not a general-purpose Font Info converter or a guarantee of reference/image fidelity. Callers must inspect the returned objects and explicitly handle document attachment and change notifications. All registered methods are static and take positional arguments. text: If you've ever edited a glyph in FontLab's glyph editor, you've clicked on nodes. A node is a single point on a Bézier curve contour — it's the fundamental building block of every letter shape you draw. When you look at a capital "S" in the glyph editor, you're looking at a collection of nodes connected by curve segments, and it's those nodes that define where the path goes and how it bends. There are two fundamental kinds of nodes: on-curve nodes and off-curve nodes (also called handles or control points). On-curve nodes lie directly on the path — they're the filled squares or circles you see in the editor. Off-curve nodes (the hollow circles connected by dotted lines) sit off to the side of the curve and act like magnets, pulling the curve toward them without the path actually passing through them. In PostScript (Type 1 / OpenType CFF) fonts, every curve segment between two on-curve nodes has exactly two off-curve control points — this is the classic cubic Bézier. In TrueType fonts, each curve segment can be described with a single off-curve point between two on-curve anchors. On-curve nodes can also be smooth or corner nodes. A smooth node keeps its two neighboring handles in a straight line through it, producing a fluid, tangent-continuous transition between the incoming and outgoing curves. A corner node lets the handles point in any direction, creating a sharp angle or cusp. In FontLab, smooth nodes are shown as circles and corner nodes as squares. When you're scripting, the smooth property tells you which kind you have, and setting it to True or False instantly changes the node's behavior.
title: What Is a Node?

text: This tutorial walks through the most common node operations you'll use in scripts: accessing nodes from a glyph, reading their properties, navigating between them, creating new nodes by hand, and performing transforms. Each section builds on the previous one. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flNode # ── Step 1: Get a contour to work with ────────────────────────────────────── # We'll use the first shape on the first layer of the glyph "A". # In practice you'd pick the glyph and layer relevant to your task. font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] contour = shape . contours [ 0 ] # ── Step 2: Inspect every node in the contour ──────────────────────────────── # node.type tells you 'on' or 'off'; node.smooth tells you if it's smooth. # This is the first script most designers write when exploring an outline. for node in contour . nodes (): print ( f " ( { node . x : .1f } , { node . y : .1f } ) type= { node . type } smooth= { node . smooth } " ) # ── Step 3: Create nodes manually and build a triangle ────────────────────── # nodeType='on' means the path passes through the point. # nodeType='off' means it's a Bézier handle — the path is pulled toward it. n1 = flNode ( 0 , 0 , nodeType = 'on' ) # bottom-left corner n2 = flNode ( 200 , 0 , nodeType = 'on' ) # bottom-right corner n3 = flNode ( 100 , 300 , nodeType = 'on' ) # apex # Adding them to a new closed contour: tri = fl . flContour () tri . closed = True for n in [ n1 , n2 , n3 ]: tri . add ( n ) shape . addContour ( tri ) # ── Step 4: Navigate between nodes ────────────────────────────────────────── # nextNode() with no argument returns the very next node (on OR off curve). # nextNode('on') skips handles and jumps to the next on-curve anchor. node = contour . nodes ()[ 0 ] nxt = node . nextNode () # next node of any type prv = node . prevNode () # previous node of any type # Find the nearest off-curve handle that follows this node: next_off = node . nextNode ( nodeType = 'off' ) if next_off and not next_off . isNull : print ( f " outgoing handle: ( { next_off . x } , { next_off . y } )" ) # ── Step 5: Change node properties ─────────────────────────────────────────── # Toggle a node between corner and smooth — the handles will snap to collinear. node = contour . nodes ()[ 0 ] node . smooth = True # make this a smooth (tangent-continuous) point node . smooth = False # revert to a corner # Move a node: node . x += 10 # nudge right by 10 units node . moveBy ( 0 , - 5 ) # nudge down by 5 units (no rounding) node . moveBy ( 5 , 0 , round = True ) # move right 5 units, snap to integer # Select it so you can see the change in the editor: node . selected = True # ── Step 6: Convert curve segments to/from lines ──────────────────────────── # convertToLine() removes handles from the incoming segment, making it straight. # convertToCurve() adds handles to prepare a node for curve editing. for node in contour . nodes (): if node . isOn (): # only work on on-curve nodes if node . isCurve (): node . convertToLine () # straighten this segment fl . Update () # refresh the display # ── Step 7: Check and use node geometry queries ────────────────────────────── # isExtreme() identifies nodes at horizontal or vertical extrema. # These are the nodes that should exist for proper PostScript hinting. for node in contour . nodes (): if node . isOn () and node . isExtreme ( x = False ): # vertical extreme print ( f " Vertical extreme at ( { node . x : .1f } , { node . y : .1f } )" ) fl . Update ()
title: Tutorial

text: These ready-to-use patterns cover the tasks designers most often automate with node-level scripting.
title: Common Scripting Patterns

text: Useful for nudging the smooth transition points in a design across all glyphs, for example when adjusting x-height in a batch operation. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if node . isOn () and node . smooth : node . moveBy ( 0 , 10 ) fl . Update ()
title: Move all smooth nodes up by 10 units

text: Select the topmost, bottommost, leftmost, and rightmost nodes on every contour. FontLab highlights these after running extremes() , but this script lets you query and select them manually. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'O' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if node . isOn (): if node . isExtreme ( x = True ) or node . isExtreme ( x = False ): node . selected = True fl . Update ()
title: Select all extremum nodes (vertical and horizontal)

text: Strips all Bézier handles from a glyph, reducing every curve to a straight line. Handy for creating a simplified or geometric version of a design. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'S' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if node . isOn () and node . isCurve (): node . convertToLine () fl . Update ()
title: Convert all curve nodes to line nodes in a glyph

text: Ensures every node in the current glyph has integer coordinates — a required step before manual hinting in many workflows. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'g' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): node . round () # snaps x and y to nearest integer fl . Update ()
title: Round all node coordinates to integers

text: Sometimes imported outlines have handles that are almost collinear but the smooth flag isn't set. This script finds and fixes them. import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'n' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] fixed = 0 for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if node . isOn () and not node . smooth : if node . canBeSmooth (): node . smooth = True fixed += 1 print ( f "Fixed { fixed } near-smooth nodes" ) fl . Update ()
title: Find nodes that are nearly smooth but flagged as corners

text: Represents one node on the canvas. This is the "live" version of an flNode — it knows where the node is on screen and can move it in glyph-space coordinates. This is what you receive when the user selects nodes in a scripted tool.
title: fontlab.flNodeInfo

text: In any tool that moves selected nodes. canvas.selectedNodes() returns a list of flNodeInfo objects, and you move those nodes by calling setGlyphPoint() on each one.
title: When do you use it?

text: flNodeInfo is the primary API for moving nodes in a custom canvas tool. Here is the standard pattern: get the selected node infos, move them, then refresh. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Move all selected nodes up by 10 units. # This is the pattern used by any tool that nudges nodes. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Open a glyph window first." ) raise SystemExit gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if gi is None : print ( "No active glyph." ) raise SystemExit selected = gi . selectedNodes () # returns list of flNodeInfo if not selected : print ( "Select at least one node first." ) raise SystemExit print ( f "Moving { len ( selected ) } selected node(s) up by 10 units:" ) for ni in selected : pt = ni . getGlyphPoint ( False ) # current position (unrounded) new_pt = QPointF ( pt . x (), pt . y () + 10 ) ni . setGlyphPoint ( new_pt ) # move the node print ( f " ( { pt . x () : .0f } , { pt . y () : .0f } ) → ( { new_pt . x () : .0f } , { new_pt . y () : .0f } )" ) fl . Update () # refresh the canvas after all moves # ============================================================ # Align all selected nodes to the same x-coordinate # (the average x of the selection). # ============================================================ if selected : xs = [ ni . getGlyphPoint ( False ) . x () for ni in selected ] avg_x = sum ( xs ) / len ( xs ) for ni in selected : pt = ni . getGlyphPoint ( False ) ni . setGlyphPoint ( QPointF ( avg_x , pt . y ())) fl . Update () print ( f "Aligned { len ( selected ) } nodes to x= { avg_x : .0f } " )

text: import fontlab as fl ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if canvas else None if gi : nodes = gi . selectedNodes () valid_nodes = [ ni for ni in nodes if ni . isValid ()] print ( f " { len ( valid_nodes ) } of { len ( nodes ) } node infos are still valid." )

text: Everything you touch in FontLab — a node, a contour, a shape, a guideline, an anchor, a glyph, a layer, even the font itself — is an flObject under the hood. It is the common base class that every FontLab model object inherits from. Think of it as the "thing" that every object in the font universe is built on top of. Because everything shares this base, there are a handful of universal superpowers that every object has, no matter what it is: An identity — every object has a unique integer id and an optional name . A type tag — you can always ask .type to find out what kind of object you're holding. Arbitrary metadata — you can attach your own key-value data to any object using properties . Boolean markers — you can tag objects with flags , perfect for "mark as processed" logic in loops. Validity checks — you can always ask whether an object is still alive, or has been deleted. History access — every object participates in FontLab's undo/redo system. You will rarely create an flObject directly. Instead, you will always be working with its subclasses — flGlyph , flLayer , flShape , flNode , etc. But understanding flObject means you understand the shared foundation all of those build on.
title: What is flObject?

text: Every object in FontLab has a unique integer ID assigned when it is created. This ID is available via the .id property. IDs are stable for the lifetime of a session — if you store an object's ID at the start of a script, you can use haveObject() and createObject() to check if it still exists later, even after operations that might have shuffled things around. IDs are particularly useful when you need to track a set of objects across multiple passes of a loop — for example, collecting node IDs in one pass and then acting on them in a second pass without worrying about the list becoming stale. node_id = some_node . id # ... do work that might reorganize things ... if fl . flObject . haveObject ( node_id ): print ( "Node still exists" )
title: The ID System

text: FontLab lets you attach arbitrary key-value metadata to any object using the setProperty / getProperty family of methods. This is a lightweight way to annotate font data with information that FontLab itself doesn't track — things like the name of the designer who created a shape, a version counter, or a flag indicating that a glyph has been reviewed. Dynamic properties hold QVariant values, including strings and numbers. They may also contain internal object links or temporary editor state. Cloning and file persistence depend on the object type and property; arbitrary properties are not guaranteed to be copied or saved. Use propertyNames() and getProperty() to inspect a snapshot before an operation. glyph . setProperty ( "reviewed_by" , "Maria" ) glyph . setPropertyInt ( "revision" , 3 ) print ( glyph . getProperty ( "reviewed_by" )) # "Maria" print ( glyph . getPropertyInt ( "revision" )) # 3
title: Properties: Attaching Your Own Metadata

text: Every object has a set of bit flags — numbered boolean markers you can set, clear, and test. These are designed for use in processing loops where you want to mark objects as "done" or "needs attention" without adding external bookkeeping. Flags are just bits in an integer, so flag(1) , flag(2) , flag(4) etc. are all independent. There is no defined meaning for any particular flag number — you choose whatever convention works for your script. for node in contour . nodes (): if needs_processing ( node ): node . setFlag ( 1 ) for node in contour . nodes (): if node . flag ( 1 ): process ( node ) node . clearFlag ( 1 )
title: Flags: Quick Boolean Markers

text: import fontlab as fl # Obtain objects at various levels — all of them are flObject subclasses font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] # ── Type inspection ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # If you're ever unsure what you're holding, check .type print ( fl . flModel . typeToStr ( shape . type )) # "Shape" print ( fl . flModel . typeToStr ( layer . type )) # "Layer" print ( fl . flModel . typeToStr ( glyph . type )) # "Glyph" # ── ID system ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── print ( shape . id ) # e.g. 4823 — unique per session # Save the ID and verify the object still exists later saved_id = shape . id # ... run an operation that might delete shapes ... if fl . flObject . haveObject ( saved_id ): print ( "Shape survived the operation" ) else : print ( "Shape was removed" ) # ── Naming objects ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── shape . name = "stem_left" print ( shape . name ) # "stem_left" # ── Properties: attach your own metadata to any object ──────────────────── # Great for scripts that need to leave notes on objects between passes glyph . setProperty ( "reviewed_by" , "Maria" ) glyph . setPropertyInt ( "revision" , 3 ) glyph . setPropertyFloat ( "stem_weight" , 92.5 ) print ( glyph . getProperty ( "reviewed_by" )) # "Maria" print ( glyph . getPropertyInt ( "revision" )) # 3 print ( glyph . getPropertyFloat ( "stem_weight" )) # 92.5 # List all properties currently set on an object for key in glyph . propertyNames (): print ( f " { key } : { glyph . getProperty ( key ) } " ) # ── Flags: mark objects during processing ───────────────────────────────── # Flag bit 1 = "needs review", flag bit 2 = "processed" for contour in layer . getContours (): for node in contour . nodes (): if node . x < 0 : node . setFlag ( 1 ) # mark nodes left of origin # Second pass: act on flagged nodes for contour in layer . getContours (): for node in contour . nodes (): if node . flag ( 1 ): node . x = 0 node . clearFlag ( 1 ) # unmark after fixing # ── Clone: make an independent copy ─────────────────────────────────────── clone = shape . clone () # The clone has a new unique ID; changes to it don't affect the original clone . name = "stem_left_copy" layer . addShape ( clone ) # ── Validity checks ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # Always guard before using objects you didn't just create if shape . isValid : print ( "Safe to use" ) if shape . isPresent : print ( "Shape is still attached to its layer" ) # ── Undo history ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── if shape . hasHistoryStates : states = shape . historyStates ( True ) # committed states only cur = shape . currentHistoryState () init = shape . initialHistoryState () print ( f "History: { len ( states ) } states, current= { cur } , oldest= { init } " ) # Undo one step programmatically (if there's a previous state) if cur > init : shape . restoreHistoryState ( cur - 1 ) # ── Mark changed and refresh UI ─────────────────────────────────────────── shape . changed () fl . Update ()

text: These are native mutable object-list wrappers, used by APIs such as flShapeData.includes . They differ from a detached Python list . Their runtime names contain angle brackets, so they are not ordinary Python identifiers; if necessary, retrieve a type with getattr(fontlab, "flObjectsList<flShape>") . Constructors accept no arguments, another compatible wrapper, an flObject , or a compatible Python sequence. They include the common flObject registrations. Use the wrapper's mutation methods to edit its contents. Changing its list snapshot does not replace the native list. Referenced drawing objects remain model objects; a list snapshot does not clone them. Manage history and notifications when editing document-owned data. text: These are native mutable object-list wrappers, used by APIs such as flShapeData.includes . They differ from a detached Python list . Their runtime names contain angle brackets, so they are not ordinary Python identifiers; if necessary, retrieve a type with getattr(fontlab, "flObjectsList<flShape>") . Constructors accept no arguments, another compatible wrapper, an flObject , or a compatible Python sequence. They include the common flObject registrations. Use the wrapper's mutation methods to edit its contents. Changing its list snapshot does not replace the native list. Referenced drawing objects remain model objects; a list snapshot does not clone them. Manage history and notifications when editing document-owned data. text: flPackage is your font file. Everything that makes up a font — every glyph, every master, the design-space axes, named instances, kerning tables, OpenType feature code, stems, alignment zones, guidelines, and all the metadata that ends up in the font's name tables — lives inside one flPackage object. Inherits from flObject .
title: fontlab.flPackage

text: When you open a .vfc , .ufo , .otf , or any other supported format in FontLab, the application creates an flPackage for it. In a script, wrap the low-level current font with fl.flPackage(fl.CurrentFont()) , after checking that fl.CurrentFont() is not None .
title: What is a Package?

text: It helps to picture the font as a set of nested containers: flPackage (the whole font) └── flGlyph (one character — "A", "g", "comma", …) └── flLayer (one drawing per master — "Regular", "Bold", …) └── flShape (a group of contours, possibly a component reference) └── flContour (one closed or open path) └── flNode (one on-curve or off-curve point) Most scripting work moves through this hierarchy: you start at the font, find a glyph, pick a layer, iterate its shapes, and then walk the contours and nodes. Understanding this chain makes the API feel logical rather than arbitrary.
title: The object hierarchy

text: In a variable font the flPackage acts as the top-level container and each master is a child flPackage stored in font.variationPackages . The master packages share glyph names and structure but hold different coordinate values. When FontLab interpolates, it travels this list and blends the numbers. For a single-master font variationPackages has just one entry — the font itself.
title: Masters and variable fonts

text: Kerning in FontLab is stored per master. The kerning(master_name) method returns a dictionary of {(glyph1, glyph2): value} pairs for a specific master. When working with class kerning, the keys use group names prefixed with @MMK_L_ and @MMK_R_ .
title: Kerning

text: The OpenType feature code you write in the Features panel is stored in the featuresContainer inside the package. You can read and write feature code programmatically, which is useful for generating or validating feature files as part of a build pipeline.
title: OpenType features

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flPackage # ============================================================ # 1. Opening and inspecting a font # ============================================================ # fl.CurrentFont() gives you the flPackage for the active font. # If no font is open it returns None, so check before using it. font = fl . CurrentFont () if font is None : print ( "No font is open!" ) else : # font.info is a structured object with all UFO-compatible metadata. # It mirrors the keys in a UFO fontinfo.plist. print ( f "Family: { font . info . familyName } " ) print ( f "Style: { font . info . styleName } " ) print ( f "UPM: { font . upm } " ) print ( f "Glyphs: { font . glyphsCount } " ) print ( f "Masters: { font . masters } " ) # ============================================================ # 2. Iterating all open fonts # ============================================================ # fl.AllFonts() returns every font currently open in FontLab. # This is useful for batch operations across a whole family. for f in fl . AllFonts (): print ( f " Open font: { f . info . familyName } / { f . info . styleName } " ) # ============================================================ # 3. Accessing and iterating glyphs # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () # Direct dictionary-style access by glyph name: glyph_A = font [ 'A' ] print ( f "Found ' { glyph_A . name } ' — width: { glyph_A . advanceWidth } " ) # Find by name (returns None if not found — safer for scripting): glyph_g = font . findName ( "g" ) if glyph_g : print ( f "Lowercase g: { glyph_g . advanceWidth } units wide" ) # Find by unicode codepoint: glyph_euro = font . findUnicode ( 0x20AC ) # € if glyph_euro : print ( f "Euro glyph: ' { glyph_euro . name } '" ) # Iterate every glyph: empty_glyphs = [] for g in font . glyphs : if not g . hasBody : empty_glyphs . append ( g . name ) print ( f "Empty glyphs: { empty_glyphs } " ) # ============================================================ # 4. Navigating the hierarchy: glyph → layer → shape → node # ============================================================ # This is the most important pattern to understand. # Everything lives inside everything else. glyph = font [ 'H' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] # first master layer print ( f "Layer ' { layer . name } ' has { len ( layer . shapes ) } shapes" ) for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : print ( f " Contour: { len ( contour . nodes ) } nodes, " f " { 'closed' if contour . closed else 'open' } " ) for node in contour . nodes : print ( f " ( { node . x : .0f } , { node . y : .0f } ) type= { node . type } " ) # ============================================================ # 5. Working with font-level guidelines # ============================================================ from fontlab import flGuideLine # Add a horizontal guideline at y=700 (e.g. for cap height): gl = flGuideLine ( 0.0 , QPointF ( 0 , 700 )) font . addGuideline ( gl ) # List all font-level guidelines: for guide in font . guidelines : print ( f "Guide at angle= { guide . angle } pos= { guide . centerPoint } " ) # ============================================================ # 6. Masters in a variable font # ============================================================ print ( f "Masters: { font . masters } " ) print ( f "Active master: { font . master } " ) # Switch to a different master: if len ( font . masters ) > 1 : font . setMaster ( font . masters [ 1 ], notify = True ) # Read the design-space location of the active master: loc = font . location () print ( f "Current location: { loc } " ) # ============================================================ # 7. Editing font metadata # ============================================================ info = font . info print ( f "Designer: { info . openTypeNameDesigner } " ) # Write metadata — these end up in the font's name tables: info . copyright = "Copyright 2026 My Foundry" info . openTypeOS2WeightClass = 400 # Regular weight info . openTypeNameDesigner = "Jane Smith" # Font-level metrics (affects line spacing and hinting zones): font . xHeight_value = 500 font . capsHeight_value = 700 font . ascender_value = 800 font . descender_value = - 200 # ============================================================ # 8. Kerning # ============================================================ master_name = font . masters [ 0 ] pairs = font . kerning ( master_name ) # Print the first 5 kern pairs: for ( g1 , g2 ), val in list ( pairs . items ())[: 5 ]: print ( f " { g1 } / { g2 } = { val } " ) # ============================================================ # 9. Saving # ============================================================ # Save to the same location the font was opened from: # font.save() # Save to a new path: # font.saveAs("/path/to/MyFont_v2.vfc")
title: Tutorial

text: Metrics view background layer.
title: fontlab.flPaper

text: The "paper" is the background layer of the metrics view canvas. It is the model object that manages the ordered list of all flGlyphInfo objects currently being rendered — the glyphs that are shown in the text string of the metrics/spacing view. It also tracks which glyph is the "active" one (the one whose outline nodes are currently visible and editable). In typical scripting you access the paper through the canvas rather than creating one directly. The paper is your gateway to understanding what is being displayed: which glyphs are on screen, which is selected for editing, and what the combined bounding rectangle of all displayed content is.
title: What is flPaper?

text: flPaper is the object you use to ask "what is on screen right now, and which glyph is active?" in the metrics view. import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Access the paper of the current metrics/glyph window canvas # and inspect what is displayed. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Open a glyph or metrics window first." ) raise SystemExit paper = canvas . paper if paper is None or not paper . hasContent (): print ( "Paper has no content — type something in the metrics view." ) raise SystemExit print ( f "Paper has content: { paper . hasContent () } " ) print ( f "Active glyph open: { paper . hasActive () } " ) # Get the bounding box of all displayed glyphs in canvas units: bounds = paper . glyphsBoundRect () print ( f "All-glyphs canvas bounds: " f "( { bounds . left () : .0f } , { bounds . top () : .0f } ) → " f "( { bounds . right () : .0f } , { bounds . bottom () : .0f } )" ) # Get the active glyph info: if paper . hasActive (): gi = paper . activeGlyphInfo () print ( f "Active glyph: ' { gi . name } '" ) # ============================================================ # Iterate all glyphs currently displayed on the paper. # ============================================================ # The paper's glyphInfoAt(i) API requires knowing the count. # Use the canvas's glyphInfos() shortcut if available, # otherwise iterate with a try-except: print ( " \n Glyphs on paper:" ) i = 0 while True : try : gi = paper . glyphInfoAt ( i ) if gi is None : break print ( f " [ { i } ] ' { gi . name } '" ) i += 1 except Exception : break # ============================================================ # Programmatically open a glyph for editing in the metrics view. # ============================================================ font = paper . package () glyph = font [ 'O' ] new_gi = paper . setActiveGlyph ( glyph ) if new_gi : print ( f " \n Opened ' { new_gi . name } ' for editing." ) fl . Update ()

text: Named anchor for mark positioning.
title: fontlab.flPinPoint

text: Anchors — represented in code as flPinPoint objects — are the small triangular markers you place on glyphs to tell FontLab how combining marks (like accents, dots, and cedillas) connect to base letters. If you've ever placed a "top" anchor on a lowercase a and a "_top" anchor on an acutecomb, you've been working with flPinPoint . The system works by pairing anchors that share the same name, one from a base letter and one from a mark: An anchor without a leading underscore (e.g. top , bottom , ogonek ) lives on the base letter . It says: "This is the spot where a combining mark can attach to me." An anchor with a leading underscore (e.g. _top , _bottom , _ogonek ) lives on the combining mark . It says: "This is my attachment point — align me here when connecting to a base." When FontLab (or the OpenType shaping engine) needs to position acutecomb on top of a , it looks for a top anchor on the a and a _top anchor on the acutecomb, then positions the mark so those two points coincide. Common anchor names you'll encounter: - top / _top — for marks that sit above a letter (acute, grave, circumflex, etc.) - bottom / _bottom — for marks below (cedilla, ogonek) - ogonek / _ogonek — for the ogonek diacritic specifically - horn / _horn — for the Vietnamese horn marks
title: What is an anchor?

text: When you enable cloud mode on an anchor, the anchor's position is no longer fixed to absolute coordinates. Instead, FontLab calculates its position dynamically from the nearest point on the glyph's outline. This is useful for anchors on glyphs whose shapes vary significantly across masters in a variable font — the cloud anchor "floats" to an optically correct position at each master rather than staying locked to coordinates that might be wrong at extreme instances.
title: Cloud mode

text: Like guidelines, anchors can have their X and Y coordinates driven by arithmetic expressions. For example, you can set expressionX = "=lsb + (rsb - lsb) / 2" to always place an anchor at the horizontal center of a glyph's advance width, no matter how wide the glyph gets.
title: Expression anchors

text: This is a common point of confusion. There are two anchor classes in FontLab: flPinPoint (Python name: flPinPoint ) — the named anchor that lives on a glyph layer and participates in mark-to-base positioning. This is the one you create, name, and inspect when building an OpenType mark feature. It's what you see as the little triangle in the glyph editor. flAnchor — a lower-level geometric link that connects a shape to a guideline or another shape within FontLab's composite/smart-corner system. You don't create these by hand; they appear on shape.anchors() as part of FontLab's internal shape-attachment mechanism. They store references to the attached objects (node, shape, guideline) and record which movement directions are constrained. Unless you're doing advanced shape scripting or building smart components, you'll rarely need to touch flAnchor directly. In short: if you're building mark-to-base or mark-to-mark positioning, work with flPinPoint . If you're exploring how shapes lock to each other in composites, you might encounter flAnchor .
title: flPinPoint vs flAnchor — what's the difference?

text:
Anchors are the most reliable way to position diacritics and combining marks. Here is the complete workflow: adding anchors to a base letter, adding anchors to a mark, and verifying the pairs. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flPinPoint # Use the native Python class name: flPinPoint = fl . flPinPoint font = fl . CurrentFont () # ============================================================ # Step 1: List existing anchors on a glyph. # ============================================================ glyph = font [ 'a' ] if glyph is None : print ( "No 'a' glyph in this font." ) raise SystemExit layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] print ( f "Anchors on ' { glyph . name } ':" ) for anchor in layer . anchors : expr = f " (formula: x= { anchor . expressionX } , y= { anchor . expressionY } )" \ if anchor . hasExpression else "" print ( f " ' { anchor . name } ': ( { anchor . point . x () : .0f } , { anchor . point . y () : .0f } ) { expr } " ) # ============================================================ # Step 2: Add a 'top' anchor to a base letter. # Place it at the top center of the glyph's bounding box. # ============================================================ bbox = layer . boundingBox () top_x = ( bbox . left () + bbox . right ()) / 2 top_y = bbox . top () existing_names = { a . name for a in layer . anchors } if 'top' not in existing_names : top_anchor = flPinPoint ( top_x , top_y ) top_anchor . name = "top" layer . addAnchor ( top_anchor ) print ( f " 
 Added 'top' anchor at ( { top_x : .0f } , { top_y : .0f } )" ) fl . Update () else : print ( " 
 'top' anchor already exists — skipping." ) # ============================================================ # Step 3: Add the corresponding '_top' anchor to a mark glyph. # The mark anchor should be at its attachment point (usually # the bottom of the accent shape). # ============================================================ mark_glyph = font [ 'acutecomb' ] if mark_glyph : mark_layer = mark_glyph . layers [ 0 ] mark_bbox = mark_layer . boundingBox () attach_x = ( mark_bbox . left () + mark_bbox . right ()) / 2 attach_y = mark_bbox . bottom () # bottom of accent = attachment point mark_names = { a . name for a in mark_layer . anchors } if '_top' not in mark_names : mark_anchor = flPinPoint ( attach_x , attach_y ) mark_anchor . name = "_top" mark_layer . addAnchor ( mark_anchor ) print ( f "Added '_top' anchor to 'acutecomb' at ( { attach_x : .0f } , { attach_y : .0f } )" ) fl . Update () # ============================================================ # Step 4: Use an expression anchor for the center-top position. # This anchor always stays at the horizontal center regardless # of the glyph width. # ============================================================ center_anchor = flPinPoint ( 0 , 0 ) center_anchor . name = "top" center_anchor . expressionX = "=(lsb + rsb) / 2 + width / 2" center_anchor . expressionY = "=xHeight" print ( f " 
 Expression anchor: x=' { center_anchor . expressionX } '" f " y=' { center_anchor . expressionY } '" ) print ( f "Has expression: { center_anchor . hasExpression } " )
title: Tutorial

text: import fontlab as fl flPinPoint = fl . flPinPoint font = fl . CurrentFont () LOWERCASE = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz' for char in LOWERCASE : glyph = font [ char ] if glyph is None : continue layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] bbox = layer . boundingBox () cx = ( bbox . left () + bbox . right ()) / 2 existing = { a . name for a in layer . anchors } if 'top' not in existing : a = flPinPoint ( cx , bbox . top ()); a . name = "top" layer . addAnchor ( a ) if 'bottom' not in existing : a = flPinPoint ( cx , bbox . bottom ()); a . name = "bottom" layer . addAnchor ( a ) fl . Update () print ( f "Added top/bottom anchors to { len ( LOWERCASE ) } glyphs." )
title: Add top/bottom anchors to all lowercase letters

text: import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () base_names = set () mark_names = set () for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for anchor in layer . anchors : if anchor . name . startswith ( "_" ): mark_names . add ( anchor . name [ 1 :]) else : base_names . add ( anchor . name ) pairs = base_names & mark_names orphans = ( base_names | mark_names ) - pairs print ( f "Paired anchor names: { sorted ( pairs ) } " ) print ( f "Unpaired: { sorted ( orphans ) } " )

text: flPreferences gives scripts read and write access to almost every setting in FontLab — the same settings you'd normally change in the Preferences dialog. You can read them to understand the current working environment, or write them to temporarily change FontLab's behavior for the duration of your script. You always access preferences through the singleton: from fontlab import flPreferences prefs = flPreferences . instance () A word of caution: Changes to preferences take effect immediately and globally . If your script changes a preference, it stays changed even after the script finishes — the user's environment is affected. For settings you change temporarily, always save the original value and restore it when you're done: prefs = flPreferences . instance () # Save original old_snap = prefs . snapToGuidelines # Change for your script prefs . snapToGuidelines = False # ... do your scripted work ... # Restore original prefs . snapToGuidelines = old_snap After changing any preferences, call flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged() so all panels and displays pick up the new values.
title: fontlab.flPreferences

text: Property Type Access Meaning generalActivateFontWindowOnOpen bool read/write Activate the Font window when opening a font; off by default. generalHideWarningDialogs bool read/write Suppress optional launch/opening dialogs; off by default. See behavior below.
title: Window-opening preferences

text: generalActivateFontWindowOnOpen is a read/write boolean, off by default . When off, opening a font with saved windows returns to its saved active window. This also applies when saving glyph-window contents without panel/window layout. Older files use their saved selected tab when available, or preserve the window activated by the restoration order when no active-window information exists. Set it to True to activate the Font window instead: flPreferences . instance () . generalActivateFontWindowOnOpen = True Window restoration must be enabled to restore a saved active window.
title: Active window when reopening a font

text: generalHideWarningDialogs is a read/write boolean, off by default, corresponding to Preferences > General > Other > Hide warning dialogs : from fontlab import flPreferences prefs = flPreferences . instance () prefs . generalHideWarningDialogs = True The change takes effect immediately and is saved for subsequent launches. Set it to False to restore dialogs. It suppresses startup prompts (including crash reporting and Welcome), font-opening warnings, legacy note encoding conversion, and Important Font Note dialogs. Pending crash reports are sent automatically without dialogs; failed uploads are retained for retry. Autosaved fonts are moved to the Keep folder without reopening them. Automatic update checks are suspended while enabled; license restrictions still apply. Imports follow the configured rounding preference. Optional repairs (merging/renaming elements, renaming masters, removing linked width expressions) and encoding conversion are skipped. Required duplicate-glyph-name and cross-layer-reference repairs still run, with messages in Output. Font collections open all faces. Known damaged autosaves and Sketchboards are skipped without deletion. Opening errors are reported in Output instead of a dialog. For temporary use, save and restore the value with try / finally . MCP exposes the same setting as general.hide_warning_dialogs through get_preferences and set_preferences .
title: Suppressing launch and font-opening dialogs

title: Common Scripting Patterns

text:
from PythonQt.QtGui import QColor import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flPreferences , flItems # ============================================================ # 1. Get the preferences singleton # ============================================================ prefs = flPreferences . instance () print ( "Preferences loaded. Dark mode:" , prefs . isDark ) print ( "Data path:" , prefs . dataPath ) # ============================================================ # 2. Reading preferences # ============================================================ # These are just attribute reads — safe, no side effects. print ( " 
 --- Editor display ---" ) print ( f " Node size: { prefs . editorNodeSize } px" ) print ( f " Fill opacity: { prefs . editorFillOpacity } %" ) print ( f " Show curve handles: { prefs . editorShowCurves } " ) print ( f " Show coordinates: { prefs . editorCoordinates } " ) print ( " 
 --- Nudge distances ---" ) print ( f " Arrow key nudge: { prefs . editorNudge1 } units" ) print ( f " Shift+arrow nudge: { prefs . editorNudge10 } units" ) print ( " 
 --- Snap settings ---" ) print ( f " Snap to guidelines: { prefs . snapToGuidelines } " ) print ( f " Snap to outline: { prefs . snapToOutline } " ) print ( f " Snap distance: { prefs . editorSnapDistance } px" ) print ( " 
 --- Grid ---" ) print ( f " Grid X: { prefs . gridDistanceX } , Grid Y: { prefs . gridDistanceY } " ) print ( f " Grid opacity: { prefs . gridOpacity } " ) # ============================================================ # 3. Safely changing a preference # ============================================================ # ALWAYS save the original value so you can restore it. # Never leave preferences in a changed state when your # script finishes, unless that's the explicit goal. orig_node_size = prefs . editorNodeSize print ( f " 
 Changing node size from { orig_node_size } to 10..." ) prefs . editorNodeSize = 10 # Tell the app to refresh all displays with the new value flItems . notifyPreferencesChanged () # ... do some work where larger nodes are helpful ... # Restore prefs . editorNodeSize = orig_node_size flItems . notifyPreferencesChanged () print ( "Node size restored." ) # ============================================================ # 4. Saving and restoring a full preferences snapshot # ============================================================ # prefs.save() returns a dict of all current preference values. # prefs.load(dict) restores from that dict. # Use this to make large temporary changes safely. snapshot = prefs . save () print ( f " 
 Saved preferences snapshot ( { len ( snapshot ) } entries)." ) # Make some temporary changes for a proofing workflow: prefs . editorFillOpacity = 0 # transparent fill prefs . editorShowCurves = False # hide handles prefs . editorCoordinates = False # hide coordinate display prefs . colorWorkspace = QColor ( 240 , 240 , 240 ) # light grey background flItems . notifyPreferencesChanged () print ( "Temporary proofing preferences applied." ) print ( "(In a real script, do your proofing work here.)" ) # Restore everything from the snapshot prefs . load ( snapshot ) flItems . notifyPreferencesChanged () print ( "Preferences fully restored from snapshot." ) # ============================================================ # 5. Temporarily disabling all snapping # ============================================================ # Useful before running a layout script where snapping # would interfere with programmatic positioning. snap_props = [ 'snapToGrid' , 'snapToGuidelines' , 'snapToFontGuidelines' , 'snapToFontMetrics' , 'snapToMetrics' , 'snapToOutline' , 'snapToBounds' , 'snapToCenters' , 'snapToDistance' ] # Save originals orig_snaps = { p : getattr ( prefs , p ) for p in snap_props } # Disable all snapping for p in snap_props : setattr ( prefs , p , False ) flItems . notifyPreferencesChanged () print ( " 
 All snapping disabled." ) # ... run your positioning script here ... # Restore all snap settings for p , v in orig_snaps . items (): setattr ( prefs , p , v ) flItems . notifyPreferencesChanged () print ( "Snap settings restored." ) # ============================================================ # 6. Configuring grid spacing # ============================================================ # For a 1000-unit UPM font, a 10-unit grid is common. # setGridDistances() sets both axes at once. orig_gx = prefs . gridDistanceX orig_gy = prefs . gridDistanceY flPreferences . setGridDistances ( 10.0 , 10.0 ) flItems . notifyPreferencesChanged () print ( f " 
 Grid set to 10×10 (was { orig_gx } × { orig_gy } )." ) # Restore flPreferences . setGridDistances ( orig_gx , orig_gy ) flItems . notifyPreferencesChanged () # ============================================================ # 7. Reading the data path (where scripts and resources live) # ============================================================ print ( f " 
 FontLab data path: { prefs . dataPath } " ) print ( f "Default data path: { prefs . dataPathDefault } " ) print ( f "Auto-save path: { prefs . pathAutoSave } " ) # ============================================================ # 8. Checking dark mode # ============================================================ # Scripts that generate colours can adapt to the current theme. if prefs . isDark : bg_colour = QColor ( 30 , 30 , 30 ) fg_colour = QColor ( 220 , 220 , 220 ) print ( " 
 Dark mode: using light-on-dark colours." ) else : bg_colour = QColor ( 255 , 255 , 255 ) fg_colour = QColor ( 0 , 0 , 0 ) print ( " 
 Light mode: using dark-on-light colours." ) print ( " 
 Preferences tutorial complete." )

text: Base class for axis-aware attributes.
title: fontlab.flProperty

text: In a variable font, certain values — a node's x-coordinate, a guideline's position, a stem width — need to change smoothly as you move between masters. Instead of storing a single fixed number, these attributes store an flProperty object: a "smart slot" that knows the attribute's name and can hold an expression formula to be evaluated at any point in design space. flProperty is the root base class. It is never used directly — you will always encounter one of its concrete subclasses: flPropertyDouble (for a single number) or flPropertyPoint (for an x,y coordinate). Understanding this base class helps you write scripts that inspect or modify axis-driven values in parametric shapes and smart components.
title: What is flProperty?

text: Properties come up when you inspect the properties map on a parametric shape or guideline. This example shows how to walk through a shape's properties and read each one's attribute name. import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Inspect axis-driven properties on a parametric shape. # Parametric shapes (smart corners, engraving elements) store # their driven values in a flPropertiesProcessor. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : processor = shape . propertiesProcessor # may be None if processor is None : continue props = processor . properties # dict-like: attr_name → property if not props : continue print ( f "Shape has { len ( props ) } axis-driven property/ies:" ) for attr_name , prop in props . items (): # prop.objectAttr tells you which attribute it controls: print ( f " attr=' { prop . objectAttr } '" ) # Cast to flPropertyDouble to read the value: try : value = prop . value expr = prop . expression . expression if prop . expression else "" print ( f " value= { value : .2f } formula=' { expr } '" ) except AttributeError : print ( f " (not a scalar property)" )

text: Scalar axis-driven attribute.
title: fontlab.flPropertyDouble

text: flPropertyDouble wraps a single numeric value (like a node's x-coordinate, a corner radius, or a stem width) and pairs it with an optional formula that computes the value from axis coordinates. When the designer moves the design-space location slider, the expression is re-evaluated and the owning object's attribute updates automatically. This is the most commonly encountered property type in parametric FontLab shapes — smart corners, engraving elements, and scriptable parametric components all expose their numeric parameters as flPropertyDouble objects.
title: What is flPropertyDouble?

text: The most practical use of flPropertyDouble in scripting is reading and optionally overriding a parametric shape's numeric parameters. import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Read all scalar axis-driven values from a parametric shape. # This prints each parameter name, its current value, and the # formula (if any) that is driving it. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'A' ] # use a glyph that has smart-corner shapes layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : proc = getattr ( shape , "propertiesProcessor" , None ) if proc is None : continue print ( f "Shape properties ( { len ( proc . properties ) } ):" ) for attr , prop in proc . properties . items (): try : val = prop . value expr = prop . expression . expression if prop . expression else "" driven = "formula-driven" if expr else "fixed" print ( f " { attr : 15s } = { val : 8.2f } ( { driven } )" + ( f " formula: ' { expr } '" if expr else "" )) except AttributeError : pass # not a scalar property # ============================================================ # Override a parametric value with a fixed number. # Useful when you want to "freeze" a parameter at a specific # value regardless of where the design-space slider is. # ============================================================ for shape in layer . shapes : proc = getattr ( shape , "propertiesProcessor" , None ) if proc is None : continue for attr , prop in proc . properties . items (): if attr == "radius" : # example: freeze the corner radius prop . value = 50.0 print ( f "Set { attr } = 50.0 (fixed)" ) # Re-evaluate to apply the new value: if layer . shapes and layer . shapes [ 0 ] . propertiesProcessor : layer . shapes [ 0 ] . propertiesProcessor . process () fl . Update ()

text: 2-D point axis-driven attribute.
title: fontlab.flPropertyPoint

text: flPropertyPoint is like flPropertyDouble but for a 2-D coordinate (x and y together). Guideline positions and anchor positions can be driven by separate formula expressions for their x and y components. flPropertyPoint holds both component expressions and the current evaluated point value. The paramType property controls how the x and y values are interpreted — whether they represent an absolute coordinate, a delta from the default position, or an angle-and-distance pair. In most scripting contexts, paramType does not need to be changed.
title: What is flPropertyPoint?

text: flPropertyPoint is most commonly encountered when inspecting formula-driven guideline or anchor positions. import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Check all font-level guidelines for expression-driven # positions. Guidelines that use formulas (like "=xHeight") # have their position stored as an flPropertyPoint internally. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () print ( "Font-level guidelines:" ) for gl in font . guidelines : # flGuideLine exposes its y-expression directly: ey = gl . expressionY if hasattr ( gl , 'expressionY' ) else None if ey and hasattr ( ey , 'hasExpression' ) and ey . hasExpression (): driven = f "formula: ' { ey . expression } '" else : pos_y = gl . centerPoint . y () driven = f "fixed y= { pos_y : .0f } " print ( f " ' { gl . name or '(unnamed)' } ': { driven } " ) # ============================================================ # Read the current evaluated position of a formula guideline. # After flPropertiesProcessor.process() the .point property # holds the computed (x, y) value. # ============================================================ for shape in font [ 'A' ] . layers [ 0 ] . shapes : proc = getattr ( shape , "propertiesProcessor" , None ) if not proc : continue for attr , prop in proc . properties . items (): # Check if this is a point property (has .point attribute) if hasattr ( prop , 'point' ) and hasattr ( prop , 'expressionX' ): pt = prop . point has_expr = prop . hasExpression () print ( f " Point property ' { attr } ': ( { pt . x () : .1f } , { pt . y () : .1f } ) " f "formula-driven= { has_expr } " )

text: Base canvas info object.
title: fontlab.flSearchInfo

text: flSearchInfo is the root of the canvas info class hierarchy. Every object that describes where something is on the FontLab canvas — a shape, a contour, a node — ultimately inherits from flSearchInfo . This base class provides two things: a link back to the rendered glyph context ( glyphInfo ) and a dist value used when searching for the nearest feature to a mouse position. You will rarely create flSearchInfo objects directly. Instead you receive them (or their subclasses) as results from canvas queries like flGlyphInfo.getNearbyContours() or canvas.selectedNodes() . Understanding this base class helps you write tool code that works generically across different info types.
title: What is flSearchInfo?

text: flSearchInfo is primarily useful through its dist property, which tells you how far a query result was from the search point. This is the basis of nearest-feature tools. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Use getNearbyContours to find all contours within a radius, # then sort them by the dist property to find the closest one. # This is the pattern used by snap and knife tools. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Open a glyph window first." ) raise SystemExit gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if gi is None : print ( "No active glyph." ) raise SystemExit # Simulate a mouse position on the canvas: mouse_pos = QPointF ( 200 , 400 ) # Get all contours within 100 canvas pixels of the mouse: nearby = gi . getNearbyContours ( mouse_pos , 100.0 , "" ) if not nearby : print ( "No contours nearby." ) else : # Sort by dist (closest first): nearby_sorted = sorted ( nearby , key = lambda ci : ci . dist ) closest = nearby_sorted [ 0 ] print ( f "Closest contour dist= { closest . dist : .1f } px" ) print ( f " Canvas bounds: { closest . brectOnCanvas () } " ) # All results share the same glyphInfo: print ( f " Glyph: { closest . glyphInfo . name } " )
title: Tutorial

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () gi = ws . getActiveCanvas () . activeGlyphInfo () if ws . getActiveCanvas () else None if gi : nearby = gi . getNearbyContours ( QPointF ( 0 , 0 ), 9999 , "" ) for ci in nearby : # Every result's glyphInfo should point back to the same glyph: assert ci . glyphInfo . name == gi . glyph . name print ( f "All { len ( nearby ) } contour results belong to ' { gi . glyph . name } '" ) Constructors: flSearchInfo() flSearchInfo(flObject) flSearchInfo(flSearchInfo) flSearchInfo(QTransform) flSearchInfo(QTransform, flObject glyph_info) Native bases: object Captured native MRO: flSearchInfo, object Native new allocation evidence (not an init overload): ( args, *kwargs) Create and return a new object. text: The Element.
title: fontlab.flShape

text: In FontLab's interface, what you see as an element in the Glyph window is an flShape in Python. Every time you draw a contour, paste artwork, or use a parametric element (like a stroke or an inline), FontLab wraps that drawing in an flShape and places it on a layer. Think of flShape as the editing shell around your drawing. It carries: - The geometric transform that positions the element within the glyph - Selection and lock state - Colour/opacity for colour font work - A reference to the actual drawing data ( flShapeData )
title: What Is an flShape?

text: Understanding which type of shape you're working with will save you a lot of confusion in scripts: Simple shape — This is the most common kind. It directly holds a list of flContour objects. When you draw an "A", the stem, the crossbar, and the counter are each contours inside one or more simple shapes. isComposite is False . The current simpleShape() implementation always returns False , so use shape type and component/composite checks when selecting editable contours. Composite shape — A composite is a shape that contains other shapes as children (its "include list"). In the UI you make a composite by grouping elements together. The sub-shapes live inside and can be rearranged, ejected back out, or merged down. isComposite is True . Component shape — A component references the shape data of another glyph . When you place an accented character like "Á" and the acute accent is reused from another glyph, it arrives as a component shape. isComponent is True and shapeData.componentGlyph tells you the source glyph name. You cannot edit the contours of a component directly — you must decompose it first. Inherits from flObject .
title: The Three Kinds of Shape

text: This tutorial walks through the most common shape scripting tasks: reading shapes from a glyph, building new shapes, and working with composites. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flShape , flContour , flNode from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] # --- Reading shapes from a layer --- # Each item in layer.shapes is an flShape. Let's see what we're working with. for sh in layer . shapes : kind = "composite" if sh . isComposite else ( "component" if sh . isComponent else "simple" ) print ( f "Shape: { kind } , contours= { sh . contoursCount } , bounds= { sh . boundingBox } " ) # --- Inspecting contours of a simple shape --- # Make sure it's a simple shape before trying to iterate contours. shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] if shape . simpleShape (): for contour in shape . getContours (): nodes = contour . nodes () print ( f " Contour: { len ( nodes ) } nodes, closed= { contour . closed } " ) # --- Building a new rectangular shape and adding it to the layer --- # First create the shape object, then build contour geometry, then add to layer. new_shape = flShape () rect = flContour () rect . closed = True # Add four corner nodes for a 200×300 rectangle for x , y in [( 0 , 0 ), ( 200 , 0 ), ( 200 , 300 ), ( 0 , 300 )]: rect . add ( flNode ( x , y , nodeType = 'on' )) new_shape . addContour ( rect ) # Add the new shape to the layer so it appears in the glyph layer . addShape ( new_shape ) print ( "Added rectangular shape. Bounds:" , new_shape . boundingBox ) # --- Moving a shape by changing its transform --- # Prepare the transform cache before any geometric operation. new_shape . prepareTransformationData () tx = QTransform () . translate ( 50 , 0 ) # move 50 units to the right new_shape . applyTransform ( tx ) new_shape . resetTransformationData () print ( "After move, bounds:" , new_shape . boundingBox ) # --- Checking and clearing selection --- # Useful at the start of a script that will set a specific selection. new_shape . unselectAllNodes () # --- Working with a composite shape --- # Check if any shapes on this layer are composites and inspect their children. for sh in layer . shapes : if sh . isComposite : print ( f "Composite with { len ( sh . includesList ) } children" ) for child in sh . includesList : print ( f " child type: { child . shapeType } " ) # To break a composite apart, use ejectTo. # apply_tx=True keeps each child in its current visual position. children = sh . ejectTo ( clone = True , apply_tx = True ) print ( f "Ejected { len ( children ) } shapes from composite" ) # --- Checking for components (references to other glyphs) --- # Components cannot be edited until you decompose them. for sh in layer . shapes : if sh . isComponent : src = sh . shapeData . componentGlyph print ( f "Component references glyph: { src } " ) # Decompose to get real editable contours: sh . decomposite () print ( " Decomposed to plain contours" ) # --- Working with anchors on a shape --- # Anchors are used for diacritic attachment. Most shapes won't have them. for sh in layer . shapes : anchors = sh . getAnchors () if anchors : for anchor in anchors : print ( f "Anchor at: { anchor . anchorPoint } " ) # --- Checking interpolation compatibility for variable fonts --- # Before writing interpolation scripts, verify shape compatibility. if len ( layer . shapes ) >= 2 : s1 , s2 = layer . shapes [ 0 ], layer . shapes [ 1 ] compat = s1 . isCompatible ( s2 , strong = True ) print ( "Shapes are compatible for interpolation:" , compat ) # Always call Update() after making changes so FontLab redraws the glyph. fl . Update ()
title: Tutorial
