text: penParameters is a readable/writable dictionary using the stroke keys stored in VFJ/VFC: thickness (or the input alias width ), join ( miter , bevel , round ), and miter_limit agree with the element's QPen . proportion and contrast use percentages; rotation uses degrees. proportion is the share of thickness on the left of the path direction: 0 is entirely on the right, 50 is centered, and 100 is entirely on the left. Reversing the path with the same proportion swaps the geometric side. cap0 and cap1 select the start/end cap. cap_offset0/1 , cap_shaping0/1 , and cap_curvature0/1 use percentages; cap_rotation0/1 uses degrees. remove_overlap is a boolean. tolerance specifies stroke approximation tolerance. Assigning a dictionary replaces the extended parameters; omitted extended values return to their defaults. Omitted width, join, miter, and cap type are initialized from the current QPen. The getter includes those values explicitly, so its result can be copied to another element. Positive thickness enables a stroke; zero disables it. The setter preserves the pen's brush/color. Non-dictionaries raise TypeError ; invalid or non-finite numeric values and negative thickness raise ValueError before changing the element. Assigning shape.pen = qpen enables a live stroke when the pen style is not NoPen . Width, join, and miter limit come from QPen. Enabling a stroke or changing QPen's cap style initializes both native end caps from that style. Changes to color, width, or join that keep the same cap style preserve explicit cap0 / cap1 and their shaping parameters. Use penParameters for different start/end caps or custom cap geometry. A fresh QPen uses miter limit 2; native PenParameters and the Add Stroke dialog default to 3. Specify miter_limit explicitly for reproducible imports. Native miter joins clip the tip when it exceeds the limit times the local side width (half the thickness for a centered circular stroke). This is not an SVG/Figma miter-to-bevel conversion rule. shape . penParameters = { "thickness" : 40 , "cap0" : "round" , "cap1" : "round" , "join" : "round" , "contrast" : 75 , "rotation" : 30 , } style = shape . penParameters other . penParameters = style expanded = shape . expandStroke () # equivalent to expandStroke(False) expandStroke([outer_only]) -> bool replaces one element's stroke with filled outlines using the native stroke engine, without requiring a canvas selection. The fill uses the former pen brush; the stroke is removed. Opacity, transform, locking, and non-spacing state are preserved. It returns False without replacing the element when there is no usable stroke or no outline can be generated. outer_only=True requests the native outer-only expansion mode. This is a geometry operation, not a guarantee of interpolation-compatible results between masters. The return value is a success flag; read shape.contours after expansion for the resulting contours. shape.inkBox() measures a live stroke without expanding it, using the native preview approximation. boundingBox remains a padded estimate. Both operations modify the model. Scripts editing document elements must manage history and send the usual change notifications themselves.
title: Stroke scripting

text: shape.addSmartCorner(node, radius=20, smooth=False) adds or updates a live smart corner and returns True when applicable. Use a negative radius for an ink trap. smooth=True enables G2 smoothing of rounded corners. The node must belong to the shape's editable source and have two nonzero, non-collinear tangents. Smooth points, handles, open endpoints, foreign nodes and locked shapes return False . Invalid radii (zero, nonfinite or outside ±10000000) raise ValueError in Python. shape.addSmartCorners(radius=20, smooth=False) adds corners to every applicable node that does not already have one, and returns the number added. Repeated calls preserve existing smart corners. Components, groups and incompatible filters are skipped. Both methods create the native Smart Corners filter automatically, preserving the element's transform and paint. Existing Smart Corners filters are reused. New filters use the owning font's corner tension and ink-trap length, or defaults for detached elements. The editable contours are cloned when the filter is first installed: reacquire nodes through shape.smartCornerSource().contours afterwards. This method returns the shape itself for plain outlines and a null shape for unsupported or locked content. # Bulk addition, with automatic filter management: added = shape . addSmartCorners ( 20 ) # Update one source node into an ink trap: source = shape . smartCornerSource () shape . addSmartCorner ( source . contours [ 0 ] . nodes ()[ 0 ], - 15 ) Notify changes once at glyph level after a script's edits. A complete current-glyph sample is in examples/python/add_smart_corners.py . MCP: inspect with get_glyph_nodes , then send edit_glyph_nodes an operation such as {"op":"smart_corner","shape_index":0,"contour_index":0,"node_index":2,"radius":20,"smooth":false} . smart_corner_applicable identifies eligible nodes; smart_radius is null for ordinary nodes. The tool creates/reuses the filter and supports atomic batches, dry_run and Undo. Reads and subsequent edits use the filter's source indices. See help(type) for accurate signature. Supplemental documentation: An editing shape with a contours collection of flContour objects. getContours() also returns its contours, and contoursCount reports their count. boundingBox is a QRectF attribute. text: Parametric Element Constructor.
title: fontlab.flShapeBuilder

text: Most shapes in FontLab are plain: they hold a list of contours you drew with the pen. But FontLab also has parametric elements — shapes whose contours are generated by an algorithm rather than drawn by hand. Examples include: Stroke elements — a centreline path that FontLab expands into two parallel outlines Engraving elements — the sharp-nibbed calligraphic strokes used in engraved type Smart-corner shapes — corners replaced by algorithmic components (ink traps, rounded corners, serifs) Inline / Outline effects — automatic outlines derived from the glyph shape Each of these lives inside an flShape , but instead of just storing fixed contours, the shape has an flShapeBuilder attached to it. The builder holds the recipe — the parameters and algorithm — and regenerates the output contours whenever those parameters change.
title: What Is flShapeBuilder?

text: When you iterate layer.shapes in a glyph that uses parametric elements, some of those shapes will have a non- None shapeBuilder property (on flShape ) or builder property (on flShapeData ). You cannot edit the contours of these shapes the same way you edit plain drawn contours — they are re-generated by the builder every time. To understand or interact with a parametric element programmatically, you go through its flShapeBuilder . Builders also appear temporarily during interactive drawing: when you are in the middle of drawing a contour with the Pen tool, FontLab uses a builder internally to manage the in-progress state. Scripts rarely need to interact with this transient builder state, but it's good to know it exists.
title: When Do You Encounter flShapeBuilder in Scripts?

text: Most scripts that encounter builders just need to detect them (check if a shape has one, read its title to know the type) and then decide to skip or decompose the shape. Directly manipulating a builder's parameters from Python is an advanced operation and depends on the specific builder type. The API documented here covers the common methods available on all builder types.
title: Reading vs Modifying

text: The BuilderFeatures enum is passed as an integer to hasFeature() . Here are the commonly used values: Value Name Meaning 1 CanAddNodes The builder accepts additional nodes (e.g., you can extend the skeleton path) 2 CanClose The skeleton path can be closed into a loop 4 CanBoolean The builder supports boolean combine operations 8 CanUngroup The builder result can be ungrouped into sub-shapes 16 CanMerge The builder can merge with adjacent shapes Note: these flags may be combined (bitwise OR). Check availability with the FontLab version you are targeting.
title: Understanding Builder Feature Flags

text: This tutorial walks through detecting parametric elements in a glyph, reading builder information, working with smart nodes, and understanding when to skip builder shapes in scripts. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flShape font = fl . CurrentFont () # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 1: Detecting parametric (builder) shapes # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # When scripting any glyph, always check whether a shape has a builder # before assuming you can edit its contours directly. glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : b = shape . shapeBuilder # None for plain drawn shapes if b is None : print ( f "Plain contour shape — { shape . contoursCount } contours, editable directly" ) else : # This is a parametric element. Its contours are generated. print ( f "Parametric shape — builder type: ' { b . title } '" ) print ( f " canUngroup= { b . canUngroup } " ) print ( f " haveResult= { b . haveResult } " ) # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 2: Identifying builder types by title # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # The builder's 'title' property is the most reliable way to identify # what kind of parametric element you are looking at. for gname in font . glyphsNames [: 20 ]: # check first 20 glyphs g = font [ gname ] for lyr in g . layers : for sh in lyr . shapes : b = sh . shapeBuilder if b is not None : print ( f " { gname } / { lyr . name } : ' { b . title } ' element" ) # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 3: Checking builder capabilities before operating # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Before calling operations that depend on specific features, always # check hasFeature() to avoid errors on builder types that don't support them. shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] b = shape . shapeBuilder if b is not None : # Feature flag constants (pass as integers): CAN_ADD_NODES = 1 CAN_CLOSE = 2 CAN_BOOLEAN = 4 print ( "Can add nodes:" , b . hasFeature ( CAN_ADD_NODES )) print ( "Can close path:" , b . hasFeature ( CAN_CLOSE )) print ( "Supports boolean:" , b . hasFeature ( CAN_BOOLEAN )) # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 4: Working with smart nodes # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Smart nodes are special control points managed by the builder. # They appear as diamond or square handles in the FontLab UI and # control parameters like corner size or serif thickness. for shape in layer . shapes : b = shape . shapeBuilder if b is None : continue smart_nodes = b . getSmartNodes () if smart_nodes : print ( f "Builder ' { b . title } ' has { len ( smart_nodes ) } smart nodes:" ) for n in smart_nodes : print ( f " smart node at ( { n . x : .1f } , { n . y : .1f } )" ) else : print ( f "Builder ' { b . title } ' has no smart nodes" ) # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 5: Applying a transform to a builder shape # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Parametric shapes need the transform cache prepared before any # geometric operation, just like plain shapes. from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform for shape in layer . shapes : b = shape . shapeBuilder if b is not None : # Prepare, transform, reset — always in this order. b . prepareTransformationData () # (Apply your transform here — e.g. via shape.applyTransform()) b . resetTransformationData () # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 6: Deactivating a builder when done # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # If you have activated a builder (e.g. by calling shape.activateBuilder()), # deactivate it when you are finished to commit the result. shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] b = shape . shapeBuilder if b is not None and b . haveResult : print ( f "Builder ' { b . title } ' has a result ready." ) b . deactivate () print ( "Builder deactivated — result committed to shape." ) # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 7: Skipping builder shapes in a contour-editing script # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Most contour-editing scripts should skip parametric shapes entirely. # Editing the output contours of a builder directly will be overwritten # the next time the builder recomputes. Always skip or decompose first. for shape in layer . shapes : if shape . shapeBuilder is not None : print ( f "Skipping parametric shape: ' { shape . shapeBuilder . title } '" ) continue # Safe to edit contours here — this is a plain drawn shape. for contour in shape . getContours (): for node in contour . nodes (): pass # your per-node processing here fl . Update ()

text: Modifying builder parameters. The flShapeBuilder class provides the common interface shared by all builder types. Each specific builder type (Stroke, Engraving, SmartCorner, etc.) exposes additional properties and methods through its own subclass. To access those, you need to cast or obtain the builder in its specific type. The title property is the safest way to determine the subclass before casting. Builder activation and the UI. When you call shape.activateBuilder() , FontLab enters the parametric editing mode for that element, as if you had double-clicked it in the UI. This changes the active tool and the edit state. If you activate a builder from a script running in the background, you may see unexpected UI changes. In batch scripts, prefer reading builder data ( title , getSmartNodes , etc.) without activating. Decomposing parametric elements. If you need editable flat contours from a parametric shape, call shape.decomposite() . This bakes the current builder output into static contours and removes the builder. The operation is destructive and cannot be undone programmatically — the shape will no longer update parametrically after decomposition. text: The Shared Drawing Record.
title: fontlab.flShapeData

text: Every flShape has an flShapeData sitting behind it. While flShape is the editing shell you interact with in the layer — it carries the transform, selection state, and lock flags — flShapeData is where the actual drawing lives: the contours, the include list for composites, and the parametric builder reference. Most of the time you work with flShape directly and never think about flShapeData . But it becomes important in two situations: Components. When a glyph reuses artwork from another glyph (for example, a shared accent in an accented character), multiple flShape objects across different glyphs can point to the same flShapeData . The referenceCount property tells you how many shapes are currently sharing that data. If referenceCount > 1 , you are looking at a shared component — editing the contours inside the flShapeData directly would affect every shape that references it, which is usually not what you want. In that case, work through the flShape and let FontLab manage the copy-on-write logic. Low-level contour assembly. Sometimes you want to build up contours and structure directly at the data level — for example, when reading from an external source and constructing a shape programmatically. flShapeData lets you manage contours, includes, and ordering without going through the full shape layer machinery.
title: What Is flShapeData?

text: Imagine you have a font with 200 accented characters, all sharing the same acute accent element. That one acute lives in one flShapeData object, referenced by 200 different flShape objects (one per glyph-layer). The referenceCount would be 200. If you need to modify only one glyph's acute, you must first make a private copy of the data. FontLab normally handles this automatically when you edit through the UI, but in scripts that manipulate flShapeData directly, you are responsible for avoiding accidental shared edits.
title: Why Does referenceCount Matter?

text: This tutorial shows how to read shape data from an existing glyph, build new shape data from scratch, and work with composite and component shapes. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flShapeData , flContour , flNode font = fl . CurrentFont () # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 1: Reading shape data from a glyph # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Access the shape data via any shape in the glyph's layer. glyph = font [ 'O' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] sd = shape . shapeData # Print the type so we know what kind of shape we're dealing with. print ( "ShapeType:" , sd . shapeType ) # Contour | Composite | Image | Component print ( "Is composite:" , sd . isComposite ) print ( "Is component:" , sd . isComponent ) # The reference count tells us how many shapes share this data. # If it's greater than 1, this is shared component data. print ( "Reference count:" , sd . referenceCount ) if sd . referenceCount > 1 : print ( " WARNING: Shared data — edits here affect all references!" ) # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 2: Inspecting contours through shape data # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # You can access contours either through flShape.contours or flShapeData.contours. # The shape data path is useful when you need to work below the shape level. for contour in sd . contours : nodes = contour . nodes () print ( f " Contour: { len ( nodes ) } nodes, closed= { contour . closed } " ) # The segments property gives you a flat list of all Bézier segments # across all contours — handy for geometric analysis. for seg in sd . segments : print ( f " Segment: p0= { seg . p0 } p3= { seg . p3 } " ) # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 3: Building shape data from scratch # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Create a fresh shape data object and add contours to it manually. new_sd = flShapeData () # Build a simple square contour and add it. c = flContour () c . closed = True for x , y in [( 0 , 0 ), ( 100 , 0 ), ( 100 , 100 ), ( 0 , 100 )]: c . append ( flNode ( x , y , nodeType = 'on' )) new_sd . addContour ( c ) # After adding contours, arrange them so outer contours precede inner ones. # This is required for correct rendering in font engines. reordered = new_sd . arrangeContours () print ( "Contours reordered:" , reordered ) # Attach a note for traceability — useful in batch-generation scripts. new_sd . note = "Generated by script — square reference mark" print ( "Note:" , new_sd . note ) # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 4: Composite shapes — inspecting and reordering children # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Find a composite shape in the font (if any) and inspect its children. for gname in font . glyphsNames : g = font [ gname ] for lyr in g . layers : for sh in lyr . shapes : if sh . isComposite : sd2 = sh . shapeData children = sd2 . includesList () print ( f " \n { gname } : composite with { len ( children ) } children" ) for child in children : print ( f " child shapeType= { child . shapeType } " ) # Move the first child to the front of the rendering stack. if len ( children ) >= 2 : moved = sd2 . sendToFront ( children [ 0 ]) print ( " Sent first child to front:" , moved ) break # just show one composite for the tutorial # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 5: Component shapes — reading the source glyph # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Components reference artwork from another glyph. # Find all components in the font and print where they come from. glyph = font . get ( 'agrave' ) if glyph : for lyr in glyph . layers : for sh in lyr . shapes : if sh . isComponent : sd3 = sh . shapeData print ( f "Component: from ' { sd3 . componentGlyph } ' layer ' { sd3 . componentLayer } '" ) # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Part 6: Sorting and normalising contours # ---------------------------------------------------------------- # Sorting is useful before comparing shapes for interpolation compatibility. shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] sd = shape . shapeData sd . sortContours ( True ) # True = apply the sort for real print ( "Contours sorted." ) fl . Update ()

text: Represents one flShape as displayed on the canvas. It knows about the compositing chain (which other shapes are layered above/below it), can be moved on-screen, and can answer hit-test questions.
title: fontlab.flShapeInfo

text: Whenever you need to know where on the canvas a shape is — for example, to show a tooltip at the correct screen position, or to find which shape the mouse cursor is hovering over.
title: When do you use it?

text: flShapeInfo is the canvas proxy you use when you need to know where a shape is on screen — for drawing overlays, for hit-testing mouse clicks, or for querying the composite hierarchy. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Get all shapes on the active glyph canvas and print their # canvas bounding boxes. This is the starting point for any # tool that needs to know where shapes are on screen. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Open a glyph window first." ) raise SystemExit gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if gi is None : print ( "No active glyph." ) raise SystemExit # Collect all shape infos via the contour infos: all_contours = gi . getNearbyContours ( QPointF ( 0 , 0 ), 9999 , "" ) seen_shapes = {} for ci in all_contours : si = ci . shapeInfo key = id ( si ) if key not in seen_shapes : seen_shapes [ key ] = si print ( f "Shapes on canvas ( { len ( seen_shapes ) } ):" ) for si in seen_shapes . values (): bbox_glyph = si . boundingBox () # text: Guideline snap geometry engine.
title: fontlab.flSnapLine

text: flSnapLine is the technical base class that powers all guideline snapping in FontLab. It holds the two geometric nodes (center and vector) that define a line's position and angle, and provides the distance and offset math that the snapping system uses to "pull" nodes toward a guide as the designer drags them. You almost never interact with flSnapLine directly — flGuideLine inherits everything from it, so you get all of these methods and properties through your flGuideLine objects. Understanding flSnapLine is most useful when writing custom snap tools or reading the snap distance from a guideline programmatically.
title: What is flSnapLine?

text: The distanceTo and offsetTo methods are the practical core of flSnapLine for scripting. Here is how to use them to measure how far nodes are from a guideline. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Measure how far each node in a glyph is from a specific # horizontal guideline. This is useful for checking whether # your nodes are properly aligned to a metric line. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'H' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] # Find the cap-height guideline (if it exists): cap_guide = next ( ( g for g in font . guidelines if 'cap' in ( g . name or '' ) . lower () or g . expression == '=capHeight' ), None ) if cap_guide is None : # Fall back to any horizontal guide near y=700 cap_guide = next ( ( g for g in font . guidelines if g . isHorizontal () and abs ( g . centerPoint . y () - 700 ) < 50 ), None ) if cap_guide is None : print ( "No cap-height guideline found." ) else : print ( f "Cap-height guide at y= { cap_guide . centerPoint . y () : .0f } " ) print () for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): pt = QPointF ( node . x , node . y ) dist = cap_guide . distanceTo ( pt , 0 ) # 0 = perpendicular if abs ( dist ) < 10 : print ( f " Node ( { node . x : .0f } , { node . y : .0f } ) " f "is { dist : +.1f } units from cap-height guide" ) # ============================================================ # Get the snap offset — the vector that moves a point exactly # onto the guideline. Useful for implementing a snap-to-guide # operation in a custom tool. # ============================================================ if cap_guide : test_pt = QPointF ( 300 , 695 ) # slightly below cap height offset = cap_guide . offsetTo ( test_pt , 0 ) snapped = QPointF ( test_pt . x () + offset . x (), test_pt . y () + offset . y ()) print ( f " \n Point ( { test_pt . x () : .0f } , { test_pt . y () : .0f } ) " f "→ snapped to ( { snapped . x () : .0f } , { snapped . y () : .0f } )" )

text: A snap target.
title: fontlab.flSnapObject

text: Every node, guideline, and metric line that can "attract" the cursor during editing is a snap object. The flSnapObject class provides the interface for querying snap distances — "how far is the cursor from this feature?" — and for controlling which snap roles (node snapping, metric snapping, guideline snapping) are active on a particular element. Most designers will never use flSnapObject directly in scripts. It is relevant when writing custom editor tools that need to implement their own snapping logic.
title: What is flSnapObject?

text: flSnapObject is the low-level snap interface used when building custom snap logic. Most scripts don't need it — but if you are writing a tool that implements its own magnetic attraction to guidelines or metric lines, here is the pattern. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Use flSnapObject through flGuideLine (which inherits it) # to measure how far the cursor is from each guideline. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () # Simulate a cursor position in glyph units: cursor = QPointF ( 303 , 498 ) # slightly off the x-height if not font . guidelines : print ( "No font-level guidelines found." ) else : print ( f "Snap distances from cursor ( { cursor . x () : .0f } , { cursor . y () : .0f } ):" ) for gl in font . guidelines : if not gl . isInUse : print ( f " ' { gl . name } ': disabled" ) continue # distanceTo returns perpendicular distance: dist = gl . distanceTo ( cursor , 0 ) offset = gl . offsetTo ( cursor , 0 ) print ( f " ' { gl . name or '(unnamed)' } ' at y= { gl . centerPoint . y () : .0f } : " f "dist= { dist : +.1f } offset=( { offset . x () : .1f } , { offset . y () : .1f } )" ) # ============================================================ # Find the closest guideline to the cursor. # ============================================================ active_guides = [ g for g in font . guidelines if g . isInUse ] if active_guides : closest = min ( active_guides , key = lambda g : abs ( g . distanceTo ( cursor , 0 ))) snap_vec = closest . offsetTo ( cursor , 0 ) snapped = QPointF ( cursor . x () + snap_vec . x (), cursor . y () + snap_vec . y ()) print ( f " \n Snapping to ' { closest . name or '(unnamed)' } ':" ) print ( f " Cursor ( { cursor . x () : .0f } , { cursor . y () : .0f } ) → " f "Snapped ( { snapped . x () : .0f } , { snapped . y () : .0f } )" ) # ============================================================ # Temporarily disable snapping on a guideline. # ============================================================ for gl in font . guidelines : if gl . name == "baseline" : gl . isInUse = False print ( f " \n Disabled snapping on 'baseline'." ) gl . isInUse = True # re-enable break

text: Hinting Stem Definition.
title: fontlab.flStem

text: A stem is a measured stroke width — the core data that PostScript hinting uses to keep your letters looking consistent at small sizes on screen. When you measure the width of the vertical uprights in your 'H' and record it as a stem, the hinting engine ensures that every glyph's vertical strokes render at the same pixel width, keeping your type even and readable. Stems come in two flavours: vertical stems ( stemsV ) describe the main upright strokes (the legs of 'H', the body of 'I'), and horizontal stems ( stemsH ) describe the thin strokes and serifs. Both are flStem objects; only the list they live in differs. Each flStem has a value (the width in font units) and a name (so you can tell your stems apart). Most fonts have one vertical stem and one horizontal stem. High-contrast designs may have several of each.
title: What is flStem?

text:
Stems are the foundation of PostScript hinting. Here is how to inspect, measure, and add stems in a real font. import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flStem # ============================================================ # Read all stems defined for the current font. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () print ( f "Font: { font . fontName } " ) print ( " 
 Vertical stems (stroke widths):" ) for s in font . ps_stemsV : print ( f " ' { s . name } ': value= { s . value : .0f } fu" ) s . guaranteeName () # auto-name if empty print ( " 
 Horizontal stems (thin strokes / serifs):" ) for s in font . ps_stemsH : print ( f " ' { s . name } ': value= { s . value : .0f } fu" ) # ============================================================ # Measure the actual stroke widths in a reference glyph ('H') # to suggest stem values. # ============================================================ glyph = font [ 'H' ] if glyph : layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] # A simple approach: find the narrowest and widest distances # between extremal x-coordinates of vertical stems. xs = [] for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): xs . append ( node . x ) if len ( xs ) >= 2 : measured = min ( xs ), max ( xs ) print ( f " 
 'H' x range: { measured [ 0 ] : .0f } – { measured [ 1 ] : .0f } " ) print ( "(Measure the actual vertical strokes for the real stem value.)" ) # ============================================================ # Add a new vertical stem. # ============================================================ new_stem = flStem () new_stem . name = "MainStem" new_stem . value = 85.0 # replace with your measured value font . ps_stemsV . append ( new_stem ) print ( f " 
 Added V-stem ' { new_stem . name } ' = { new_stem . value : .0f } " ) # Remove it again (demo only): font . ps_stemsV . remove ( new_stem )

text: Canvas Annotation.
title: fontlab.flSticker

text: A sticker is a text label that you can attach to a shape in the glyph editor. It appears directly on the canvas as a coloured text box, floating next to the shape it belongs to. Stickers are a handy way to annotate specific shapes during a review or proofing process — you can leave notes like "check spacing", "needs smoother curve", or "discuss with client" directly on the glyph. In scripts, flSticker lets you add, read, move, or remove these canvas annotations programmatically. For example, you could write a script that audits all glyphs and attaches stickers to flag potential problems.
title: What is flSticker?

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flSticker # ============================================================ # Add an annotation sticker to a shape in the current glyph. # This is useful for leaving review comments directly on # the canvas, visible to anyone editing the glyph. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] if not layer . shapes : print ( "No shapes in 'A'." ) else : shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] # Create the sticker and set its text: sticker = flSticker () sticker . text = "Check the apex" # Position it near the top of the shape's bounding box: bbox = shape . boundingBox sticker . move ( QPointF ( bbox . center () . x (), bbox . top () + 20 )) # Attach to the shape: shape . addSticker ( sticker ) fl . Update () print ( f "Added sticker: ' { sticker . text } '" ) print ( f "Position: { sticker . textRect } " ) # ============================================================ # Read back all stickers on all shapes in the glyph. # Useful for a review script that collects all annotations. # ============================================================ print ( " \n All stickers in 'A':" ) for shape in layer . shapes : for s in shape . stickers : print ( f " Shape ' { shape . name } ': ' { s . text } ' at { s . textRect } " ) # ============================================================ # Remove all stickers from a shape. # Use this after a review pass to clean up annotations. # ============================================================ for shape in layer . shapes : shape . clearStickers () fl . Update () print ( "All stickers cleared." )

text: A TrueType hinting instruction.
title: fontlab.flTTHCommand

text: TrueType fonts can contain a hint program — a small sequence of instructions embedded in each glyph that tells the rasterizer how to snap outlines to the pixel grid at small display sizes. Each individual instruction in that program is one flTTHCommand . The instructions you will most commonly see are: - Align — snap a single point to a zone boundary (e.g. snap the top of 'x' to the x-height zone) - Single Link — constrain the distance between two points to match a stem width (e.g. the two edges of a stroke) - Double Link — constrain three points so that the stem width is centred on the midpoint - Delta — a manual pixel-level correction at a specific PPEM size (e.g. "at 11px, move this node 1/8 pixel to the right") Most designers using FontLab's automatic TrueType hinting will not need to create flTTHCommand objects manually — the autohinting engine handles this. But if you are auditing, exporting, or modifying TT hints programmatically, these are the objects you work with.
title: What is flTTHCommand?

text: import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () # ============================================================ # Inspect TT hinting commands on a glyph layer. # Run this after applying TT autohinting to a glyph to see # what instructions were generated. # ============================================================ glyph = font [ 'H' ] # 'H' is a good test — it has vertical stems layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] commands = layer . tthCommands () print ( f "TT hint commands on 'H': { len ( commands ) } " ) for i , cmd in enumerate ( commands ): direction = "V" if cmd . isVertical () else "H" if cmd . isDelta (): kind = "Delta" elif cmd . isFinal (): kind = "FinalDelta" else : kind = f "code= { cmd . code } " print ( f " [ { i } ] [ { direction } ] { kind } " ) print ( f " Points: { cmd . point_names } " ) print ( f " Parameters: { cmd . parameters } " ) # For link commands, show which stem they reference: stem_idx = cmd . stemIndex () if stem_idx >= 0 : stems = layer . stems if stem_idx < len ( stems ): print ( f " Stem: ' { stems [ stem_idx ] . name } ' " f "width= { stems [ stem_idx ] . value } " ) # For delta commands, decode the PPEM/value pairs: if cmd . isDelta (): params = cmd . parameters print ( f " Delta corrections: { params } " ) # ============================================================ # Find all delta commands — these are the manual corrections # a hinting engineer has added on top of the autohinting. # ============================================================ print ( " \n --- Delta commands only ---" ) deltas = [ cmd for cmd in commands if cmd . isDelta ()] print ( f "Found { len ( deltas ) } delta command(s)." ) for d in deltas : print ( f " Points: { d . point_names } Params: { d . parameters } " ) # ============================================================ # Count commands by direction across the whole font. # ============================================================ v_count = 0 h_count = 0 d_count = 0 for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for cmd in layer . tthCommands (): if cmd . isVertical (): v_count += 1 if cmd . isHorizontal (): h_count += 1 if cmd . isDelta (): d_count += 1 print ( f " \n Font-wide TT hints: " f "V= { v_count } H= { h_count } Deltas= { d_count } " )

text: Text layout and editing engine.
title: fontlab.flTextBlock

text: The flTextBlock is both a layout engine (it knows how to arrange glyphs on screen, apply features, handle line wrapping) and an interactive widget (it receives mouse clicks and key presses and updates accordingly). There are two editing modes you will encounter in scripts: - Text mode ( EditMode.Text ): the user is typing characters. Key presses insert/delete characters from the string. - Metrics mode ( EditMode.Metrics ): the user is adjusting sidebearings and kerning. Clicking a glyph selects it for metric editing. The text block maintains a cursor position (which glyph is active), a selection (which glyphs are selected), and a symbol list (the full string of characters being shown).
title: Understanding flTextBlock

title: Creating an flTextBlock

Pass the flCanvas you want the text to appear on. removedFromCanvas() Cleans up internal rendering state when the text block is detached from its canvas. Call this before destroying a text block that was previously attached. setParentTextBlock(flTextBlock) Sets a parent text block for nested text block hierarchies (used internally for composite metrics views).

If shrink is also True , it shrinks to fit content if content is smaller than the fixed height. setFrameWidth(double) Sets the maximum width for word-wrapped text. When content exceeds this width, it wraps to a new line. setFrameSize(QSizeF canvas_size) Sets both width and height for framed (word-wrapped) text layout. After calling this, text will wrap within the specified frame. setShowCursor(bool) Shows or hides the text insertion cursor (the blinking I-beam). Set to False when displaying text that isn't actively being edited. setShowNodes(bool) Shows or hides the glyph outline nodes inside the text block. Set to True when you want to display node positions in the metrics view — useful for comparing node positions across glyphs. setLayoutProcessing(bool) Enables or disables GSUB (glyph substitution) processing. When disabled, OpenType substitutions (ligatures, small caps, etc.) are not applied even if the features are listed. setKerningProcessing(bool) Enables or disables kerning. When disabled, all pairs are shown at zero kerning regardless of the font's kern data. Useful for checking un-kerned spacing. setMarksProcessing(bool) Enables or disables mark attachment (GPOS mark/mkmk features). When disabled, combining marks are displayed without positioning. drawContent(QPainter*, flCanvas, QRectF painted_nodes_screen_rect) Renders the text block's content to a QPainter . Used in custom rendering code. Pass the canvas for coordinate mapping and the screen rect of visible nodes for performance optimisation.
title: Content & Layout

text: Signature Description flGlyphInfo/Nothing getActiveGlyph() Returns the flGlyphInfo for the glyph at the current cursor position, or Nothing if the cursor is not inside any glyph. This is the "currently selected glyph" in metrics mode. flGlyphInfo/Nothing getHitGlyph(QPointF canvas_pos) Returns the flGlyphInfo for whichever glyph's bounding box (advance width rectangle) contains the given canvas point. Use this for "click to select glyph" in metrics mode. flGlyphInfo/Nothing getHitToShapeGlyph(QPointF canvas_pos) Like getHitGlyph but tests against the actual ink shapes rather than the bounding box. A click in the white space between strokes of an 'H' would return Nothing with this method, but a result with getHitGlyph . Use this for more precise click-to-select. list(flContourInfo)/Nothing getHitToShapes(QPointF canvas_pos) Returns the flContourInfo objects whose filled shapes contain the given canvas point. Useful for finding exactly which contour was clicked when a glyph has complex overlapping shapes. list(flGlyphInfo)/Nothing getIntersectsGlyphs(QRectF canvas_rect) Returns all glyph infos whose bounding boxes intersect the given canvas rectangle. Use this for rubber-band selection (drag a selection box and find all glyphs touched by it). flGlyphInfo/Nothing getNextGlyphInLine(int glyph_index) Returns the flGlyphInfo for the glyph immediately after glyph_index in the text line. Returns Nothing at the end of the line. Use for sequential navigation. flGlyphInfo/Nothing getPrevGlyphInLine(int glyph_index) Returns the flGlyphInfo for the glyph immediately before glyph_index . Returns Nothing at the start of the line. flGlyphInfo/Nothing getGlyphAt(int glyph_index) Returns the flGlyphInfo at absolute index glyph_index in the symbol list. The first glyph is index 0. Returns Nothing if out of range. flGlyphInfo/Nothing getGlyphInfo(fgSymbol, &) Returns the flGlyphInfo for a specific fgSymbol object. Useful when you already have a symbol reference (e.g. from symbolList[2] ) and want to get its canvas info. list(flGlyphInfo)/Nothing getGlyphsInLine(flGlyphInfo | int lineIndex) Returns all glyph infos in the same text line. Pass either a glyph info (to find its line-mates) or a line index directly. Returns Nothing if the line index is out of range. list(flGlyphInfo)/Nothing getAllGlyphs([int line_index = -1]) Returns every glyph info in the text block. If line_index >= 0 , returns only glyphs in that specific line. This is your "get everything" method for iterating the metrics view. list(flGlyphInfo)/Nothing getNearbyGlyphs(QPointF text_block_point, double max_dist) Returns all glyph infos within max_dist text-block units of the given point. Useful for implementing magnetic selection or automatic nearest-glyph queries. setActiveGlyph(flGlyphInfo) Programmatically moves the editing cursor to the given glyph. Use this to set focus on a specific glyph in metrics mode — for example, after a script identifies a problem glyph, jump the cursor to it. setCheckMouseHoverNode(bool) Enables or disables per-frame node hover detection during mouse movement. Disabling this improves performance when you do not need hover highlights on individual nodes. setExclusiveEditing(bool) When True , this text block captures all mouse events exclusively, preventing clicks from reaching other canvas items. Use in custom tool implementations when the text block should own all interaction.
title: Glyph Queries

text: Signature Description fgSymbolList/Nothing getSelectedCharacters() Returns the selected characters as an fgSymbolList , or Nothing if no characters are selected. This gives you the Unicode/name information for the selection, independent of canvas coordinates. list(flGlyphInfo)/Nothing getSelectedGlyphs() Returns the selected glyph infos. This is the same selection as getSelectedCharacters but as canvas info objects, with position and bounds available. list(flShape)/Nothing visibleShapes() Returns the flShape objects that are currently visible within the viewport. Useful for selective rendering or for knowing which shapes to include in a measurement. flNodeInfo/Nothing getMouseHitNode() Returns the flNodeInfo for the node currently under the mouse cursor, or Nothing . Useful in canvas overlay scripts that want to highlight or annotate the hovered node. flNodeInfo/Nothing getScvNode() Returns the current smooth-curve-vector node for G2 curvature editing mode, or Nothing if not in G2 mode.
title: Selection & Navigation

text: Signature Description setRightMetric(QPointF canvas_pos, flGlyphInfo glyph_info, bool measurement) Sets the right sidebearing of glyph_info by moving the right metric line to canvas_pos . If measurement is True , a ruler line is shown but the metric is not committed — useful for a preview. If False , the change is committed to the font. setLeftMetric(flGlyphInfo glyph_info, bool measurement) Sets the left sidebearing for glyph_info . Works the same way as setRightMetric — measurement=True for preview, False to commit.

Use this to position a custom cursor overlay exactly where the text cursor is. QRectF activeRowRect() Returns the bounding rectangle of the currently active row (the row containing the text cursor), in canvas coordinates. Use this to draw a row-highlight background. QRectF paintedNodesScreenRect() Returns the total screen rectangle that contains all rendered glyph nodes. Access the text block. # The metrics view has exactly one text block controlling # the main text display. # ============================================================ # For demonstration, we create a fresh text block: from fontlab import flTextBlock tb = flTextBlock . createInstance () tb . init ( canvas ) # Attach the current font: font = fl . CurrentFont () tb . package = font print ( "Font attached." ) # ============================================================ # 2. Check what is currently displayed. # ============================================================ print ( f "Has text: { tb . haveText () } " ) print ( f "Characters: { tb . charsCount () } " ) print ( f "Rendered glyphs: { tb . glyphsCount () } " ) # ============================================================ # 3. Iterate all rendered glyphs and print their names # and canvas positions. # ============================================================ all_glyphs = tb . getAllGlyphs () if all_glyphs : print ( f "

text: A transform is a recipe for repositioning, resizing, rotating, or slanting something. In type design you use transforms constantly: you move a shape to adjust its position, scale it up or down, rotate it to create swash variants, or skew it to fake an italic slant. Mathematically, all of these operations — move, scale, rotate, skew — can be described with a single 3×3 table of numbers called a transformation matrix . You don't need to understand the maths; what matters is knowing that: Translate = move. The transform shifts every point by a fixed amount in X and/or Y. Scale = resize. A scale of 2.0 doubles the size; 0.5 halves it. You can scale X and Y independently (e.g. make something taller without making it wider). Rotate = spin. Points are rotated around the origin by an angle. Shear/skew = slant. Points are pushed sideways in proportion to their Y position — this is what makes something look italic. Most transforms are a combination of the above. A slant plus a scale is still just one matrix.
title: What is a Transform?

text: FontLab uses Qt's QTransform type for the raw matrix arithmetic. flTransform wraps QTransform and adds a convenient scale property that reads the uniform scale factor out of the matrix automatically. flTransform is what you find on shapes ( shape.fl_transform ) and on canvas views ( canvas.viewTransform ). In practice: - Read the transform on a shape via shape.fl_transform — this is an flTransform . - Build a new matrix using QTransform methods ( .translate() , .scale() , .rotate() , .shear() ), then wrap it in flTransform to apply it. - Apply a transform to a shape using shape.transformBy(qt_transform) or glyph.applyTransform(qt_transform) .
title: flTransform vs. QTransform

text: from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform # Move 50 units to the right, 0 units vertically: move_right = QTransform () . translate ( 50 , 0 ) shape . transformBy ( move_right )
title: Moving a shape by a fixed amount

text: from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform # Scale everything by a factor of 1.1 (10% larger): scale_up = QTransform () . scale ( 1.1 , 1.1 ) glyph . applyTransform ( scale_up )
title: Scaling a glyph to a new UPM

text: from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform # Scale X by -1 to mirror left-to-right: mirror = QTransform () . scale ( - 1.0 , 1.0 ) shape . transformBy ( mirror )
title: Flipping a shape horizontally (mirror)

text: from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform # First move to the origin, then scale, then move back: t = QTransform () t = t . translate ( - centre_x , - centre_y ) # move pivot to origin t = t . scale ( 0.8 , 0.8 ) # scale down 20% t = t . translate ( centre_x , centre_y ) # move back shape . transformBy ( t )
title: Composing multiple operations into one transform

text: from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF , QRectF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flTransform from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'A' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] # ============================================================ # Creating transforms from scratch # ============================================================ # The identity transform: wrapping an empty QTransform means # "apply no change at all". Useful as a starting point. identity = flTransform () # A pure translation: move 50 units to the right. # QTransform().translate(dx, dy) builds the move matrix. move_right = flTransform ( QTransform () . translate ( 50 , 0 )) # A pure scale: double the width while leaving height unchanged. # scale(sx, sy) — values > 1 enlarge; values < 1 shrink. double_wide = flTransform ( QTransform () . scale ( 2.0 , 1.0 )) # A uniform scale: make everything 80% of its original size. shrink = flTransform ( QTransform () . scale ( 0.8 , 0.8 )) # A rotation: spin 15 degrees clockwise around the origin. # Qt uses clockwise-positive angles (in a Y-down coordinate system). rotate15 = flTransform ( QTransform () . rotate ( 15 )) # ============================================================ # Inspecting a transform # ============================================================ # Read the raw Qt matrix object: print ( "Matrix:" , move_right . transform ) # Read the uniform scale factor (useful for checking canvas zoom): print ( "Scale factor:" , shrink . scale ) # should be 0.8 # ============================================================ # Mapping points and rectangles # ============================================================ # Use map() to find where a point ends up after the transform. # This is useful for calculating where outlines will land BEFORE # you actually apply the transform. pt = QPointF ( 100 , 200 ) moved_pt = move_right . map ( pt ) print ( f "Original: ( { pt . x () } , { pt . y () } )" ) print ( f "After move +50: ( { moved_pt . x () } , { moved_pt . y () } )" ) # → (150.0, 200.0) # Map a bounding rectangle to find the new bounds: bounds = QRectF ( 0 , 0 , 300 , 700 ) new_bounds = double_wide . mapRect ( bounds ) print ( f "New width: { new_bounds . width () } " ) # → 600.0 # ============================================================ # Translating an existing transform # ============================================================ # translate() modifies the transform in place by adding a move. # Here we add a vertical shift to the existing horizontal move: move_right . translate ( QPointF ( 0 , 100 )) # also move 100 up # Now move_right will shift (+50 in X, +100 in Y) when applied. # ============================================================ # Applying transforms to shapes and glyphs # ============================================================ # Apply a QTransform directly to a shape (the standard way): shape . transformBy ( double_wide . transform ) # Apply to every shape in the glyph across all layers: glyph . applyTransform ( shrink . transform ) # ============================================================ # Composing multiple transforms # ============================================================ # You can chain Qt operations to build a single combined matrix. # Operations apply right-to-left (last call is first applied). # Here: rotate first, then move the result 200 units right. combined = QTransform () combined *= QTransform () . rotate ( 45 ) combined *= QTransform () . translate ( 200 , 0 ) shape . transformBy ( combined ) # ============================================================ # Resetting to identity (undo any transform) # ============================================================ # Applying an identity matrix undoes all previous transforms # by effectively resetting the shape to no-transform state # (only if you are replacing the transform, not composing). no_transform = QTransform () # identity matrix shape . transformBy ( no_transform ) fl . Update () Inherited binding members: flObject. text: Guideline-anchored nodes.
title: fontlab.flVectorNode

text: A vector node (called a "vector point" in the FontLab UI) is a special node that is pinned to a guideline. When the guideline moves, the node moves with it — automatically, across all glyphs that reference that guideline. This is the mechanism behind FontLab's power guidelines : you draw a guideline, attach nodes from multiple glyphs to it, and moving the guideline moves all the attached nodes at once. This makes vector nodes a powerful tool for variable font design. If you define a guideline at the x-height and attach the top of your lowercase letters to it, raising the x-height guideline automatically raises every attached node in every glyph. flAbstractVectorNode is the base class (provides the interface); flVectorNode is the concrete implementation you create and use in scripts.
title: What are vector nodes?

text: Signature Description flVectorNode createInstance() Creates a detached flVectorNode ready to be attached to a guideline. bool isVectorNode(flObject) Returns True if the given object is an flVectorNode . Use this for type checking when iterating mixed node lists.

text: Vector nodes are most useful in variable fonts where you want multiple glyphs to share a common alignment target. Here is how to check for and inspect existing vector nodes in a glyph. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flVectorNode # ============================================================ # Check whether any nodes in the active glyph are vector nodes # (i.e. attached to guidelines). # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'a' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] print ( f "Checking ' { glyph . name } ' for vector nodes:" ) found = 0 for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if flVectorNode . isVectorNode ( node ): vn = node # it IS an flVectorNode print ( f " Vector node at ( { vn . x : .0f } , { vn . y : .0f } )" f " attached to guideline: { vn . guideline } " ) found += 1 if found == 0 : print ( " No vector nodes found in this glyph." ) # ============================================================ # Create a vector node and attach it to a guideline. # ============================================================ # First, find or create a guideline to attach to: x_height_guide = next ( ( g for g in font . guidelines if g . expression == "=xHeight" ), None ) if x_height_guide : # Create a vector node at the x-height position: vn = flVectorNode . createInstance () vn . setPosition ( QPointF ( 250 , x_height_guide . centerPoint . y ())) print ( f " \n Created vector node at ( { 250 } , { x_height_guide . centerPoint . y () : .0f } )" ) print ( "Attach this node to a contour via contour.addVectorNode(vn)." ) else : print ( " \n No x-height expression guideline found." ) print ( "Create one first: guide.expression = '=xHeight'" )
title: Tutorial

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flVectorNode font = fl . CurrentFont () total = 0 for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if flVectorNode . isVectorNode ( node ): total += 1 print ( f "Total vector nodes in font: { total } " )
title: Count vector nodes across the entire font

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flVectorNode font = fl . CurrentFont () used_guides = set () for glyph in font . glyphs : for layer in glyph . layers : for shape in layer . shapes : for contour in shape . contours : for node in contour . nodes (): if flVectorNode . isVectorNode ( node ): gl = node . guideline if gl : used_guides . add ( id ( gl )) print ( f " { len ( used_guides ) } guideline(s) have attached vector nodes." )

text: Base class for all canvas objects.
title: fontlab.flVisualItem

text: Every visible, interactive object on the canvas — shapes, text blocks, stickers, and the transform frame — is an flVisualItem . This class provides the common interface: visibility, selection state, transform, paint, and coordinate mapping between glyph space and canvas space. In practice, you won't create flVisualItem objects directly. Instead you will call its methods on concrete subclasses like flShapeInfo or flTextBlock . Understanding flVisualItem helps you write tool code that works generically with any canvas object.
title: What is flVisualItem?

text:
flVisualItem is the API for controlling visibility, selection, and on-screen appearance of canvas objects. Here is how to use it through concrete canvas items. from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Access canvas items in the active glyph window. # flShapeInfo, flTextBlock, and the TransformFrame are all # flVisualItem subclasses — they share the same interface. # ============================================================ ws = fl . flWorkspace . instance () canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas is None : print ( "Open a glyph window first." ) raise SystemExit gi = canvas . activeGlyphInfo () if gi is None : print ( "No active glyph." ) raise SystemExit # Get all shape info objects (each is an flVisualItem): all_contours = gi . getNearbyContours ( QPointF ( 0 , 0 ), 9999 , "" ) shapes = { id ( ci . shapeInfo ): ci . shapeInfo for ci in all_contours } print ( f "Canvas objects ( { len ( shapes ) } ):" ) for si in shapes . values (): print ( f " selectable= { si . isSelectable () } " f "on_canvas= { si . haveCanvas () } " f "zoom= { si . itemScale () : .2f } × " f "bounds= { si . boundingRectOnCanvas () } " ) # ============================================================ # Select and deselect items. # ============================================================ for si in shapes . values (): si . select () # select all shapes fl . Update () print ( " 
 All shapes selected." ) import time ; time . sleep ( 0.5 ) for si in shapes . values (): si . unselect () # deselect all fl . Update () print ( "All shapes deselected." ) # ============================================================ # Show/hide a shape temporarily (e.g. for a "before/after" # comparison — not recommended for permanent edits). # ============================================================ shape_list = list ( shapes . values ()) if shape_list : target = shape_list [ 0 ] target . hide () fl . Update () print ( f " 
 Hid shape. Canvas = { target . haveCanvas () } " ) import time ; time . sleep ( 0.5 ) target . show () fl . Update () print ( "Showed shape." ) # ============================================================ # Use itemScale() to draw decorators at a fixed screen size. # A circle of radius 5 screen pixels regardless of zoom: # ============================================================ if shape_list : si = shape_list [ 0 ] zoom = si . itemScale () # In a real paint() override: radius = 5.0 / zoom print ( f " 
 For decorator: screen-radius 5px → glyph-radius { 5.0 / zoom : .2f } fu" )

text: flWorkspace is the FontLab application itself — represented as a Python object. It knows which fonts you have open, which glyph window is in front, what tool is active, and what zoom level you're looking at. When you want to do anything at the application level — loop over all open fonts, switch to a different window, change the active tool, or trigger an export — flWorkspace is where you start. You always get to it the same way: ws = flWorkspace . instance () That gives you the running FontLab application. There's only ever one. As a type designer writing scripts, you'll use flWorkspace for: Finding open fonts — ws.packages() gives you a list of every font currently open. Knowing which font is in focus — ws.currentPackage is the font whose window is active. Accessing the active glyph window — ws.getActiveCanvas() gives you the editor window you're looking at. Switching tools — ws.setToolEditor() , ws.setToolPen() , etc. Exporting fonts — ws.exportCurrentFont() or ws.exportFont(pkg, options) . Batch scripts — loop over ws.packages() to process every open font.

Which font is active right now? # ============================================================ active_font = ws . currentPackage if active_font : print ( f "Active font: { active_font . info . familyName } " ) else : print ( "No font is currently active." ) # ============================================================ # 2. Loop over every open font # ============================================================ all_fonts = ws . packages () print ( f " 
 { len ( all_fonts ) } font(s) open: 
 " ) for pkg in all_fonts : info = pkg . info # info.familyName and info.styleName give you the font's # family and style names as they appear in Font Info print ( f " { info . familyName } { info . styleName } " ) # ============================================================ # 3. Do something to every glyph in every open font # ============================================================ # Example: print the glyph count for each open font. for pkg in ws . packages (): glyph_count = len ( pkg . glyphs ) name = pkg . info . familyName or "(unnamed)" print ( f " { name } : { glyph_count } glyphs" ) # ============================================================ # 4. Batch edit with update suppression # ============================================================ # When making many edits across many glyphs, block screen # updates first to avoid flickering and speed things up. changed_ids = set () ws . blockUpdate ( 10000 ) # suppress updates for up to 10 seconds try : for pkg in ws . packages (): for glyph in pkg . glyphs : # Example: shift every glyph's first layer right by 10 units if not glyph . layers : continue layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : shape . transform = QTransform () . translate ( 10 , 0 ) changed_ids . add ( glyph . id ) finally : # Always unblock, even if the script errors partway through ws . unblockUpdate () # Notify FontLab about all the changes at once flModel . notifyGlyphsChanged ( changed_ids ) ws . updateActiveViewport () # ============================================================ # 5. Export every open font to a folder # ============================================================ # Note: exportCurrentFont() uses the settings from Font Info. # For custom export options, use exportFont(pkg, ExportControl). # for pkg in ws.packages(): # ws.currentPackage = pkg # make it active # ws.exportCurrentFont() # ============================================================ # 6. Access the active canvas and glyph # ============================================================ canvas = ws . getActiveCanvas () if canvas : print ( f " 
 Canvas is active: { canvas . isActiveCanvas () } " ) # The currentGlyph property tells you which glyph is in # the editor right now glyph_info = ws . currentGlyph if glyph_info : print ( f "Currently editing: { glyph_info . name } " ) else : print ( " 
 No canvas is open — open a glyph window to get the canvas." ) # ============================================================ # 7. Switching tools at the end of a script # ============================================================ # Good practice: leave the user in a sensible tool state # after your script finishes. The node editor is usually # the right choice. ws . setToolEditor () print ( "

text: registerPythonTool(name, icon, object) -> int adds a tool to the palette/menu and returns a cleanup token. icon must be a PythonQt QIcon or None . unregisterPythonTool(token) -> bool removes the registered tool and deactivates it if necessary. Run both operations on the GUI thread. The callback object can implement activate() and deactivate() with no arguments; mouse callbacks mousePressed(event, canvas) , mouseMoved(event, canvas) , mouseReleased(event, canvas) and mouseDoubleClicked(event, canvas) ; key callbacks keyPressed(event, canvas) and keyReleased(event, canvas) ; and paint(painter, canvas) . Event callbacks receive borrowed Qt QMouseEvent/QKeyEvent wrappers, not flMouseEvent . Return a truthy value to consume an event, or false/None to allow normal processing. Painter coordinates are viewport coordinates. import fontlab as fl class ExampleTool : def mousePressed ( self , event , canvas ): print ( event . pos ()) return False workspace = fl . flWorkspace . instance () tool_token = workspace . registerPythonTool ( "Example Python tool" , None , ExampleTool ()) # Retain tool_token; later, during plugin/script cleanup: workspace . unregisterPythonTool ( tool_token ) The registry keeps the callback object alive while registered. Do not retain borrowed event/painter wrappers beyond their callbacks. Keep cleanup tokens and unregister before unloading a plugin. Callback errors are printed to Python output. The registration does not itself select the tool.

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import flStem , flZone font = fl . CurrentFont () master_name = font . masters [ 0 ] # e.g. "Regular" # ============================================================ # 1. Inspect the existing stems # ============================================================ # Vertical stems are the main uprights — the stroke you see in # the leg of "H" or the body of "I". These control the weight # of the predominant strokes in your font. print ( "Vertical (PS) stems:" ) for s in font . ps_stemsV : print ( f " ' { s . name } ' = { s . value } units" ) # Horizontal stems are the thin strokes — crossbars, serifs, # or the thin parts of a high-contrast design. print ( "Horizontal (PS) stems:" ) for s in font . ps_stemsH : print ( f " ' { s . name } ' = { s . value } units" ) # ============================================================ # 2. Create new stems # ============================================================ # Measure a vertical stem from your "H" glyph and add it. # The value should be the width of the upright stroke in font # units — something like 80–100 for a regular-weight text font # at 1000 UPM. v_stem = flStem () v_stem . name = "Stem" # short, descriptive name v_stem . value = 85.0 # adjust to match your design v_stem . guaranteeName () # ensures name is unique font . ps_stemsV . append ( v_stem ) # For a high-contrast font you'd also add a horizontal stem: h_stem = flStem () h_stem . name = "HStem" h_stem . value = 40.0 h_stem . guaranteeName () font . ps_stemsH . append ( h_stem ) # ============================================================ # 3. Inspect the existing zones # ============================================================ # Top zones snap the tops of uppercase and lowercase letters # to consistent pixel rows. print ( " \n Top alignment zones:" ) for z in font . ps_zonesT : print ( f " ' { z . name } ' position= { z . position } " f "overshoot= { z . width } " ) # Bottom zones snap the bottoms of letters and descenders. print ( "Bottom alignment zones:" ) for z in font . ps_zonesB : print ( f " ' { z . name } ' position= { z . position } " f "overshoot= { z . width } " ) # ============================================================ # 4. Set up all standard alignment zones # ============================================================ # A typical Roman font needs these zones: # Bottom: baseline (0), descender # Top: x-height, cap height, ascender # --- Baseline (bottom zone, extends downward) --- baseline = flZone () baseline . name = "Baseline" baseline . position = 0 # A negative width means the zone extends BELOW position 0. # This covers the baseline overshoot of rounded letters like # "o" and "c" that dip slightly below. baseline . width = - 16 baseline . guaranteeName ( False ) # False = it's a bottom zone font . ps_zonesB . append ( baseline ) # --- Descender (bottom zone) --- desc = flZone () desc . name = "Descender" desc . position = int ( font . descender_value ) # e.g. -200 desc . width = - 16 desc . guaranteeName ( False ) font . ps_zonesB . append ( desc ) # --- X-height (top zone, extends upward) --- xh = flZone () xh . name = "XHeight" xh . position = int ( font . xHeight_value ) # e.g. 500 # A positive width means the zone extends ABOVE the position. # This covers the overshoot of rounded lowercase letters. xh . width = 16 xh . guaranteeName ( True ) # True = it's a top zone font . ps_zonesT . append ( xh ) # --- Cap height (top zone) --- cap = flZone () cap . name = "CapHeight" cap . position = int ( font . capsHeight_value ) # e.g. 700 cap . width = 20 cap . guaranteeName ( True ) font . ps_zonesT . append ( cap ) # --- Ascender (top zone) --- asc = flZone () asc . name = "Ascender" asc . position = int ( font . ascender_value ) # e.g. 800 asc . width = 20 asc . guaranteeName ( True ) font . ps_zonesT . append ( asc ) # ============================================================ # 5. Run auto-hinting with the new stems and zones in place # ============================================================ # Auto-hint every glyph in the font. # make_hints=True means actually write the hints (not just analyse). font . autohintGlyphs ( list ( font . glyphs ), True ) # ============================================================ # 6. Convert zones to guidelines for visual reference # ============================================================ # This creates font-level guidelines at each zone boundary, # which you can see while drawing. Useful to check that your # zones match your actual letterforms. font . convertZonesToGuidelines ( font . ps_zonesT , font . ps_zonesB ) fl . Update ()

title: fontlab.CurveEx.bcp1

title: fontlab.CurveEx.bcv1

title: fontlab.CurveEx.brect

text: contourIx : Any int Index of the parent contour within its shape. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.contourIx

title: fontlab.CurveEx.countPoints

text: empty () -> bool bool empty() Returns True if this segment is degenerate — all four points coincide, or the segment has not been initialised. A segment with countPoints == 1 (a line) is not considered empty. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.empty

text: extremum ( prev : Any ) -> bool bool extremum(CurveEx prev) Checks whether the shared node between this segment and prev is at a local extremum — the topmost, bottommost, leftmost, or rightmost point of the curve at that junction. Returns True if it is an extremum. Use this when auditing a glyph for missing extremum nodes. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.extremum

text: fastLength () -> float double fastLength() Computes a quick approximation of the arc length (the actual measured length along the curve). The approximation uses the chord length plus a fraction of the handle distances — it is fast and good enough for most layout purposes, but not numerically exact. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.fastLength

text: improve ( curvature : Any = ... ) -> bool bool improve([double curvature = 1.0]) Adjusts the off-curve control points to improve the visual quality of the curve, targeting the given curvature factor. A factor of 1.0 preserves the approximate arc length while making the curve more balanced. Returns True if the points were changed. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.improve

text: leftIdx : Any int Index of the left node ( p0 ) within the parent contour's node list. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.leftIdx

text: p0 : Any QPointF p0 The left (start) on-curve point of this segment. This is the node at the beginning of the segment. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.p0

text: p1 : Any QPointF p1 The right (end) on-curve point of this segment. The node at the end. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.p1

text: paramT : Any int The parametric position (0..1) of the most recently queried point on this segment. Set by hit-test operations; read to find where on the segment a query point landed. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.paramT

text: rightIdx : Any int Index of the right node ( p1 ) within the parent contour's node list. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.rightIdx

text: smooth ( prev : Any ) -> bool bool smooth(CurveEx prev) Checks whether this segment and the previous segment prev join smoothly (G1 continuity — the tangent direction is the same on both sides of the shared node). Returns True if smooth. Use this to find which nodes in an outline are already smooth before applying a smoothing script. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.smooth

text: smoothCurvature ( c1 : Any , complete : bool ) -> Any CurveEx smoothCurvature(CurveEx c1, bool complete) Returns a new CurveEx with its handles adjusted for smooth curvature continuity (G2) between this segment and c1 . If complete is True , both ends of the returned segment are adjusted; if False , only the join end is adjusted. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.smoothCurvature

text: split ( * args : Any , ** kwargs : Any ) -> Any bool split(CurveEx, CurveEx) Splits this segment at its stored paramT value into two new segments. The two result segments are written into the two CurveEx arguments passed in. Returns True on success. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.CurveEx.split

title: fontlab.CurveEx.updateBRect

text: canBeFixed : Any bool True if calling fix() will automatically resolve this issue. False for issues that require manual intervention (e.g. a very complex curve that the auto-fixer doesn't know how to improve). Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.canBeFixed

text: contour : Any flContour The contour this issue is associated with, or Nothing if the issue is at a higher level (e.g. a font-level metric problem). Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.contour

text: fix () -> Any flGlyph/Nothing fix() Attempts to automatically fix the outline problem described by this record. For example: closes an open contour, corrects a reversed path direction, or adds a missing extremum node. Returns the modified flGlyph if the fix was applied, or Nothing if the issue cannot be auto-corrected (some issues require manual designer judgement). Always call fl.Update() after fixing to refresh the canvas. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.fix

text: id : Any int The numeric code identifying which audit rule produced this finding. Stable across FontLab versions. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.id

text: location : Any QPointF The glyph-space coordinates of where the issue is located. Use this with flAuditInfo.glyphLocation() to convert to canvas coordinates for drawing an indicator. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.location

text: nodeIndex : Any int The index of the specific node involved in this issue within its contour. -1 if the issue is not associated with a particular node. Use this with contour.nodeAtIndex(nodeIndex) to retrieve the problematic node. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.nodeIndex

text: priority : Any int The severity of this issue. Higher numbers are more important. Use this to sort issues by priority when generating a report. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.priority

text: report : Any QString The full detailed description of the issue, including measurements, coordinate values, and fix recommendations. This is the text that FontLab shows in its audit panel. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.report

text: title : Any QString A brief, human-readable name for this type of issue, such as "Open contour" , "Wrong direction" , "Almost flat curve" . Use this in log output or a custom report. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.title

text: vector : Any QPointF A direction vector associated with the issue. For example, for a "node should move to extremum" issue, this vector points from the current position to the target extremum position. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr.vector

title: fontlab.FontMetrics.lineGap

title: fontlab.FontMetrics.xHeight

text: name_id : Any uint The glyph ID of the base glyph being referenced. Use with font.glyph(id) to retrieve the actual flGlyph . If you created the component with a name string, name_id will be 0 until the component is resolved. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.GlyphComponent.name_id

text: transform : Any QTransform The 2-D transform applied to the base glyph when it is drawn as part of this composite. A simple translation (e.g. QTransform().translate(0, 300) ) shifts the component 300 units up. For accented letters with use_anchors = False , the translation typically places the accent above the base letter. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.GlyphComponent.transform

text: use_anchors : Any bool If True , the component is positioned by matching its attachment anchor to the base glyph's anchor — for example, the _top anchor on the accent snaps to the top anchor on the base letter. If False , the explicit transform is used for positioning. For mark-to-base composites (accented letters), True is the standard approach and is required for the font to correctly place diacritics. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
title: fontlab.GlyphComponent.use_anchors

text: width_scale : Any double Scale factor applied to the component's advance width when compositing. 1.0 uses the base glyph's normal width. Values other than 1.0 are unusual. Source: FontLab Proteus API documentation
